Compound.name: a 3-(3-hydroxyalkanoyloxy)alkanoate
Comment: This class contains molecules that are composed of two 3-hydroxy fatty acid chains of varying length (represented here in part by R1 and R2) linked to each other through an ester bond between the beta-hydroxyl group of one chain and the carboxyl group of another chain. They have been found to be constituents of rhamnolipids (see |FRAME: Mono-Rhamnolipids| and a |FRAME: Di-Rhamnolipids|) |CITS: [11813309] [16160828] [20336292]|.

Compound.name: a gibberellin
Comment: Gibberellins (GAs) are plant hormones that regulate growth and influence various developmental processes, including stem elongation, germination, dormancy, flowering, sex expression, enzyme induction, and leaf and fruit senescence. All known gibberellins are diterpenoid acids that are synthesized by the terpenoid pathway in plastids and then modified in the endoplasmic reticulum and cytosol until they reach their biologically-active form (see |FRAME: PWY-5052|). The gibberellins are named GA1 through GAn in order of discovery. All gibberellins have either 19 or 20 carbon units grouped into either four or five ring systems (see |FRAME: CPD1F-95| and |FRAME: CPD1F-134|, respectively). The fifth ring is a lactone ring. GAs containing a tetracyclic ent -gibberellane structure (|FRAME: CPD1F-95|) are called C 20 -GAs, whereas GAs containing a pentacyclic 20-nor- ent -gibberellane structure (|FRAME: CPD1F-134|) are called C 19 -GAs. C 20 -GAs do not usually have biological activity but can be metabolized to active C 19 -GAs (note that not all C 19 -GAs are bioactive).

Compound.name: an L-arabinan
Comment: L-arabinan is a common hemicellulosic component of the cell wall of higher plants. It is a branched polysaccharide with a backbone of alpha-(1,5)-linked arabinofuranosyl residues with alpha-(1,2)- and alpha-(1,3)-linked arabinofuranosyl side chains and is involved in covalent cross-lining of cell wall polysaccharides. It is usually associated with pectic substrates, and pectins with attached arabinans can be isolated from many fruits and vegetables such as apples, sugar beet, apricots, carrots, cabbage, onion and pears.

Compound.name: a galactan
Comment: Galactans are polymers composed of repeating units of galactose residues. In many plants galactans are often found as a constituent of complex polysaccharides such as |FRAME: Arabinogalactan arabinogalactan|, often forming a component of hemicellulose. Two main classes of arabinogalactans are found in nature: |FRAME: Plant-Arabinogalactans "plant arabinogalactan"| and |FRAME: Mycobacterial-Arabinogalactans "microbial arabinogalactan"|. A completely different form of galactan polymers is found in red algae. |FRAME: Red-Alage-Galactans "Red algal galactans"| are polysaccharides having usually a linear backbone built up of alternating 3-linked beta-D-galactopyranose and 4-linked alpha-galactopyranose residues. The beta-galactose residues always belong to D-series, whereas the alpha-galactose residues are D in carrageenans and L in agars. A substantial part of the alpha-galactose residues may exist in the form of a 3,6-anhydro derivative Truus06. Red algal galactans are usually sulfated.

Compound.name: a beta-(1,4)-mannan oligosaccharide
Synonyms: a (1->4)-beta-D-mannooligosaccharide // a short beta-(1,4)-mannoglycan // a short beta-(1,4)-mannan
Comment: Mannan is a plant polysaccharide that is a polymer of the sugar mannose. This compound class represents short mannan saccharides that are produced by the action of mannanase enzymes. The structure that is shown here represnts a tetrasaccharide and is provided only as an example.

Compound.name: phosphatidylglycerol-34:3

For each of the group members, the total number of carbon atoms in the two acyl chains adds up to 34, and the total number of double bonds in the two acyl groups adds up to 3.

Compound.name: a 6,7-dihydropterin
Comment: |FRAME: Pterins Pterins| are heterocyclic compounds based on fused |FRAME: CPD-26401| and |FRAME: PYRIMIDINE-RING| rings (a |FRAME: CPD-15307| ring system) where the pyrimidine ring has an amino group in the 2-position and an oxo group in the 4-position, resulting in four double bonds within the ring system. When one of the double bonds is reduced the compounds is referred to as a dihydropterin (the most common form of which is |FRAME: CPD0-1718|). When two of the double bonds are reduced, the compound is referred to as |FRAME: Tetrahydropterins|. |FRAME: 67-Dihydropterins "6,7-dihydropterin"| is a different form of a dihydropterin. Older literature often refers to it as quinonoid dihydrobiopterin.

Compound.name: a benzopyran
Comment: Benzopyran is an polycyclic organic compound that results from the fusion of a benzene ring to a heterocyclic pyran ring.

Compound.name: a glycosphingolipid
Comment: |FRAME: Glycosphingolipids Glycosphingolipids| are a family of complex lipids composed of |FRAME: Ceramides| and mono- or oligosaccharide moieties that play an important role in various cellular functions including recognition, cell adhesion, proliferation and differentiation 8490246. The lipid portion is embedded in the outer plasma membrane leaflet and the sugar chains extended to the outer environment, acting as an antigen. Together with |FRAME: Glycoproteins glycoproteins| and |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans glycosaminoglycans|, the glycosphingolipids contribute to the glycocalyx that covers eukaryotic cell surfaces. Glycoshphingolipids have been classified into the following 12 series based on their structure: |FRAME: Arthro-Series-GSLs arthro|, |FRAME: Gala-Series-GSLs gala|, |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs ganglio|, |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs globo|, |FRAME: Isoglobo-Series-GSLs isoglobo|, |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs lacto|, |FRAME: Muco-Series-GSLs muco|, |FRAME: Mollu-Series-GSLs mollu|, |FRAME: Neogala-Series-GSLs neogala|, |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs neolacto|, |FRAME: Schisto-Series-GSLs schisto| and |FRAME: Spirometo-Series-GSLs spirometo| 25969757. Glycosphingolipids are synthesized by the sequential addition of sugar residues to ceramide by glycosyltransferases that are specific to each glycosidic linkage. |FRAME: Lactosyl-Ceramides Lactosylceramide|, a product of the second glycosylation step in the biosynthesis of many glycosphingolipids, is an important branching point, being a common precursor for the synthesis of the four major classes of glycosphingolipids: the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|, the |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs "globo series"|, the |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs "lacto series"|, and the |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs "neolacto series"| 10320813. In the diagram below, R1 describes the variable part of the sphingoid base, R2 describes the fatty acid, and R3 describes the glycan moiety.

Compound.name: a (1->3)-beta-D-xylan
Comment: |FRAME: 13-BETA-D-XYLANS "beta-1,3-D-xylan"| is a polysaccharide composed of beta-1,3-linked |FRAME: BETA-D-XYLOSE| residues. This polysaccharide was first found in the siphonous green seaweed |FRAME: TAX-148944| as a water-insoluble and alkaline-soluble component of cell walls Mackie59. It was subsequently found in cell walls of some red (|FRAME: TAX-2784| and |FRAME: TAX-31346|) and green (|FRAME: TAX-76312|, |FRAME: TAX-3128| and |FRAME: TAX-170436|) algae |CITS: [13852998][Fukushi86][Yamagaki96][12860427]|. It has not been detected in cell walls of land plants, which contain |FRAME: 1-4-beta-Xylan| instead. Analysis of |FRAME: 13-BETA-D-XYLANS "beta-1,3-D-xylan"| from the siphonous green alga |FRAME: TAX-177073| showed that it is a linear heteropolysaccharide also containing glucose residues linked by beta(1,3) linkages as well as some xylose residues linked by beta(1,4) linkages. Both of these are thought to be located within the beta-1,3-xylose chain and linked via covalent bonds 16891637.

Compound.name: a steroid hormone
Comment: Steroid hormones are steroids that act as hormones. Steroid hormones are divided into five groups based on the receptors to which they bind: |FRAME: Glucocorticoids glucocorticoids|, |FRAME: Mineralocorticoids mineralocorticoids|, |FRAME: Androgens androgens|, |FRAME: Steroidal-Estrogens "steroidal estrogens"|, and |FRAME: Progestogens progestogens|. Certain vitamin D derivatives (e.g. |FRAME: CALCITRIOL|) are sometimes considered a sixth steroid hormone group. The natural steroid hormones of mammals are generally synthesized from cholesterol in the gonads and adrenal glands.

Comment: |FRAME: Pterins Pterins| are heterocyclic compounds based on fused |FRAME: CPD-26401| and |FRAME: PYRIMIDINE-RING| rings (a |FRAME: CPD-15307| ring system) where the pyrimidine ring has an amino group in the 2-position and an oxo group in the 4-position, resulting in four double bonds within the ring system. However, the term amide also refers to compounds where the nitrogen is bonded to a non-carbon atom (see for example |FRAME: Sulfonamides|).

Compound.name: a [lipoyl-carrier protein]- N 6 -[( R )-lipoyl]-L-lysine
Synonyms: protein N6-(lipoyl)lysine // lipoyl-domain // a lipoylated protein lipoyl-domain // an [enzyme] N 6 -(lipoyl)lysine // an enzyme N 6 -(lipoyl)lysine
Comment: |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID "Lipoate"| is an organosulfur compound that is used as an essential cofactor by many enzyme complexes. The functional group of lipoate is a ditholane ring, which is a cyclic disulfide. The enzyme complexes that require lipoate have a dedicated |FRAME: Lipoyl-Protein "lipoyl domain"|, and lipoate is actually produced on this domain. The precursor |FRAME: CPD-195| molecule is first attached to a specific |FRAME: LYS| residue within the lipoyl domain (producing |FRAME: Octanoylated-domains|), and is then converted to lipoate by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX0-782|, resulting in |FRAME: Lipoyl-Protein-N6-lipoyllysine|. |FRAME: CPLX0-782 "Lipoate synthase"| not only catalyzes the reaction, but is also the source of the two sulfur atoms.

Compound.name: a galactoglucomannan
Comment: |FRAME: Glucomannans Glucomannans| (GM) and |FRAME: Galactoglucomannans galactoglucomannans| (GGM) are the major hemicellulosic components of the secondary cell walls of softwoods, but occur only in minor amounts in the secondary cell walls of hardwoods. Both polymers consist of a bakbone composed of beta(1->4)-linked glucopyranose and mannopyranose residues. GGM chains are substituted by galactopyranose residues and are often branched. Both polymers show some variations in structural features depending on the plant species and stage of plant development Ebringerova05. The mannan backbone of GGM from spruce wood consists of galactose, glucose, and mannose in the mole ratio 1 : 8 : 33, and contains segments of more than four mannopyranose residues, interrupted with a segment composed of both mannopyranose and glucopyranose, or two glucopyranose residues. Branches terminated by single galactose residues are attached at positions 2, 3, and 6 of mannose residues and at positions 3 and 6 of glucose residues of the backbone. Many of the mannose residues are acetylated at positions 2 and 3 11128591. The extent of GGM galactosylation governs its association tendency to the cellulose microfibrils Ebringerova05.

Compound.name: a sphingomyelin
Comment: |FRAME: Sphingomyelins Sphingomyelins| are a type of |FRAME: SPHINGOLIPIDS sphingolipids| found in animal cell membranes, especially in the membranous myelin sheath that surrounds some nerve cell axons. It usually consists of |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-CHOLINE| and |FRAME: Ceramides|, but |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-ETHANOLAMINE| can replace |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-CHOLINE|. Sphingomyelins are found in all tissues and lipoproteins; for example, they account for ~5% of the lipid phosphate in liver and 25% in pancreas 2187537. Sphingomyelins have a function in signal transduction 8086039. Sphingomyelins are highly enriched in the plasma membrane of cells, and were considered to be found largely in the exoplasmic leaflet of the cell membrane. However, there is some evidence that there may also be a sphingomyelin pool in the inner leaflet of the membrane 2187537. Moreover, neutral sphingomyelinase-2, an enzyme that breaks down sphingomyelins into ceramides, has been found to localize exclusively to the inner leaflet, further suggesting that there may be sphingomyelin present there. Sphingomyelin can accumulate in a rare hereditary disease called Niemann-Pick Disease . The disease is caused by a deficiency in the enzyme sphingomyelinase, rsulting in accumulation of sphingomyelin in the spleen, liver, lungs, bone marrow, and the brain, causing irreversible neurological damage.

Compound.name: a pyrimidine nucleotide
Comment: A pyrimidine nucleotide is composed of |FRAME: Pyrimidine-Bases|, a five-carbon sugar (either |FRAME: CPD0-1110 ribose| or |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE|), and one to three phosphate groups. When joined together, nucleotides make up the structural units of RNA and DNA. The nucleotides are called |FRAME: Ribonucleotides| when the sugar is |FRAME: CPD0-1110 ribose|, and |FRAME: Deoxynucleotides| when it is |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE|.

Compound.name: an i antigen
Synonyms: a beta-D-galactosyl-(1,4)- N -acetyl-beta-D-glucosaminyl-(1,3)-beta-D-galactosyl-(1,4)- N -acetyl-D-glucosaminyl-[glycoprotein] // a beta-D-galactosyl-(1->4)- N -acetyl-beta-D-glucosaminyl-(1->3)-beta-D-galactosyl-(1->4)- N -acetyl-beta-D-glucosaminyl-R // an i histo-blood group antigen // a beta-D-Gal-(1->4)-beta-D-GlcNAc-(1->3)-beta-D-Gal-(1->4)-beta-D-GlcNAc-R
Comment: The |FRAME: Lower-case-i-Antigens "i antigen"| is found on membrane proteins in red blood cells and many other cell types as well as various body secretions of developing fetuses and newborn infants |CITS: [13767181][4971635]|, while the |FRAME: Upper-case-I-antigens "I antigen"| is found in all adults 13292836. The i antigen undergoes gradual conversion to the I antigen in newborn infants, a process that completes in about 18 months. Both antigens are based entirely on Type 2 (|FRAME: BETA-D-GALACTOSYL-ETCETERA-GLUCOSAMINE " N -acetyllactosamine"|) chains. The basic i structure is an unbranched polylactosamine comprising at least two N - acetyllactosamine units connected by a beta(1->3) linkage |CITS: [823020][22356451]|. The crucial step in the transition from the i antigen to the I antigen is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.150|, also known as the I-branching enzyme, which introduces the branching by adding a GlcNAc residue by a beta(1->6) linkage to the galactose residue to which other residues are already attached by a 1,3 linkage 6490658. Note that the structure shown here is the core structure that defines I antigenicity. Most i antigens are further glycosylated. (Reviewed in Daniels13).

Compound.name: a dextrin
Comment: Dextrins are a group of low-molecular-weight carbohydrates produced by the hydrolysis of the D-glucose polymers |FRAME: Starch| or |FRAME: Glycogens glycogen|. The term is usally used to describe a mixture of polymers of various sizes, where the glucose units are linked by either alpha-(1->4) or alpha-(1->6) glycosidic bonds. When the polymers were hydrolyzed sufficiently to produce chain lengths that are under 20 monomers, the mixture is referred to as |FRAME: Maltodextrins|. The enzymatic degradation of starch by certain bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-44252| results in formation of cyclical molecules known as |FRAME: Cyclodextrins cyclodextrins|.

Compound.name: a bacteriochlorophyll e
Comment: Green sulfur bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-191412|) and green flimentous bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-1106|) contain chlorosomes - large organelles that are believed to be the most efficient light-harvesting antennae in nature |CITS: [20130996][Saga10]|. Green sulfur bacteria can grow at light intensities that are too low to support growth of any other phototroph, up to a million times lower light than normal sunlight Overmann92. Chlorosomes contain about 1,500 bacteriochlorophyll molecules per reaction center. They are filled with 10 30 rod-shaped elements which are oriented parallel to the long axis of the chlorosomes and have a diameter of 10 nm. Each rod consists of a tubular bilayer formed by self-organization of the antenna bacteriochlorophyll molecules. Unlike all other known photosynthetic antenna, in which the chlorophyll molecules are bound to proteins, chlorosomes do not contain accessory proteins. The chlorosomal bacteriochlorophyll pigments are able to self-aggregate due to their unique chemical characteristics. The bacteriochlorophylls found in chlorosomes are either |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d "| or |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e "|, depending on the species. They all possess a hydroxyl group at the C-3 1 position that allows them to chelate the Mg atom of a neighboring molecule and to interact with the C-13-oxo carbonyl group of another neighboring pigment molecule, affording the self-aggregation |CITS: [16121276][19435848][22210764]|. In addition, all of these bacteriochlorophylls lack C-13 2 -methylcarboxyl side chains, which are found in all other (bacterio)chlorophylls but would interfere with the ability to form aggregates 16245042. Despite of their names, |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d "| and |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e "| are actually chlorins rather than bacteriochlorins. All three are usually found with an unsaturated farnesyl tail rather than phytyl tails |CITS: [2350541][Borrego99]|, although exceptions have been reported. In chlorosomes of |FRAME: TAX-191412| (but not |FRAME: TAX-1106| |CITS: [Risch79][3442679]|) all three types of bacteriochlorophyll appear in several forms with different degrees of methylation at the C-8 2 and C-12 1 carbons |CITS: [12656478][14610639]|. The variety in methylation is depicted in the structure shown here by the R groups. In general, pimgents produced by cultures grown at lower light intensities are more highly methylated at the C-8 2 position than pigments produced by cells of the same organism grown at higher light intensities. Different methylation states result in different aggregation properties and light absorbance of the chlorosome, and thus methylation is used as an adaptation to altering envireonmental conditions. Most of the green sulfur bacteria growing in stratified lakes contain CPD-9093. CPD-9094 has been isolated from the chlorosomes of several strains of brown-colored |FRAME: TAX-191412|, including |FRAME: TAX-34090| and |FRAME: TAX-1096| 12029393.

Compound.name: a beta-lactam
Comment: This compound class stands for |FRAME: Lactams lactams| in which the amide bond is contained within a four-membered ring, which includes the amide nitrogen and the carbonyl carbon. beta-Lactam compounds imitate the naturally occurring |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| substrate for the group of enzymes known as penicillin binding proteins (PBPs), which cross-link the peptidoglycan in bacterial cell wall, and thus act as powerful antibiotics 6109324. Naturally occurring |FRAME: Beta-Lactams "beta-lactam antibiotics"| are classified into several groups according to their chemical structure: In |FRAME: Monolactams monolactams| the beta-lactam ring is not fused to another ring. This class includes compounds such as the |FRAME: Nocardicins nocardicins| 3427723 and the |FRAME: Monobactams monobactams| 3909315. In |FRAME: Penams penams| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a saturated five atom ring (a 4:5 structure). Penams contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring (for example, the |FRAME: PENICILLIN penicillins|) 6335599. Related classes include the |FRAME: Carbapenams carbapenams|, which contain a carbon atom in that position 12890666, and the |FRAME: Clavams oxopenams| (also known as clavams), which contain an oxygen atom at that position (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9261|) 3304182. |FRAME: Penems Penems| are molecues similar to penams in which the five atom ring is unsaturated at positions 2-3. Similarly, penems contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring, while |FRAME: Carbapenems carbapenems| contains a carbon atom in that position 16413506. In |FRAME: Cephams cephams| and |FRAME: Cephems cephems| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a six-atom ring (a 4:6 strcuture) that contains a sulfur atom at position 1. In cephams the ring is saturated, while cephems have an unsaturated bond at positions 3-4 |CITS: [1164170][12722308]|. 1-Oxocephams/1-oxacephems conain an oxygen atom at position 1 |CITS: [11671696][11078187]|.

Compound.name: a ceramide NP

Comment: The nomenclature of isoprenoids and their derivatives is somewhat confusing. Here are some guidelines for understanding these names: Isoprenoids are composed of repeating isoprene units. The units can be attached in either a trans conformation (the two carbons are on opposite sides of the double bond) or a cis conformation (the two carbons are on the same side of the double bond). It is common to use E and Z instead of trans and cis , respectively. The numbering of carbons in the molecule starts from the carbon attached to the hydroxyl or phosphate group. The isoprene unit furthest from the C1 carbon is called the ω unit. Unlike all other isoprene units, the ω unit is not a stereo center since the last carbon is attached to two identical methyl groups. There are two widely used naming systems, and unfortunately they refer to the isoprene units in opposite order. One method describes the molecule starting with the unit with the lowest carbon number (ie the one furthest from the ω unit), naming each of the stereo-active carbons by its number, followed by its stereo designation. For example, CPD-11977 is referred to as 2,6- cis ,10- trans -tetraprenyl diphosphate or (2 Z ,6 Z ,10 E )-tetraprenyl diphosphate. According to the other method, the molecule is described by the stereoconfiguration of the molecule starting with the ω unit. For example CPD-11977 is referred to as ω, E,Z,Z tetraprenyl diphosphate. On top of this, many of the shorter molecules have trivial names that are commonly used. Some of these names are specific for a particular stereoisomer and some are used for all stereoisomer. For example, |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP "geranylgeranyl diphosphate"| is commonly used for the all- trans isomer of the molecule with four isoprene units, while farnesyl diphosphate is used for all four isomers of the molecule with three isoprene units - FARNESYL-PP, CPD-9444, CPD-11293 and CPD-11990.

Comment: Iron-sulfur centers consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways. They serve as cofactors of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers with a low reduction potential. In addition to their roles in electron t ransfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes and the storage of iron and sulfur. They can also act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression 16466637. In some cases iron-sulfur clusters serve as sources of sulfur in enzymatic reactions 29051382 (see below). Two main types of [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters are low-potential (bacterial-type) clusters and high-potential (HiPIP) clusters. The bacterial clusters shift between the oxidation states +1 and +2, while the HiPIP clusters shift between the oxidation states +2 and +3. In some enzymes the [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters bind substrates. For example, in radical SAM enzymes the cluster binds and reduces S-adenosylmethionine, generating a radical that interacts with the enzyme's substrate. In a few cases, as in |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.8|, the cluster serves as the source of sulfur atoms for a sulfuration reaction. Siderophores are very common in pathogenic bacteria, since iron in the host organism is usually tightly bound to proteins, resulting in an extremely low concentration of free iron in the blood. Most siderophores belong to one of three major groups: the |FRAME: Catecholate-siderophores "catechols"|, |FRAME: Hydroxamate-siderophores "hydroxamates"| and |FRAME: Thiazoline-siderophores "thiazolines"|. Some grasses are known to make siderophores as well. These |FRAME: Phytosiderophores "phytosiderophores"| are also known as mugineic acids.

Based on the notation GlcCer(m:n)-p used to name subclasses of glucosylceramides, the total number of carbons present in the sphingoid base and the fatty amide is "m" while the total number of double bonds is "n." The length, hydroxylation position, double bond position, and double bond orientation of the groups attached at R1 and R2 will differ between individual members of this group of compounds.

Compound.name: hyaluronan
Comment: |FRAME: Hyaluronan Hyaluronan| is an anionic, nonsulfated |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycan"| distributed widely throughout connective, epithelial, and neural tissues, including the vitreous humor of the eye, the aorta, blood, brain, liver and skin 354500. It is produced by almost all members of the animal kingdom as well as by certain members of streptococci 9260563. Hyaluronan can be very large, with its molecular weight often reaching the millions. It forms a strikingly viscous solution and functions primarily as a joint lubricant and shock absorber, although it is also thought to be involved in cell proliferation, migration and differentiation. Hyaluronan is composed of repeating disaccharide unit of [|FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| (beta1,4) |FRAME: CPD-12521|] (|FRAME: HYALURONATE|) linked by beta 1,3 linkages. Though classified as a glycosaminoglycan, it differs from other members of this family. While all other glycosaminoglycans are synthesized by resident Golgi enzymes and covalently attached to core proteins, hyaluronan is synthesized at the inner face of the plasma membrane as a free linear polymer without any protein core. In addition, it is the only glycosaminoglycan that is not sulfated 17408700.

Compound.name: a [DsrC protein] with an intramolecular disulfide bond
SMILES.ID: C(=O)([a DsrC sulfur carrier protein])[C@@H]1(CSSC[C@@H](C(=O)[R]N1)N[a DsrC sulfur carrier protein])
Comment: The dissimilatory sulfite reductase, DsrAB, is an essential enzyme in prokaryotic sulfur-based energy metabolism. In sulfur reducers it catalyzes the reduction of sulfite to sulfide, while in sulfur oxidizers it catalyzes the opposite reaction Schedel79. This reaction involves the small protein DsrC, which is present in all organisms that contain DsrAB, including sulfate/sulfite reducing organisms, sulfur-oxidizing bacteria, and organosulfonate reducers. DsrC contains two redox-active conserved cysteines in a flexible C-terminal arm. A crystal structure of |FRAME: TAX-881| DsrAB in complex with DsrC has shown that the C-terminal arm of DsrC projects inside DsrAB in a way that brings its last Cys (CysA) right next to the active site. In |FRAME: TAX-1049| DsrC is the final sulfur-accepting protein, receiving the sulfur from the sulfur-carrier protein |FRAME: DsrE-Protein DsrE| and forming |FRAME: DsrC-persulfides "a perthiol on CysA"|. This perthiol serves as a direct substrate for |FRAME: CPLX-7133| (DsrAB), which catalyzes the oxidation of the sulfane sulfur while still attached to DsrC. The oxidized sulfur is then released is the form of sulfite, leaving DsrC with |FRAME: DsrC-disulfide-form "an intramolecular disulfide bond"| between the two cysteine residues 18656485. This disulfide bond can be dissociated by the action of the DsrK protein, part of the DsrMKJOP complex 20952577. In sulfite reducing bacteria, where the reaction occurs in the opposite direction, the two substrates for DsrAB are DsrC and a sulfite molecule. During the reaction the sulfite sulfur is added to CysA of DsrC and reduced, forming a perthiol. The sulfur then leaves as a sulfide, leaving DsrC with intramolecular disulfide bond between the two cysteine residues as described above 24662917. In the structure shown below, the R residue represents a stretch of amino acids that separate the two conserved L-cysteines.

Compound.name: an N 10 -formyltetrahydrofolate
Comment: |FRAME: THF-GLU-N Tetrahydrofolate| (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are required in a variety of reactions in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, where they act as carriers of one-carbon units in various oxidation states. These one-carbon units are utilized in the biosynthesis of various cellular components, including glycine, methionine, formylmethionine, thymidylate, pantothenate and purine nucleotides. During folate biosynthesis (as described in FOLSYN-PWY) the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.12|, adds a glutamate residue to |FRAME: 7-8-DIHYDROPTEROATE|, resulting in |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE|, also known as H 2 PteGlu 1 . This molecule in turn is reduced by EC-1.5.1.3 (FolA) to |FRAME: THF| (H 4 PteGlu 1 , or tetrahydrofolate), which can be converted to several other folate molecules 11501996. Most folate molecules are modified in cells by successive additions of glutamate residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-gamma-glutamates). The glutamate residues are added by an amide linkage to the gamma-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are not the normal amide bonds they are not hydrolyzed by peptidases or proteases, which are specific for alpha-carboxyl-linked peptide bonds. The addition of glutamyl residues probably occurs after the reduction of newly synthesized dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and its conversion to other tetrahydrofolate derivatives. The glutamylation of folate residues serves several goals: it prevents the efflux of folates out of the cell, it increases the binding of folate cofactors to the enzymes of folate interconversion and biosynthesis, and in mammals, it allows the accumulation of folates in the mitochondria, which is required for glycine synthesis 10598551. This class stands for 10-formyltetrahydrofolates with an unspecified number of glutamate residues.

Compound.name: an anthracycline

This group of antibiotics is defined by the presence of a four fused-ring aromatic system, based on a 7,8,9,10-tetrahydro-5,12-naphthacenequinone framework, which usually occurs as a glycoside with a deoxy(amino)sugar. The framework is synthesized by a polyketide-synthase from an acetyl-CoA or propanoyl-CoA starter unit and malonyl-CoA extender units, and subsequently modified by other enzymes 11851469. The anthracyclines intercalate between base pairs of the DNA/RNA strand, inhibit topoisomerase II enzymes, and prevent DNA replication. They are among the most effective anticancer treatments ever developed and are effective against more types of cancer than any other class of chemotherapeutic agents.

Compound.name: an H antigen
Synonyms: an alpha-L-fucosyl-(1->2)-beta-D-galactosyl-R // a glycoprotein-alpha-L-fucosyl-(1,2)-beta-D-galactose // a 2-O-(6-deoxy-alpha-L-galactopyranosyl)-beta-D-galactopyranosyl // an alpha-L-fucosyl-1,2-beta-D-galactoside // an alpha-L-fucosyl-1,2-beta-D-galactosyl-R
Comment: The |FRAME: H-antigen "H antigens"| are fucosylated oligosaccharides that decorate proteins on the surface of red blood cells in people with O blood type. These fucosylated structures are found not only on blood cells but also on many other cell types (mainly epithehal), and it has been suggested that they should be called histo-blood group antigens. The majority of the A, B and H antigens are linked to the ends of long polylactosamine chains attached mainly to band 3 protein (encoded by SLC4A1), the anion exchange protein of the red blood cells. A minor fraction of the antigens is attached to a ceramide moiety, forming neutral glycosphingolipids. Several H antigens exist, differing in their core disaccharide 2093726. The different types are: |FRAME: Type-1-H-Antigen "Type 1"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->3)-betaGlcNac-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-2-H-Antigen "Type 2"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->4)-betaGlcNac-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-3-H-Antigen "Type 3"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->3)-alphaGalNac-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-4-H-Antigen "Type 4"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->3)-betaGalNac-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-5-H-Antigen "Type 5"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->3)-betaGal-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-6-H-Antigen "Type 6"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->4)-betaGlc-(1->R) Most of the H antigens found in the cell are either type 1 or type 2, followed by type 3 and 4. Type 1 is found in secretions and in the serum, while type 2 is found exclusively on the surface of red blood cells. Type 6 molecules have been described in exocrine secretions. It is not clear if type 5 H antigens exist, although the type 5 precursor has been characterized 2093726.

PKSs can be divided to two types: multifunctional polyproteins (type I) and discrete protein (type II). Some grasses are known to make siderophores as well. These |FRAME: Phytosiderophores "phytosiderophores"| are also known as mugineic acids. Thiazoline siderophores are named based on the presence of a thiazoline (5-membered heterocyclic compound containing both sulfur and nitrogen in the ring) element in their structures.

Compound.name: a 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate
Synonyms: (-)CH 2 H 4 folate // (-)5,10-methylene-5,6,7,8-tetrahydrofolate // methylene-H4PteGlu(n) // methylene-THF(glu) n // methylene-H 4 PteGlu n // methylene-tetrahydropteroylpolyglutamates
Comment: |FRAME: THF-GLU-N Tetrahydrofolate| (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are required in a variety of reactions in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, where they act as carriers of one-carbon units in various oxidation states. These one-carbon units are utilized in the biosynthesis of various cellular components, including glycine, methionine, formylmethionine, thymidylate, pantothenate and purine nucleotides. During folate biosynthesis (as described in FOLSYN-PWY) the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.12|, adds a glutamate residue to |FRAME: 7-8-DIHYDROPTEROATE|, resulting in |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE|, also known as H 2 PteGlu 1 . This molecule in turn is reduced by EC-1.5.1.3 (FolA) to |FRAME: THF| (H 4 PteGlu 1 , or tetrahydrofolate), which can be converted to several other folate molecules 11501996. Most folate molecules are modified in cells by successive additions of glutamate residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-gamma-glutamates). The glutamate residues are added by an amide linkage to the gamma-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are not the normal amide bonds they are not hydrolyzed by peptidases or proteases, which are specific for alpha-carboxyl-linked peptide bonds. The addition of glutamyl residues probably occurs after the reduction of newly synthesized dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and its conversion to other tetrahydrofolate derivatives. The glutamylation of folate residues serves several goals: it prevents the efflux of folates out of the cell, it increases the binding of folate cofactors to the enzymes of folate interconversion and biosynthesis, and in mammals, it allows the accumulation of folates in the mitochondria, which is required for glycine synthesis 10598551. This class stands for 5,10-methylene-tetrahydrofolates with an unspecified number of glutamate residues.

The length of a fatty acid is determined by the length of the longest carbon chain, including the carbon of the carboxy group. Common natural fatty acids usually have an even number of carbons in the longest chain and can be either saturated or unsaturated. In many organisms they are often modified by branching, hydroxylation, methylation, epoxidation and other types of modifications. Inside living cells fatty acids are rarely found in free form. They are usually bound to coenzyme A or acyl-carrier proteins, or form part of |FRAME: Triacylglycerides triglycerides|, |FRAME: Phospholipids phospholipids|, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides|, and |FRAME: Cholesterol-esters cholesterol esters|. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "Short-chain fatty acids"| (SCFA) have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "Medium-chain fatty acids"| (MCFA) have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "Long-chain fatty acids"| (LCFA) have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "Very-long-chain fatty acids"| (VLCFA) have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "Ultra-long-chain fatty acids"| (ULCFA) have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain. Most of the natural fatty acids have an even number of carbon atoms, since their biosynthesis involves the addition of two-carbon-atom units. When a fatty acid contains only single bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Saturated-Fatty-Acids|. When it contains one or more double bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Unsaturated-Fatty-Acids|. Since globo H is not expressed in normal tissue except for weak expression in the apical epithelial cells at lumen borders, a site that is inaccessible to the immune system |CITS: [6711680][9334808]|, it is considered an ideal target for immunotherapy of many epithelial cancers. Two phase I trials of a Globo H-based vaccine in breast and prostate cancer, respectively, have shown promising results |CITS: [10318949][11248068]|, and efforts to develop a globo H cancer vaccine are continues 25665650.

Compound.name: a stephacidin

The stephacidins belong to a diverse family of biologically active prenylated indole alkaloids isolated mainly from various |FRAME: TAX-5073| and |FRAME: TAX-5052| species of fungi that contains a unique bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane core ring system, and are derived from |FRAME: TRP|, a cyclic amino acid (|FRAME: PRO|, |FRAME: L-PIPECOLATE| or a derivative of one of those compounds), and one or two isoprene units. In addition to their structural diversity, members of this family have been attributed a variety of bioactivities, including (but not limited to) insecticidal, cytotoxic, anthelmintic, and antibacterial properties. The bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane-containing compounds can be divided into two sub-categories: the diketopiperazines (DKPs) and the monoketopiperazines (MKPs). DKPs include the |FRAME: Stephacidins stephacidins|, |FRAME: Brevianamides brevianamides|, and |FRAME: Notoamides notoamides|, while MKPs include the |FRAME: Paraherquamides paraherquamides|, |FRAME: Asperparalines asperparalines|, |FRAME: Marcfortines marcfortines|, |FRAME: Chrysogenamides chrysogenamides|,and |FRAME: Malbrancheamides malbrancheamides|.

The estrogens that occur naturally in the body are steroids, however other types of molecules acquired in the diet are known to bind to the estrogen receptors and are thus also considered estrogens. They include molecules produced by plants (phytoestrogens), molecules produced by fungi (mycoestrogens), and synthetic compounds (xenoestrogens). The main steroidal |FRAME: Estrogens estrogens| in humans are |FRAME: ESTRONE|, |FRAME: CPD-352| and |FRAME: ESTRIOL|, which differ in the number of hydroxyl groups (one for |FRAME: ESTRONE|, two for |FRAME: CPD-352| and three for |FRAME: ESTRIOL|). |FRAME: CPD-352| is about 10 times as potent as |FRAME: ESTRONE| and about 80 times as potent as |FRAME: ESTRIOL| in its estrogenic effect. |FRAME: CPD-352| is the predominant estrogen in non-pregenant women during their reproductive years in terms of serum levels. |FRAME: ESTRONE Estrone| is the predominant circulating estrogen in women during menopause and |FRAME: ESTRIOL| is the predominant circulating estrogen during pregnancy.

Compound.name: a terpenoid
Comment: |FRAME: Terpenoids Terpenoids| make up a very large family of natural products, containing more than 50,000 structurally diverse compounds, that are derived from five-carbon |FRAME: CPD-9436| units. They are categorized by the number of C5 isoprene units as follows: |FRAME: Hemiterpenes Hemiterpenoids| (one C5 unit), |FRAME: Monoterpenes monoterpenoids| (C10; two C5 units), |FRAME: Sesquiterpenes sesquiterpenoids| (C15; three C5 units), |FRAME: Diterpenes diterpenoids| (C20; four C5 units), |FRAME: Sesterterpenes sesterterpenoids| (C25; five C5 units), |FRAME: Triterpenes triterpenoids| (C30; six C5 units), |FRAME: C35-Terpenes "sesquarterpenoids"| (C35; seven C5 units), and |FRAME: Tetraterpenes tetraterpenoids| (C40; eight C5 units). Larger compounds are referred to as polyterpenoids.

Compound.name: a pectate
Synonyms: poly(1,4-alpha-D-galacturonate)(n) // (1,4-alpha-D-D-galactosyluronate)n // 1,4-alpha-D-galacturonide // a pectic acid // an alpha-D-polygalacturonic acid // a poly(1,4-alpha-D-galacturonate)
Comment: |FRAME: Pectin "Pectin"| is a structural heteropolysaccharide consisting of a complex set of polysaccharides that is present in most primary cell walls and is particularly abundant in the non-woody parts of terrestrial plants. It s involved in crosslinking cellulose and hemicellulose fibers, which provides rigidity to the cell wall. The characteristic structure of pectin is a linear chain of alpha-(1-4)-linked |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| that forms the pectin-backbone, |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl|. Different components of pectin have different substitutions and additions. A common type is |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "rhamnogalacturonan I"| (RG-I), which makes up 20-35% of pectin. In RG-I some of the |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| units in the backbone are replaced by (1-2)-linked |FRAME: L-rhamnose|, to which side chains of various neutral sugars branch off, mostly |FRAME: D-Galactose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| and |FRAME: CPD-25028|. Another common type is |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan II"| (RG-II), which makes up about 10% of pectin. RG-II is based on a backbone of 8-9 galacturonate units, which are decorated by four side chains consisting of 12 different types of sugars in more than 20 different linkages. RG-II usually forms dimeric structures via the formation of crosslinks by a 1:2 borate diol ester between apiosyl residues in one of the side chains. Other types of pectin include chains of apiogalacturonan, homogalacturonan, and xylogalacturonan. There is currently no consensus as to how the pectic polysaccharides are linked to each other, or to other polymers, in the wall. However, it is thought that the different peptides are covalently linked to each other via their backbones, forming a large linear structure with many side branches |CITS: [11423143][12162553][Coenen07]|. In nature, around 80% of the carboxyl groups of the galacturonate units are esterified with |FRAME: METOH|. Some plants, including sugar beet, potatoes and pears, contain pectins with acetylated galacturonate in addition to methyl esters. Partially esterified pectins are often referred to as pectinate, and if the degree of esterification is below 5%, |FRAME: PECTATE|.

Compound.name: an oligosaccharide
Comment: An oligosaccharide is a saccharide polymer containing a small number (typically three to six) of component monosaccharides (also known as simple sugars). Oligosaccharides are often found either O - or N -linked to compatible amino acid side chains in proteins or to lipid moieties.

Compound.name: a very-long-chain 3-oxoacyl-CoA
Comment: ACYL-COA are oxoacids that have been activated by |FRAME: CO-A|. They are often classified by the length of their acyl moiety. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Medium-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from fatty acids with aliphatic tails of 6-12 carbons. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Long-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from fatty acids with aliphatic tails of 13-21 carbons. |FRAME: VERY-LONG-CHAIN-FATTY-ACYL-COA "Very long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from fatty acids with aliphatic tails of 22 carbons or longer.

Compound.name: a xyloglucan oligosaccharide
Comment: Xyloglucan oligosaccharides are produced from |FRAME: Xyloglucan xyloglucan| by the action of endo- or exo-(1,4)-beta-glucanases. A study that analyzed the products of tamarind xyloglucan digestion by several endoglucanases from different organisms found that all enzymes produced oligosaccharides with the composition |FRAME: CPD-13375 XXXG|, |FRAME: CPD-13376 XXLG|/|FRAME: CPD-13377 XLXG| and |FRAME: CPD-13378 XLLG| as the end products of xyloglucan hydrolysis 15541296 (see |FRAME: Xyloglucan| for explanation of this terminology). Xyloglucan from |FRAME: TAX-3702| is comprised of repeating subunits of |FRAME: CPD-13418 XXFG|, |FRAME: CPD-13375 XXXG|, |FRAME: CPD-13376 XXLG|, |FRAME: CPD-13417 XLFG|, |FRAME: CPD-13378 XLLG|, and |FRAME: CPD-13377 XLXG| |CITS: [12837954][17011813]|.

Compound.name: a proanthocyanidin
Comment: Proanthocyanidins are a class of polyphenols found in a variety of plants. They are flavonoid oligomers obtained by the condensation of two or more units of |FRAME: Flavanols flavanols|. Many proanthocyanidins are oligomers of |FRAME: CPD-1961| and |FRAME: CPD-7630| and their gallic acid esters. More complex polyphenols, having the same polymeric building block, form the group of tannins. The structure shown here is for illustration only, and shows a generic dimeric proanthocyanidin. Natural procyanidins are highly diverse in size and composition, and the monomers are usually lined up by C-4/C-8 or C-4/C-6 linkages 12788945.

Compound.name: a protein-bound uremic retention solute
Comment: Uremic retention solutes are toxic compounds that accumulate in blood and tissues of patients with uremia (chronic renal failure). They may be free or protein-bound. The common protein-bound solutes include |FRAME: CPD-108| ( p -cresol), |FRAME: CPD-16817|, |FRAME: CPD-425|, |FRAME: CPD-16818| (CMPF), and |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| 14681860. Protein-bound compounds pose challenges to treatment since their removal by conventional hemodialysis is low.

Compound.name: a phosphatidylinositol
Comment: Phosphatidylinositols are a group of compounds that include one |FRAME: L-PHOSPHATIDATE phosphatidyl| group esterified to one of the hydroxy groups of |FRAME: Inositols inositol|. Unlike |FRAME: Glycerophosphoinositols|, it always contains two fatty acids.

Compound.name: a secondary alcohol
Comment: A secondary alcohol is a compound in which a hydroxy group, -OH, is attached to a saturated carbon atom that has two other carbon atoms attached to it.

Compound.name: a cardenolide glycoside
Comment: Cardiac glycosides are plant-made compounds (mostly by members of the |FRAME: TAX-4163| genus, or Foxgloves) that have beneficial effects over patients with cardiac failure. The treatment of congestive heart failure (dropsy), among other ailments like tuberculosis, by the use of Foxglove is mentioned in writings as early as 1250 A. D., when the Welsh Physicians of Myddva collected foxglove as one of their many herbs and included it in their remedies. 28561136. The cardiac glycosides are composed of two structural features: a sugar moiety that may contain one or more saccharides, and a steroid aglycone. Cardiac glycosides having a terminal glucose are called primary glycosides whereas those lacking such a sugar are termed secondary glycosides. There are two classes of cardiac glycosides differing by the group attached at the 17-position of the aglycone: the |FRAME: Cardenolide-Glycosides "cardenolides"|, which have a five-membered unsaturated lactone ring (but-2-en-4-olide ring) and the |FRAME: Bufadienolide-Glycosides bufadienolides|, which have a six membered doubly unsaturated lactone ring (penta-2,4-dien-5-olide ring). The steroid nucleus of the cardiac glycosides have a unique configuration: rings A/B and C/D are cis - fused while rings B/C are trans - fused. The nucleus has beta configured hydroxyls at the positions C-3 and C-14, and many compounds have additional hydroxyl groups at positions 12 and 16. The sugars found in the glycoside moiety range from common hexoses and pentoses (such as |FRAME: D-Glucose|, |FRAME: L-rhamnose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-Xylose|) to very uncommon sugars, some of which have only been found in cardiac glycosides (e.g. |FRAME: D-quinovopyranose|, |FRAME: CPD-22597|, |FRAME: D-Digitoxose|, |FRAME: CPD-22572|, |FRAME: D-Olivose|, and |FRAME: D-Fucoses|). While the mechanism whereby cardiac glycosides cause a positive inotropic effect and electrophysiologic changes of the hurt is still not completely clear, the most widely accepted mechanism involves the ability of cardiac glycosides to inhibit the membrane bound Na+/K+-ATPase pump responsible for Na+/K+ exchange KAUTE08.

Compound.name: an E vitamin
Comment: The term |FRAME: Vitamin-E| (tocochromenols) is a collective term for the eight forms of |FRAME: Tocotrienols tocotrienols| and |FRAME: Tocopherols tocopherols|, each existing as alpha, beta, gamma, and delta species. Structurally tocotrienols and tocopherols differ only in the degree of unsaturation of their side-chain. The tocotrienol chain comprises three trans -double bonds, whereas the tocopherol chain is fully saturated. In addition, the alpha, beta, gamma, and delta species of both compound groups vary in the methylation pattern of the chromanol ring 12897790. Vitamin E compounds are synthesized only by photosynthetic organisms, although they are essential dietary components for animals (including humans), where they act primarily as antioxidants. Their presumed role in plants involve protection of chloroplast lipids and chlorophylls against oxidative damages. The tocotrienols are mostly found in monocots Padley94 and a few dicots 17110122, whereas tocopherols are wider spread in the plant kingdom and dominate in the dicots 8827691.

Compound.name: a cannabinoid
Comment: Cannabinoid are a diverse group of pharmacologically active secondary metabolites. While they are named after the Cannabis plant, which forms many of these compounds, some cannabinoids are produced natively by humans and animals.

Compound.name: an isoflavonoid
Comment: An isoflavanoid is a type of |FRAME: Flavonoids| with an aryl substituent at position 3. They are biologically active compounds, such as the phytoestrogens produced by pea family plants.

Compound.name: a medium-chain fatty aldehyde
Comment: Fatty-Aldehydes are aldehydes that are formed by the reduction of the carboxylic acid group of |FRAME: Fatty-Acids fatty acids|. Many enzymes that act on fatty acids, as well as the corresponding |FRAME: Fatty-Acyl-CoAs "fatty acyl-CoAs"|, |FRAME: Fatty-Alcohols alcohols|, and |FRAME: Fatty-Aldehydes aldehydes|, have evolved to recognize substrates with a limited range of chain lengths. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-Chain-Aldehydes "Short-chain fatty aldehydes"| are derived from |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Aldehydes "Medium-chain fatty aldehydes"| are derived from |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Aldehydes "Long-chain fatty aldehydes"| are derived from |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "fatty acids that have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Very-Long-Chain-Aldehydes "Very-long-chain fatty aldehydes"| are derived from |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Ultra-Long-Chain-Aldehydes "Ultra-long-chain fatty aldehydes"| are derived from |FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain"|.

Compound.name: a ω-3 fatty acid
Comment: Omega 3 fatty acids (popularly referred to as ω-3 fatty acids or n-3 fatty acids) are fats commonly found in marine and plant oils. They are polyunsaturated fatty acids with a double bond (C=C) starting after the third carbon atom from the end of the carbon chain. The fatty acids have two endsthe acid (COOH) end and the methyl (CH3) end. The location of the first double bond is counted from the methyl end, which is also known as the omega (ω) end or the n end.

Compound.name: a carotenoid
Comment: |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A. Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest. The prominent |FRAME: CPD1F-119|, as well as |FRAME: CPD1F-130|, are involved in the reduction of cataract and macular degeneration; others are exploited as coloring agents in flowers and fruits to attract pollinators (and in industry as food colorant) and agents of seed dispersal. Carotenoids serve as precursors for the plant growth hormone |FRAME: Abscisic-Acid| and |FRAME: Vitamin-A| (for a succinct review of the applications of carotenoids, see 15012246). In addition, they may be cleaved to |FRAME: Apocarotenoids apocarotenoids|, whose functions include serving as a cofactor for light-sensing proteins, acting as hormones, or acting as antifungals. Carotenoids have been the subject of metabolic pathway engineering studies because microbial carotenoid production is environmentally preferable to chemical synthesis. Over 700 carotenoids have been identified. The two main structural classes of carotenoids are the |FRAME: Carotenes carotenes| and the |FRAME: Xanthophylls xanthophylls|, which are composed of hydrocarbons and oxygenated hydrocarbons, respectively. Most carotenoids have a C40 chain length derived from the symmetric precursor |FRAME: CPD-12321| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6287|). |FRAME: CPD-12321| is derived from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|, which is in turn derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5120|). Larger, C50 carotenoids also occur in nature and appear to be derived from the addition of two isoprene units to a C40 carotenoid. Although biosynthetic intermediates and novel bacterial genes involved in C50 carotenoid biosynthesis from |FRAME: CPD1F-114| have been identified and biosynthetic pathways postulated, details of all of the enzyme reactions involved in these pathways remain to be determined (as in |CITS: [20802040] [17008032] [11511870] [11432736]|). Smaller, C30 carotenoids have also been found in plants and microorganisms. In microorganisms they appear to be synthesized by a distinct C30 pathway, whereas in plants they appear to result from cleavage of C40 carotenoids. |FRAME: CPD-9911| is a bacterial C30 carotenoid derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|. It is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite |FRAME: CPD-9916| in |FRAME: TAX-1280| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5875|). |FRAME: CPD-9911| has also been identified in a few other bacteria |CITS: [20303609] [9297464]|. Genes encoding the enzymes of carotenoid biosynthesis have been cloned from many plants, cyanobacteria and other microorganisms (|CITS: [20582313][11511870][18535920] [17257797] [17912511][12730708]|. Extensive comparative genomics analysis of microbial carotenoid biosynthetic proteins has shown new phylogenetic and evolutionary patterns of these pigments that had not been found in previous, more limited, analyses 20582313.

Compound.name: a phthiodiolone A
Comment: |FRAME: Phthiodiolones Phthiodiolones| are intermediates in |FRAME: Phthiocerols phthiocerol| biosynthesis. They contain an oxo group where phthiocerols contain a methoxyl group. Two types of phthiodiolone exist. In |FRAME: Phthiodiolone-A "phthiodiolone A"| the oxo and the methyl groups are attached at positions 3 and 4, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 9 and 11. In |FRAME: Phthiodiolone-B "phthiodiolone B"| a methyl group is missing from the beginning of the molecule, and thus the oxo and methyl groups are attached at positions 2 and 3, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 8 and 10.

Compound.name: a long-chain primary alcohol
Comment: A primary alcohol is a compound in which a hydroxy group, -OH, is attached to a saturated carbon atom that is connected to no more than one other carbon atom. Primary alcohols are also classified based on their length. |FRAME: Short-Chain-Primary-Alcohols "Short-chain primary alcohols"| have alkyl chains with fewer than six carbons. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Primary-Alcohols "Medium-chain primary alcohols"| have alkyl chains of 6-12 carbons. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Primary-Alcohols "Long-chain primary alcohols"| (also known as fatty alcohols) have alkyl chains of 13-22 carbons. |FRAME: Very-Long-Chain-Primary-Alcohols "Very long-chain primary alcohols"| have alkyl chains of 23 carbons or longer.

Compound.name: a long-chain fatty alcohol
Comment: Fatty alcohols are aliphatic |FRAME: Alcohols alcohols| consisting of a chain of 3 or more carbon atoms. They may be saturated or unsaturated and may be branched or unbranched. Many enzymes that act on |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "fatty acids"|, as well as the corresponding |FRAME: Fatty-Acyl-CoAs "fatty acyl-CoAs"|, |FRAME: Fatty-Alcohols alcohols|, and |FRAME: Fatty-Aldehydes aldehydes|, have evolved to recognize substrates with a limited range of chain lengths. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-Chain-Alcohols "Short-chain alcohols"| have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Alcohols "Medium-chain alcohols"| have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Long-chain-alcohols "Long-chain alcohols"| have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Very-Long-Chain-Alcohols "Very-long-chain alcohols"| have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Ultra-Long-Chain-Alcohols "Ultra-long-chain alcohols"| have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain.

Compound.name: a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug
Comment: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAIDs) are a group of anti-inflammatory drugs that do not belong to the steroid family. In addition to anti-inflammatory actions, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs have analgesic, antipyretic, and platelet-inhibitory actions. They act by blocking the synthesis of |FRAME: Prostaglandins prostaglandins| by inhibiting cyclooxygenase, which converts |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| to cyclic endoperoxides, precursors of |FRAME: Prostaglandins prostaglandins|.

Compound.name: an isoquinoline alkaloid
Comment: Isoquinoline alkaloids have a structure based on an |FRAME: ISOQUINOLINE| nucleus. They are derived from amino acids like |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: PHE|.

Compound.name: a carbapenam
Comment: This compound class stands for |FRAME: Lactams lactams| in which the amide bond is contained within a four-membered ring, which includes the amide nitrogen and the carbonyl carbon. beta-Lactam compounds imitate the naturally occurring |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| substrate for the group of enzymes known as penicillin binding proteins (PBPs), which cross-link the peptidoglycan in bacterial cell wall, and thus act as powerful antibiotics 6109324. Naturally occurring |FRAME: Beta-Lactams "beta-lactam antibiotics"| are classified into several groups according to their chemical structure: In |FRAME: Monolactams monolactams| the beta-lactam ring is not fused to another ring. This class includes compounds such as the |FRAME: Nocardicins nocardicins| 3427723 and the |FRAME: Monobactams monobactams| 3909315. In |FRAME: Penams penams| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a saturated five atom ring (a 4:5 structure). Penams contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring (for example, the |FRAME: PENICILLIN penicillins|) 6335599. Related classes include the |FRAME: Carbapenams carbapenams|, which contain a carbon atom in that position 12890666, and the |FRAME: Clavams oxopenams| (also known as clavams), which contain an oxygen atom at that position (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9261|) 3304182. |FRAME: Penems Penems| are molecues similar to penams in which the five atom ring is unsaturated at positions 2-3. Similarly, penems contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring, while |FRAME: Carbapenems carbapenems| contains a carbon atom in that position 16413506. In |FRAME: Cephams cephams| and |FRAME: Cephems cephems| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a six-atom ring (a 4:6 strcuture) that contains a sulfur atom at position 1. In cephams the ring is saturated, while cephems have an unsaturated bond at positions 3-4 |CITS: [1164170][12722308]|. 1-Oxocephams/1-oxacephems conain an oxygen atom at position 1 |CITS: [11671696][11078187]|.

Compound.name: an aldoxime
Comment: |FRAME: Oximes "An oxime"| is a class of chemical compounds with the general formula (R1)(R2)HC=NOH. |FRAME: Aldoxime An aldoxime| is an oxime where R1 is a hydrogen, and is is usually generated by the reaction of |FRAME: HYDROXYLAMINE| and |FRAME: Aldehydes aldehydes|. The term oxime is derived from a condensation of the words oxygen and |FRAME: Imides imide|.

Compound.name: a retinoid
Comment: Retinoids are a group of compounds that are related to vitamin A, including all-trans forms such as |FRAME: CPD-13524|, |FRAME: RETINAL| and |FRAME: RETINOATE|, cis forms such as |FRAME: CPD-882|, |FRAME: CPD-881|, |FRAME: CPD-13549| and |FRAME: CPD-13548|, and |FRAME: Retinyl-Esters "retinyl esters"| such as |FRAME: CHOCOLA_A|. Retinoids have many important and diverse functions throughout the body including roles in vision, regulation of cell proliferation and differentiation, growth of bone tissue, immune function, and activation of tumor suppressor genes. Structurally, all retinoids possess a beta-ionone ring and a polyunsaturated side chain, with either an alcohol, aldehyde, a carboxylic acid group or an ester group. The side chain is composed of four isoprenoid units, with a series of conjugated double bonds which may exist in trans - or cis -configuration.

Compound.name: phosphatidylcholine-34:3

For each of the group members, the total number of carbon atoms in the two acyl chains adds up to 34, and the total number of double bonds in the two acyl groups adds up to 3.

Compound.name: a [lipoyl-carrier protein] N 6 -octanoyl-L-lysine
Comment: |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID "Lipoate"| is an organosulfur compound that is used as an essential cofactor by many enzyme complexes. The functional group of lipoate is a ditholane ring, which is a cyclic disulfide. The enzyme complexes that require lipoate have a dedicated |FRAME: Lipoyl-Protein "lipoyl domain"|, and lipoate is actually produced on this domain. The precursor |FRAME: CPD-195| molecule is first attached to a specific |FRAME: LYS| residue within the lipoyl domain (producing |FRAME: Octanoylated-domains|), and is then converted to lipoate by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX0-782|, resulting in |FRAME: Lipoyl-Protein-N6-lipoyllysine|. |FRAME: CPLX0-782 "Lipoate synthase"| not only catalyzes the reaction, but is also the source of the two sulfur atoms.

Compound.name: a bacteriochlorophyll c
Comment: Green sulfur bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-191412|) and green flimentous bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-1106|) contain chlorosomes - large organelles that are believed to be the most efficient light-harvesting antennae in nature |CITS: [20130996][Saga10]|. Green sulfur bacteria can grow at light intensities that are too low to support growth of any other phototroph, up to a million times lower light than normal sunlight Overmann92. Chlorosomes contain about 1,500 bacteriochlorophyll molecules per reaction center. They are filled with 10-30 rod-shaped elements which are oriented parallel to the long axis of the chlorosomes and have a diameter of 10 nm. Each rod consists of a tubular bilayer formed by self-organization of the antenna bacteriochlorophyll molecules. Unlike all other known photosynthetic antenna, in which the chlorophyll molecules are bound to proteins, chlorosomes do not contain accessory proteins. The chlorosomal bacteriochlorophyll pigments are able to self-aggregate due to their unique chemical characteristics. The bacteriochlorophylls found in chlorosomes are either |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d "| or |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e "|, depending on the species. They all possess a hydroxyl group at the C3 1 position that allows them to chelate the Mg atom of a neighboring molecule and to interact with the C13-oxo carbonyl group of another neighboring pigment molecule, affording the self-aggregation |CITS: [16121276][19435848][22210764]|. In addition, all of these bacteriochlorophylls lack C-13 2 -methylcarboxyl side chains, which are found in all other (bacterio)chlorophylls but would interfere with the ability to form aggregates 16245042. Despite of their names, |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d "| and |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e "| are actually chlorins rather than bacteriochlorins. All three are usually found with an unsaturated farnesyl tail rather than phytyl tails |CITS: [2350541][Borrego99]|, although exceptions have been reported. In chlorosomes of |FRAME: TAX-191412| (but not |FRAME: TAX-1106| |CITS: [Risch79][3442679]|) all three types of bacteriochlorophyll appear in several forms with different degrees of methylation at the C-8 2 and C-12 1 carbons |CITS: [12656478][14610639]|. The variety in methylation is depicted in the structure shown here by the R groups. In general, pimgents produced by cultures grown at lower light intensities are more highly methylated at the C-8 2 position than pigments produced by cells of the same organism grown at higher light intensities. Different methylation states result in different aggregation properties and light absorbance of the chlorosome, and thus methylation is used as an adaptation to altering envireonmental conditions. Most of the green sulfur bacteria growing in stratified lakes contain CPD-9093, and species containing |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "| are rarely found vanGemerden95. Some examples for bacteria that possess |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "| are the green sulfur bacteria |FRAME: TAX-1092| and |FRAME: TAX-1097| and the green filamentous bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1108|.

Compound.name: a phosphatidylcholine
Synonyms: a (3- sn -phosphatidyl)choline // a 1,2-diacyl- sn -glycero-3-phosphocholine // a choline phosphatide // an L-alpha-phosphatidylcholine // lecithin // a phosphatidyl- N -trimethylethanolamine
Comment: |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE "A phosphatidylcholine"| is |FRAME: Phosphoglycerides| composed of a |FRAME: GLYCEROL| backbone esterified to |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-CHOLINE| and two |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "fatty acids"|. Phosphatidylcholine is a major component of eukaryotic cell membranes, in which it accounts for 40-60% of total phospholipids. It is also found in an estimated 1015% of bacterial taxa, and especially in bacterial symbionts and pathogens of eukaryotes. Phosphatidylcholine is often referred to by the name lecithin, obtained from ancient Greek for egg yolk (lekithos), from which it was originally isolated. Compound.name: a glycogen
Comment: Glycogen is a highly branched glucose polymer found in archaea, bacteria, and eukaryotes. It resembles plant-produced |FRAME: Starch starch| and is sometimes called "animal starch". Glycogen serves multiple functions, including energy reserve, osmotic regulation, blood glucose homeostasis, and pH maintenance. Glycogen is formed of small chains of 8 to 12 glucose molecules linked together by alpha (1->4) bonds. These small chains, also known as |FRAME: Maltodextrins maltodextrins|, are in turn linked together by alpha (1->6) bonds. The alpha-1,4 linkages make up approximately 95% of the total molecule. The alpha-1,6 branches accounts for 7–10% of the linkages and are evenly distributed within the glycogen particle. Since each chain (with the exception of the outer unbranched chains) supports two branches, glycogen particles grow spherically by adding tiers (a tier corresponds to the spherical space separating two consecutive branches from all chains located at similar distance from the center of the particle). Two structural levels of glycogen particles have been reported, which are tightly associated with their physiological functions: small quasi-spherical beta particles, as found in muscle cells, and large rosette-shaped alpha particles, as found in liver cells. The diameter of beta particles normally range from 10 to 50 nm, with an average at around 20—30 nm. The beta particles can stick together to form large alpha particles with diameters up to 300 nm |CITS: [20196533][31244022][33996916]|. Two types of alpha particles have been observed: fragile and dense particles, which comprise large and dense beta particles with long average chain length, and stable light particles, which comprise smaller, compact beta particles with short average chain length 31244022. Mathematical modelling predicts a maximal size for the beta particle beyond which further growth is impossible, as there would not be sufficient space for interaction of the chains with the catalytic sites of glycogen metabolism enzymes. The predicted upper limit is a particle consisting of 12 tiers corresponding to a 42 nm maximal diameter and including about 55,000 glucose residues. 36% of this total number rests in the outer (unbranched) shell and is thus readily accessible to glycogen catabolism without the need for debranching 12179957. Although glycogen and starch are two distinct physical states of the same type of storage polysaccharide, starch is solid semi-crystalline while glycogen particles are entirely hydrosoluble 21220783.

Most of them are glycoconjugates containing one or more sugars attached at different positions of the angucyclinone framework 11026547.

Compound.name: a 5,10-methenyltetrahydrofolate
Comment: |FRAME: THF-GLU-N Tetrahydrofolate| (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are required in a variety of reactions in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, where they act as carriers of one-carbon units in various oxidation states. These one-carbon units are utilized in the biosynthesis of several cellular components, including glycine, methionine, formylmethionine, thymidylate, pantothenate and purine nucleotides. During folate biosynthesis (as described in FOLSYN-PWY) the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.12|, adds a glutamate residue to |FRAME: 7-8-DIHYDROPTEROATE|, resulting in |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE|, also known as H 2 PteGlu 1 . This molecule in turn is reduced by EC-1.5.1.3 (FolA) to |FRAME: THF| (H 4 PteGlu 1 , or tetrahydrofolate), which can be converted to several other folate molecules 11501996. Most folate molecules are modified in cells by successive additions of glutamate residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-gamma-glutamates). The glutamate residues are added by an amide linkage to the gamma-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are not the normal amide bonds they are not hydrolyzed by peptidases or proteases, which are specific for alpha-carboxyl-linked peptide bonds. The addition of glutamyl residues probably occurs after the reduction of newly synthesized dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and its conversion to other tetrahydrofolate derivatives. The glutamylation of folate residues serves several goals: it prevents the efflux of folates out of the cell, it increases the binding of folate cofactors to the enzymes of folate interconversion and biosynthesis, and in mammals, it allows the accumulation of folates in the mitochondria, which is required for glycine synthesis 10598551. This class stands for 5,10-methenyltetrahydrofolates with an unspecified number of glutamate residues.

Compound.name: a melleolide
Comment: The |FRAME: Melleolides melleolides| are a large family of aryl ester secondary metabolites produced by species of the basidiomycete genus |FRAME: TAX-47424|, which are composed of an |FRAME: CPD-47| moiety esterified to a tricyclic sesquiterpene (|FRAME: CPD-14796|) alcohol |CITS: [Midland82][Donnelly82]|. Both |FRAME: CPD-47| and protoilludane derivatives have been described from numerous other organisms |CITS: [11281843][12714063][19666480]|, but these two elements are combined into a single entity only in the melleolides, which are not found outside the |FRAME: TAX-47424|. Biosynthesis of the sesquiterpene protoilludene moiety is achieved by cyclization of |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.2.3.135|, and results in the tricyclic |FRAME: CPD-14796| backbone 21148562. In |FRAME: TAX-47429|, |FRAME: CPD-47| is biosynthesized by a seven-domain polyketide synthase whose terminal thioesterase domain also catalyzes the coupling of |FRAME: CPD-47| to protoilludene-based alcohols 23993460. Modifications of the basic structure include hydroxylation at various positions of the sesquiterpene, oxidation of the primary alcohol at C-1 to an aldehyde or carboxy group, shift or reduction of the cyclohexene double bond, methyl ether formation at O-5', and chlorination at C-6' 26655762, resulting in excess of 60 melleolide analogs and making the melleolides one of the most diverse groups of fungal natural products Misiek12. Various melleolides have been shown to inhibit microbial growth |CITS: [Arnone86][10805573]| and display phytotoxicity 1418682. The antifungal activity has been linked to the position of the double bond within the sesquiterpene moiety 24906293. Melleolides have also been reported to have cytotoxic effects on human cancer cell lines by decreasing DNA synthesis 21376582.

Compound.name: a lipid A
Comment: Lipid A is a lipid component of the |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides "lipopolysaccharides"| (LPS) of Gram-negative bacteria. Its hydrophobic nature allows it to anchor the LPS to the outer membrane. Lipid A consists of two glucosamine units attached by a beta(1->6) linkage and decorated with four to seven acyl chains and one or two phosphate groups. Up to four acyl chains, often with a beta hydroxy group and usually 10 to 18 carbons in length, are attached directly to the glucosamine sugars at positions N-2 and O-3 (and N'-2 and O'-3, respectively), while additional acyl chains are attached to the beta hydroxy groups of some of those primary acyl chains. Phosphate groups can be attached at position O-1, O'-4, or both. Many variations are found in the structures of lipid A molecules. Further modifications are commonly observed, such as the addition or removal of phosphate groups (see |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.29|, |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.M9|, and |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.M11|), the addition of |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-ETHANOLAMINE| (see |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.43|, |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.42|, and |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.M9|), the addition of |FRAME: 4-AMINO-4-DEOXY-L-ARABINOSE| units (see |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.43|), and further addition or removal of fatty acyl units (see |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.251| and |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.77|). Many bacterial species produce lipid A molecules that contain |FRAME: CPD-24440| (see |FRAME: PWY-8273|). Since the fully acylated lipid A is assembled only when attached to the core oligosaccharide, a "stand alone" lipid A, as depicted here, does not occur naturally.

Compound.name: a b-series ganglioside
Comment: About the nomenclature of gangliosides Ganglioside naming is somewhat complex. Two ganglioside nomenclature systems are currently in use. The most commonly used is a short-hand nomenclature suggested by Svennerholm, which was initially based on the migration order of |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio-series"| gangliosides in chromatography 14066623. The more comprehensive system formulated by IUPAC 9826173 is applied much less frequently. A typical ganglioside name using the old system looks like |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"|. The first letter refers to the glycosphingolipid series. For example, the "G" stands for the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|. The next letter describes the number of sialic acid residues: (A = 0, M =1, D = 2, T = 3, Q = 4, P = 5, H = 6, S = 7). The following number describes the number of the non-sialic residues, and is derived in a rather complex manner. It was initially assumed that the number of such residues does not exceed 5. The number in the name was calculated as (5 - the number of uncharged carbohydrates). In addition, several sub-series of gangliosides have been defined based on the number of sialic acids attached to the galactose residue of the lacosylceramide core. If no sialic residues are present at that position, the compounds belong to the |FRAME: 0-Series-Ganglioside "0-series |. Those with one sialic acid at that position are named the |FRAME: A-Series-Gangliosides a-series |, those with two sialic acids belong to the |FRAME: B-Series-Gangliosides b-series |, and so on. |FRAME: C-Series-Gangliosides "C-series"| or higher gangliosides are rare in adult mammals and birds, but are abundant in fish and amphibians. Confusingly, GM1b and GD1c are both 0-series gangliosides, despite having a b and c in their names. So, for example, the |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"| is named as follows: G = belongs to the ganglio series, Q = 4 sialic acids, 1 = 4 non-sialic residues, and b = belongs to the b-series, meaning two of the sialic acids are attached to the inner galactose.

Quinones are conjugated but not aromatic. A classic example of a quinone is |FRAME: P-BENZOQUINONE|. Quinones are commonly named with a prefix that indicates the parent aromatic hydrocarbon (for example, "benzo-" for benzene, "naphtho-" for naphthalene, and "anthra-" for anthracene) with a "-quinone" suffix. Several types of quinones serve as electron acceptors in electron transport chains. Those quinones are usually prenylated with a lipid-soluble isoprenyl tail that anchors them in the membrane lipid bilayer. Quinones can carry two electrons, and when fully reduced they are referred to as |FRAME: Reduced-Quinones quinols|. The addition of a single H atom to a quinone results in formation of a free radical called |FRAME: Semiquinones|. Many quinone derivatives often have other biological activities, such as |FRAME: CPD-11501 "vitamin K"|.
