Compound.name: a penicillin
Comment: Penicillins are medically important |FRAME: Beta-Lactams "beta-lactam"| antibiotics biosynthesized as end products by certain filamentous fungi, including |FRAME: TAX-5076| and |FRAME: TAX-162425|. Β-Lactam antibiotics inhibit the formation of peptidoglycan cross-links in the bacterial cell wall by the irreversible binding of their four-membered beta-lactam ring to the so-called |FRAME: Penicillin-Binding-Proteins "penicillin binding proteins"| (PBPs). The PBPs are proteins that contain a D,D-peptidase domain, most commonly used for hydrolyzing the |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| bond found in the pentapetide moiety of peptidoglycans. Since the beta-lactam moiety of |FRAME: PENICILLIN "penicillins"| is similar to the D-Ala-D-Ala structure, these enzymes bind penicillin irreversibly and become inactive. Several groups of enzymes belong to this family - carboxypeptidases, transpeptidases, and endopeptidases. The carboxypeptidase remove the terminal |FRAME: D-ALANINE| from the pentapeptide, the transpeptidase form crosslinks between the pentapeptides of adjacent glycan threads, and the endopeptidases hydrolyze these crosslinks. This irrevesible binding prevents the enzyme from catalyzing the formation of these cross-links, resulting in a defective cell wall and cell death. Penicillin antibiotics were the first drugs that were effective against many previously serious diseases, such as syphilis, and infections caused by staphylococci and streptococci. They are still widely used today, although more and more types of bacteria have acquired resistance.

They have been used in a variety of agricultural and urban environments around the world. Due to their relatively high water solubilities some phenylurea herbicides and their metabolites have been detected as contaminants of groundwater, streams, lakes, and seawater in different areas worldwide. In addition, ecotoxicological data show that phenylurea herbicides and their main metabolites are environmental hazards and are carcinogenic to animals and humans |CITS: [2279779][8402576]|.

Compound.name: a vitamin B6
Comment: |FRAME: Vitamins-B6 Vitamin B6| is a group term for PYRIDOXAL (PL), PYRIDOXINE (PN), PYRIDOXAMINE (PM) and their 5'-phosphorylated derivatives PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE (PLP), PYRIDOXINE-5P (PNP) and PYRIDOXAMINE-5P (PMP), which are also referred to as vitamers. Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) is the biochemically active form, and is an essential cofactor in all living systems 7748903. It plays an important role in amino acid and carbohydrate metabolism and has been implicated in singlet oxygen resistance 10687384. Most bacteria, archaea, fungi, and plants synthesize PLP in a single reaction, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6466|, although some bacteria, such as E. coli , use a longer, more complex pathway (|FRAME: PYRIDOXSYN-PWY|) |CITS: [9696782][12896974]|. Animals do not synthesize this compound, making it an essential nutrient in their diet. PLP is an essential cofactor of numerous metabolic enzymes, predominantly in amino acid metabolism. It is one of the most versatile cofactors and participates in transamination, decarboxylation, racemization, Calpha-Cbeta cleavage and alpha-beta elimination reactions. In humans this vitamin has a role in numerous functions ranging from modulation of hormone function to potent antioxidant activity.

Compound.name: beta-carrageenose
Comment: |FRAME: Carrageenans Carrageenans| and |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| are sulfated polysaccharides that are extracted from sea weeds belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-2763| (red algae), mainly from |FRAME: TAX-2769|, and species from the |FRAME: TAX-31444| and |FRAME: TAX-33664| genera. They are laid out in the cell wall at a high density and can constitute up to 50% of the algae dry mass. The basic units of |FRAME: Carrageenans carrageenans| are repeats of alternating alpha-1,3-linked D-galactose and beta-1,4-linked D-galactose units, which are often substituted by sulfate. Carrageenans are classified according to the number and the position of sulfated ester 1367970. In |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| the alpha-1,3-linked galactose units are modified by having a 3,6-anhydro bridge. These bridges, which form a double helix during aggregation, are responsible for the gelation that is typical to these compounds. Despite this distinction, carrageenoses are often referred to as carrageenans. The three most industrially exploited carrageenans, namely, |FRAME: kappa-Carrageenan|, |FRAME: iota-Carrageenan| and |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan|, are distinguished by the presence of one, two or three ester-sulfate groups per repeating disaccharide unit respectively. |FRAME: beta-Carrageenan| is the only carrageenose polymer that is not sulfated.

Compound.name: xanthan
Comment: |FRAME: Xanthan Xanthan| is an exopolysaccharide produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-339| and related species. Because of its rheological properties, including high viscosity and pseudo-plasticity, and stability in extreme conditions, xanthan gum has been used in food, agriculture and industry as an emulsifying, thickening or suspending agent. It was approved for use in foods in 1968. Xanthan gum has been implicated as the pathogenic substance causing black rot in crucifers 9144435. The polymer is composed of repeating pentasaccharide units with the structure of a beta-1,4-linked D-glucose backbone with trisaccharide side chains composed of mannose-(beta-1,4)-glucuronic acid-(beta-1,2)-mannose attached to alternate glucose residues in the backbone by alpha-1,3 linkages 1212669. The terminal repeat unit is anchored to the cytoplasmic membrane by an undecaprenyldiphosphate lipid carrier, and assembley of the polymer occurs while anchored. Acetyl and pyruvyl residues are often added to one of the mannose units as non-carbohydrate decorations.

Compound.name: a mercapturate

In contrast, sphinganine, 4-hydroxysphinganine, and 4-hydroxy-8-sphingenine are the prevalent long-chain bases in plants. The acyl chain of plant ceramides contains alpha-hydroxylated very long chain fatty acids. The plant ceramide (IV) in MetaCyc represents plant ceramides with 4-hydroxy-8-sphingenine as the long-chain base.

Compound.name: a pyranoside

Compound.name: a 2,3,4-saturated fatty acyl CoA
Comment: This class describes ACYL-COA that do not contain any double bonds in the 2, 3, and 4 positions. Acyl-CoAs are oxoacids that have been activated by |FRAME: CO-A|. This class includes the following sub-classes: |FRAME: Short-Chain-234-Saturated-acyl-CoAs "Short-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "2,3,4-saturated fatty acids with aliphatic chains shorter than 6 carbons"|. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-234-Saturated-acyl-CoAs "Medium-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids with aliphatic chains of 6-12 carbons"|. |FRAME: Long-Chain-234-Saturated-acyl-CoAs "Long-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Long-Chain-234-Saturated-Fatty-Acids "2,3,4-saturated fatty acids with aliphatic chains of 13-22 carbons"|. |FRAME: Very-long-Chain-234-Saturated-acyl-CoAs "Very-long-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids with aliphatic chains of 23 carbons or longer"|.

Compound.name: an arabinoglucuronoxylan
Comment: |FRAME: Glucuronoarabinoxylans Glucuronoarabinoxylans| (GAX) and |FRAME: Arabinoglucuronoxylans arabinoglucuronoxylans| (AGX) are components of |FRAME: Hemicelluloses| that have a similar structure - a beta(1->4)-D-xylopyranose backbone with single 4- O -methylglucuronate and alpha-L-arabinofuranose residues attached at position 2 and 3, respectively. The AGX type polymers occur in appreciable quantity in coniferous species, although it is usually not the dominant hemicellulosic component (an exception is the hemicellulose of the tropic conifer |FRAME: TAX-1030197| Bochicchio03). They are also the dominant hemicelluloses in the cell walls of lignified supporting tissues of grasses and cereals.

Compound.name: a glucosaminoglycan

Comment: |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| (often referred to as simply linolenate) is a polyunsaturated fatty acid (18:3) that is an important constituent of plant membranes. It is also known as an ω-3 fatty acid, referring to the position of the first double bond from the methyl end of the fatty acid. Seed oils are the richest sources of |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID|, especially those of rapeseed (canola), soybeans, walnuts, flaxseed (Linseed), perilla, chia and hemp. It is also common in the lipids that are found in thylakoid membranes in the green leaves of broadleaf plants, and in cyanobacteria and algae |CITS:[4621688][414660]|. |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| is an essential fatty acid for animals, and is considered an essential dietary requirement for all mammals. Like other fatty acids, |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| is rarely found in its free form. It is usually found either as |FRAME: LINOLENOYL-COA| or |FRAME: Alpha-linolenoyl-groups "incorporated into a lipid"|.

Synonyms: beta-D-galactosyl-1,3- N -acetyl-alpha-D-galactosaminyl-R // glycoprotein D-galactosyl-1,3- N -acetyl-alpha-D-galactosamine // beta-D-galactosyl-1,3- N -acetyl-D-galactosaminyl-R // beta-D-galactosyl-(1->3)- N -acetyl-alpha-D-galactosaminyl-L-seryl/L-threonyl-[protein] // T antigen

Compound.name: a cardiac glycoside
Comment: Cardiac glycosides are plant-made compounds (mostly by members of the |FRAME: TAX-4163| genus, or Foxgloves) that have beneficial effects over patients with cardiac failure. The treatment of congestive heart failure (dropsy), among other ailments like tuberculosis, by the use of Foxglove is mentioned in writings as early as 1250 A. D., when the Welsh Physicians of Myddva collected foxglove as one of their many herbs and included it in their remedies. 28561136. The cardiac glycosides are composed of two structural features: a sugar moiety that may contain one or more saccharides, and a steroid aglycone. Cardiac glycosides having a terminal glucose are called primary glycosides whereas those lacking such a sugar are termed secondary glycosides. There are two classes of cardiac glycosides differing by the group attached at the 17-position of the aglycone: the |FRAME: Cardenolide-Glycosides "cardenolides"|, which have a five-membered unsaturated lactone ring (but-2-en-4-olide ring) and the |FRAME: Bufadienolide-Glycosides bufadienolides|, which have a six membered doubly unsaturated lactone ring (penta-2,4-dien-5-olide ring). The steroid nucleus of the cardiac glycosides have a unique configuration: rings A/B and C/D are cis - fused while rings B/C are trans - fused. The nucleus has beta configured hydroxyls at the positions C-3 and C-14, and many compounds have additional hydroxyl groups at positions 12 and 16. The sugars found in the glycoside moiety range from common hexoses and pentoses (such as |FRAME: D-Glucose|, |FRAME: L-rhamnose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-Xylose|) to very uncommon sugars, some of which have only been found in cardiac glycosides (e.g. |FRAME: D-quinovopyranose|, |FRAME: CPD-22597|, |FRAME: D-Digitoxose|, |FRAME: CPD-22572|, |FRAME: D-Olivose|, and |FRAME: D-Fucoses|). While the mechanism whereby cardiac glycosides cause a positive inotropic effect and electrophysiologic changes of the hurt is still not completely clear, the most widely accepted mechanism involves the ability of cardiac glycosides to inhibit the membrane bound Na+/K+-ATPase pump responsible for Na+/K+ exchange KAUTE08.

Compound.name: a [glycerolipid]-oleate
Comment: |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD Oleate| (oleic acid) is the first unsaturated fatty acid that is generated from the saturated fatty acids produced by the fatty acid synthase. It's name is derived from the olive tree, since it makes up 55-80% of olive oil. Oleate synthesis occurs with membrane-bound systems. The desaturase enzymes that produce oleate have been isolated from fungi, yeast, and mammalian liver and found to be specific for |FRAME: STEAROYL-COA|. In plants, on the other hand, oleate is produced via |FRAME: Stearoyl-ACPs|, an acyl-carrier-protein bound intermediate 4831331. |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD Oleate| has also been reported from a few bacteria, including the obligate anaerobic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1520| and the saprophytic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1377|. Bacterial biosynthesis of |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| does not require oxygen and involves elongation of |FRAME: CPD-17289| |CITS: [14498314][5554109][6886674][12583708][23972938]|. Like other fatty acids, |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| is rarely found in its free form. It is usually found as either |FRAME: Oleoyl-ACPs oleoyl-[acp]|, |FRAME: OLEOYL-COA|, or |FRAME: Oleoyl-lipid "incorporated into a lipid"|.

Compound.name: a linoleate-derived metabolite
Comment: The oxidation of the polyunsaturated fatty acids |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID|, |FRAME: CPD-8120|, |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|, |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID|, |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE icosapentaenoate| (EPA) and |FRAME: CPD-10244 docosahexaenoate| (DHA) results a wide array of lipid metabolites, including (but not limited to) |FRAME: Prostaglandins prostaglandins|, |FRAME: Thromboxanes thromboxanes|, |FRAME: Leukotrienes leukotrienes|, |FRAME: Lipoxins lipoxins|, |FRAME: Resolvins resolvins|, and |FRAME: Eoxins eoxins|. The best-studied of these are the compounds derived from C20 acids, which are known as |FRAME: Icosanoids icosanoids|. Many of these compounds act as signaling molecules that play prominent roles in many physiological processes. In mammals they participate in the regulation of many key biological processes in the cardiovascular, renal, reproductive and other systems, with a particular important role in inflammation.

Compound.name: a bryostatin
Comment: The |FRAME: Bryostatins bryostatins| are a family of structurally related macrolide compounds originally found in the bryozoan |FRAME: TAX-10212|. The |FRAME: TAX-10205| are marine colonial filter-feeders, with each member (polypide) enclosed in a separate unit (zooecium). |FRAME: CPD-21475 "Bryostatin 1"|, the first member to have its structure reported, was identified from samples collected from the California coast. The authors noted its anticancer activity, which they described as "remarkable" Pettit82. Other samples, collected in the Gulf of Mexico, the Gulf of California, and other locations, afforded other members. Currently 20 members of the bryostatin family are known Pettit91. In 1990 it was suggested that the bryostatins may be produced by endosymbiotic bacteria Anthoni90. The presence of such endosymbionts was confirmed in 1997, and based on small-subunit rRNA gene sequence the organisms were found to belong to a new genus within the gamma-proteobacteria. They were named |FRAME: TAX-62101| 9361448. The bacteria cannot be cultivated outside the host; however, the discovery of genes encoding polyketide synthases in the bacterial DNA provided proof for a bacterial origin of the bryostatins 11571152. Most, but not all, of the bryostatins pharmacological effects are attributed to their interaction with the |FRAME: Diacyl-sn-Glycerols diacylglycerol| binding site of the C-1, C-19 and C-26 regulatory domain of |FRAME: EC-2.7.11.13| 20971628. In addition, bryostatins can function as very potent immunostimulants (in 24033119). More than 30 clinical trials have been conducted with |FRAME: CPD-21475| in monotherapy or in combination with clinically used cytotoxic drugs, testing its efficacy against different tumor types such as sarcoma, melanoma, ovaria, cervical, neck and head carcinoma, esophageal, gastric, pancreatic, renal cell carcinoma, as well as a variety of leukemias, e.g., chronic lymphocytic leukemia, non-Hodgkin s lymphoma, or multiple myeloma. However, phase II studies of |FRAME: CPD-21475| have failed to demonstrate any clinically meaningful activity, and bryostatin has not progressed to phase III clinical trials as a cancer treatment Newman12. On the other hand, |FRAME: CPD-21475| has been shown to reverse synaptic loss and facilitate synaptic maturation in animal models of Alzheimer's disease, Fragile X, stroke, and other neurological disorders. Advanced Alzheimer patients treated with bryostatin demonstrated return of major functions such as swallowing, vocalization, and word recognition, and currently Phase II clinical trials are conducted with |FRAME: CPD-21475| as a potential treatment for Alzheimer's disease 28482641.

Compound.name: an A antigen
Synonyms: an A histo-blood group antigen // a histo-blood group substance A // an N -acetyl-alpha-D-galactosaminyl-(1,3)-[alpha-L-fucosyl-(1,2)]-beta-D-galactosyl-R // a [glycoprotein]- N -acetyl-alpha-D-galactosaminyl-(1,3)-[alpha-L-fucosyl-(1,2)]-D-galactose
Comment: The A antigen is an oligosaccharide that decorates proteins on the surface of red blood cells in people with A blood type. It is generated from |FRAME: H-antigen|, which is found in people with O blood type, by the attachement of an |FRAME: CPD-12557| residue by a 1,3 linkage to one of the beta-D-galactosyl residues of the H antigen. People with AB blood type contain both |FRAME: A-antigen "A antigens"| and |FRAME: B-antigen "B antigens"|. The majority of the A, B and H antigens are linked to the ends of long polylactosamine chains attached mainly to band 3 protein (encoded by SLC4A1), the anion exchange protein of the red blood cells. A minor fraction of the antigens is attached to a ceramide moiety, forming neutral glycosphingolipids.

Compound.name: a pyrimidine nucleoside
Comment: Nucleosides are glycosylamines consisting of |FRAME: Bases| bound to a |FRAME: CPD0-1110 ribose| or |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE| sugar via a beta-glycosidic linkage. The nucleosides are called |FRAME: Ribonucleosides ribonucleosides| when the sugar is |FRAME: CPD0-1110 ribose|, and |FRAME: Deoxy-Ribonucleosides deoxyribonucleosides| when it is |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE|. Common |FRAME: Ribonucleosides ribonucleosides| include |FRAME: CYTIDINE|, |FRAME: URIDINE|, |FRAME: ADENOSINE|, |FRAME: GUANOSINE| and |FRAME: INOSINE|. Examples of |FRAME: Deoxy-Ribonucleosides deoxyribonucleosides| include |FRAME: THYMIDINE| and |FRAME: DEOXYADENOSINE|. When nucleosides are phosphorylated on the sugar's primary alcohol group, the resulting phosphonucleosides are called |FRAME: Nucleotides nucleotides|. Pyrimidine is a heterocyclic aromatic compound similar to benzene, containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3 of the ring. The name pyrimidines is also used for compounds derived from the basic pyrimidine compound, including three of the nucleosides found in nucleic acids, namely |FRAME: CYTIDINE|, THYMIDINE, and |FRAME: URIDINE|.

Compound.name: a glycoside
Comment: A glycoside is any molecule in which a sugar group is bonded through its anomeric carbon to a non-acyl group via a glycosidic bond. Glycosides can be linked by a C-O bond (an O-glycoside), C-N bond (a glycosylamine), C-S bond (a thioglycoside) or a C-C bond (a C-glycoside). When the sugar is bound to a non-carbohydrate moiety, the sugar group is known as the glycone and the non-sugar group as the aglycone or genin part of the glycoside.

Compound.name: a brassinosteroid
Comment: |FRAME: Brassinosteroids Brassinosteroid|s are steroidal phytohormones that regulate various important physiological and developmental processes, such as cell elongation and division, pollen fertility, photomorphogenesis, differentiation of vascular elements, and stress resistance |CITS: [16056912][Mandava88][15012241]|. Brassinosteroids, which have structural similarity to |FRAME: ECDYSONE|, the molting hormone of insects, are C 27 , C 28 and C 29 steroids depending on their C-24 alkyl substituents. More than 70 free, naturally occurring brassinosteroids have been identified in plants. The C 28 brassinosteroid |FRAME: CPD-697| (BL) is the most biologically active and together with its C 28 congeners is distributed widely in the plant kingdom 15012241.

Compound.name: a penam
Comment: This compound class stands for |FRAME: Lactams lactams| in which the amide bond is contained within a four-membered ring, which includes the amide nitrogen and the carbonyl carbon. beta-Lactam compounds imitate the naturally occurring |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| substrate for the group of enzymes known as penicillin binding proteins (PBPs), which cross-link the peptidoglycan in bacterial cell wall, and thus act as powerful antibiotics 6109324. Naturally occurring |FRAME: Beta-Lactams "beta-lactam antibiotics"| are classified into several groups according to their chemical structure: In |FRAME: Monolactams monolactams| the beta-lactam ring is not fused to another ring. This class includes compounds such as the |FRAME: Nocardicins nocardicins| 3427723 and the |FRAME: Monobactams monobactams| 3909315. In |FRAME: Penams penams| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a saturated five atom ring (a 4:5 structure). Penams contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring (for example, the |FRAME: PENICILLIN penicillins|) 6335599. Related classes include the |FRAME: Carbapenams carbapenams|, which contain a carbon atom in that position 12890666, and the |FRAME: Clavams oxopenams| (also known as clavams), which contain an oxygen atom at that position (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9261|) 3304182. |FRAME: Penems Penems| are molecues similar to penams in which the five atom ring is unsaturated at positions 2-3. Similarly, penems contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring, while |FRAME: Carbapenems carbapenems| contains a carbon atom in that position 16413506. In |FRAME: Cephams cephams| and |FRAME: Cephems cephems| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a six-atom ring (a 4:6 strcuture) that contains a sulfur atom at position 1. In cephams the ring is saturated, while cephems have an unsaturated bond at positions 3-4 |CITS: [1164170][12722308]|. 1-Oxocephams/1-oxacephems conain an oxygen atom at position 1 |CITS: [11671696][11078187]|.

Compound.name: a glycosaminoglycan
Comment: Glycosaminoglycans (also known as mucopolysaccharides) are important components of connective tissues. They are composed of long unbranched polysaccharides consisting of a repeating disaccharide unit. The repeating units consist of an N -acetyl-hexosamine and a hexose or hexuronic acid, either or both of which are often sulfated. Members of the glycosaminoglycan family vary in the type of hexosamine, hexose or hexuronic acid unit they contain (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-12521|, |FRAME: CPD-12515|, galactose, CPD-12557, |FRAME: CPD-12541|). Glycosaminoglycans are divided into four main classes: |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates| and |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate|; |FRAME: HEPARIN| and |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate|; |FRAME: Hyaluronan|; and |FRAME: KERATAN-6-SULFATE "keratan sulfate"|. With the exception of hyaluronan, the polysaccharide chains are linked covalently at the reducing end to a core protein through an O -glycosidic linkage to a serine residue. The modified proteins are known as |FRAME: Proteoglycans proteoglycans|. Most glycosaminoglycans are attached via a specific tetrasaccharide known as the |FRAME: GlcA-Gal-Gal-Xyl-Proteins "glycosaminoglycan-protein linkage region"|.

Compound.name: chitin
Comment: |FRAME: CHITIN Chitin| is a polymer of repeating units of beta-(1,4)-linked |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| (GlcNAc) n . It may be the second most abundant biopolymer in the world, after cellulose. It is the main component of the cell walls of fungi, the exoskeletons of arthropods such as crustaceans and the insects, the radula of mollusks, and the beaks of the cephalopods. Chitin polymers have a high degree of polymerization and are insoluble in water 20559485.

Compound.name: an oxopenam
Comment: This compound class stands for |FRAME: Lactams lactams| in which the amide bond is contained within a four-membered ring, which includes the amide nitrogen and the carbonyl carbon. beta-Lactam compounds imitate the naturally occurring |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| substrate for the group of enzymes known as penicillin binding proteins (PBPs), which cross-link the peptidoglycan in bacterial cell wall, and thus act as powerful antibiotics 6109324. Naturally occurring |FRAME: Beta-Lactams "beta-lactam antibiotics"| are classified into several groups according to their chemical structure: In |FRAME: Monolactams monolactams| the beta-lactam ring is not fused to another ring. This class includes compounds such as the |FRAME: Nocardicins nocardicins| 3427723 and the |FRAME: Monobactams monobactams| 3909315. In |FRAME: Penams penams| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a saturated five atom ring (a 4:5 structure). Penams contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring (for example, the |FRAME: PENICILLIN penicillins|) 6335599. Related classes include the |FRAME: Carbapenams carbapenams|, which contain a carbon atom in that position 12890666, and the |FRAME: Clavams oxopenams| (also known as clavams), which contain an oxygen atom at that position (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9261|) 3304182. |FRAME: Penems Penems| are molecues similar to penams in which the five atom ring is unsaturated at positions 2-3. Similarly, penems contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring, while |FRAME: Carbapenems carbapenems| contains a carbon atom in that position 16413506. In |FRAME: Cephams cephams| and |FRAME: Cephems cephems| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a six-atom ring (a 4:6 strcuture) that contains a sulfur atom at position 1. In cephams the ring is saturated, while cephems have an unsaturated bond at positions 3-4 |CITS: [1164170][12722308]|. 1-Oxocephams/1-oxacephems conain an oxygen atom at position 1 |CITS: [11671696][11078187]|.

Compound.name: a mycolate
Comment: Mycolic acids are the hallmark of the cell envelope of |FRAME: TAX-1773| and related species and genera. They comprise a homologous series of C60-C90 (2 R )-alkyl-(3 R )-hydroxy very long-chain fatty acids, and are found as either esters of |FRAME: Arabinogalactan| or as free lipids in the form of trehalose dimycolate (TDM). Both forms contribute to forming the two leaflets of the mycobacterial outer membrane, also called the mycomembrane, which protects the organism from antibiotics and the host's immune system |CITS: [15653820][17555433][15353567]|. There is a significant variability in the structure of mycolic acids among different species. Acids from |FRAME: TAX-1716| species contain 22-38 carbon atoms, |FRAME: TAX-697025| and |FRAME: TAX-697025| spp. contain 30-36, |FRAME: TAX-37914| spp. contain 34-38, |FRAME: TAX-1827| spp. contain 34-52 in, |FRAME: TAX-1817| spp. contain 46-60, |FRAME: TAX-2053 Gordonia | spp. contain 46-66, |FRAME: TAX-2060| spp. contain 64-78 , |FRAME: TAX-1763| spp. contain 60-90, and |FRAME: TAX-286801| spp. contain up to 100 carbon atoms 24374164. The acids are formed by a Claisen-type condensation of two components - the meromycolic chain and a fatty acid. The meromycolic chain of |FRAME: TAX-1773| typically incorporates a hydroxy group at C-1, a cyclopropyl ring fused onto the C-16/C-17 bond (at either a cis or a trans configuration), a methoxyl or oxo group at C-35, and a methyl group at C-36. The modifications and their positions may change among strains and species. Several structural classes of mycolic acids exist. In |FRAME: TAX-1773| the most apolar ones, known as alpha-mycolic acids, contain 74-80 carbon atoms (out of which 22-26 carbons are located in the fatty acid moiety and the rest on the mero-chain) and generally two double bonds (that can be in either cis - or trans -configuration) or two cis -cyclopropyl groups located in the meromycolic chain. The cyclopropane rings are believed to protect the organism from oxidative stress 15653820. alpha-Mycolic acids usually comprise more than 70 percent of the total mycolic acids in the cell. Other classes are defined by additional oxygen functions located in the distal part of the meromycolic chain, and include keto-, methoxy-, wax ester-, epoxy-, and hydroxy-types. In |FRAME: TAX-1773| the oxygenated mycolic acids (keto-, methoxy-, and hydroxy-types) contain ~84-88 carbon atoms, and are thus four to six carbons longer than the alpha-mycolic acids from the same strains. The biosynthesis of mycolic acids is described in |FRAME: PWYG-321|.

Compound.name: a gamma-butyrolactone
Comment: The Gram-positive, soil-inhabiting, filamentous bacteria of the genus |FRAME: TAX-1883| use a number of chemical compounds including |FRAME: Gamma-Butyrolactones "gamma-butyrolactones"|, |FRAME: MMFs "methylenomycin furans"|, |FRAME: CPD-19905|, and |FRAME: Butenolides "gamma-butenolides"|, as chemical signalling molecules or microbial hormones, which, together with their specific receptors, regulate morphological and/or physiological differentiation 2268871. At least 60% of Streptomyces species appear to produce gamma-butyrolactones, although (as of 2011), only a small number of which have been identified 21090718. Based on their structures, these gamma-butyrolactones have been classified into three types: the |FRAME: A-factor-type-lactones "A-factor type"|, |FRAME: Virginiae-butanolides "virginiae butanolide (VB) type"|, and |FRAME: IM-2-type-lactones "IM-2 type"|, all of which share the cyclic butanolide skeleton |CITS: [14523609][19778723]|.

Compound.name: a [glycerolipid]-crepenynate
Comment: |FRAME: CREPENYNATE Crepenynate| (crepenynic acid) is a fatty acid with an 18-carbon chain containing a cis double bond at position 9 and a triple bond at position 12. Like other fatty acids, |FRAME: CREPENYNATE| is rarely found in its free form. It is usually found |FRAME: Glycerolipid-crepenynate "incorporated into a lipid"|. |FRAME: CREPENYNATE Crepenynate| makes up to 70% of the fatty acids in triacylglycerol from the seed oil of the plant |FRAME: TAX-72610| Banas97.

Compound.name: a phenylpropanoid
Comment: The phenylpropanoids are a large family of compounds, mostly found in plants, that are synthesized from |FRAME: PHE| and, to a lesser extent, |FRAME: TYR|. The pathway that starts from |FRAME: PHE| forms |FRAME: COUMARATE| as a main intermediate. The name "phenylpropanoid" is derived from this compound, which consists of an aromatic phenyl group and a propene tail. Further processing results in the biosynthesis of many types of compounds, including |FRAME: Lignols monolignols| (precursors to |FRAME: Lignins lignin| and lignocellulose), |FRAME: Flavonoids flavonoids|, |FRAME: Coumarins coumarins|, |FRAME: Stilbenoids stilbenoids|, and phenolic acids. Phenylpropanoids are found throughout the plant kingdom, where they serve as essential components of a number of structural polymers, provide protection from ultraviolet light, defend against herbivores and pathogens, and also mediate plant-pollinator interactions as floral pigments and scent compounds.

Compound.name: a phenolphthiocerol A
Comment: |FRAME: Phthiocerols Phthiocerol|-based lipids and glycolipids have been found in many species of |FRAME: TAX-1762|, including |FRAME: TAX-1773|, |FRAME: TAX-1765|, |FRAME: TAX-33894|, |FRAME: TAX-1781|, |FRAME: TAX-1768|, |FRAME: TAX-1777|, |FRAME: TAX-1769| and |FRAME: TAX-1809| 3149973. For example, in |FRAME: TAX-78331| the trisaccharide (2,3,4-tri- O -methyl L-fucopyranosyl-(alpha1->3)-rhamnopyranosyl-(alpha1->3)-2- O -methyl L-rhamnopyranose) is attached. Compound.name: a kanamycin
Comment: |FRAME: Kanamycins Kanamycins| are a group of |FRAME: Aminoglycoside-Antibiotics "aminoglycoside antibiotics"| produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1967|. The compounds were discovered in 1957 by researchers in the National Institute of Health of Tokyo, Japan |CITS: [13513509][13595489]|. Due to their wide range of activity, especially against severe staphylococcal and mycobacterial infections, these antibiotics gained almost immediate acceptance, and the most common form, |FRAME: CPD-4821|, was produced commercially within a year of its discovery 13566481. Kanamycins interact with the 30S subunit of the prokaryotic ribosome, inducing substantial amounts of mistranslation and indirectly inhibiting translocation during protein synthesis, resulting in death |CITS: [391568][9662506]|. Kanamycins are currently used to treat a wide variety of infections. Kanamycins share several biosynthetic intermediates with other aminoglycosides, including the core moiety |FRAME: CPD-10151| and the pseudodisaccharides |FRAME: CPD-14126|, |FRAME: CPD-14125| and |FRAME: CPD-14137|. While the main product produced by |FRAME: TAX-1967| is |FRAME: CPD-4821| (R1 = NH2; R2 = OH), additional products are also produced, including |FRAME: CPD-4822| (R1 = R2 = NH 2 ), |FRAME: CPD-4823| (R1 = OH; R2 = NH 2 ) |CITS: [13563334][13587408]|, |FRAME: CPD-14138| (similar to |FRAME: CPD-4821|, but contains a glucose moiety instead of the kinosamine moiety) Adams96 and |FRAME: CPD-4824| (R1 = R2 = OH) Chang80.

Compound.name: a 5,6,7,8-tetrahydropterin

When one of the double bonds is reduced the compounds is referred to as a dihydropterin (the most common form of which is |FRAME: CPD0-1718|). When two of the double bonds are reduced, the compound is referred to as |FRAME: Tetrahydropterins|.

Compound.name: a beta-lactone

It is characterized by a closed ring consisting of two or more carbon atoms and a single oxygen atom, with a ketone group in one of the carbons adjacent to the ring oxygen. Compound.name: a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster
Synonyms: an iron-sulfur center (ambiguous) // Fe 2 S 2 iron-sulfur cluster // a 2Fe-2S center // a 2Fe-2S cluster // 2Fe-2S // Fe 2 S 2 // an Fe 2 S 2 iron-sulfur center // [2Fe-2S] // [2Fe-2S] cluster // Iron-sulfur (2Fe-2S)
Comment: |FRAME: FeS-Centers "Iron-sulfur clusters"| consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways. They serve as prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers with a low reduction potential. In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes and the storage of iron and sulfur. They act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression regulation 16466637. In |FRAME: CPD-6| the irons are coordinated to the sulfurs of 4 cysteine side chains.

However, GAX-type polymers consist of |FRAME: Arabinoxylan| backbone that contains about ten times more alpha-L-arabinofuranose side chains than glucuronate ones, while AGX-type polymers are |FRAME: Glucuronoxylans| with a small proportion of the xylopyranose residues of the backbone disubstituted by two alpha-L-arabinofuranose residues Ebringerova05. Another difference is that GAX contain some xylopyranose units that are doubly substituted by both 4- O -methylglucuronate and alpha-L-arabinofuranose Ebringerova05. Unlike glucuronoxylans, glucuronoarabinoxylans are not acetylated 15944805. Some of the arabinofuranose side chains in GAX are further substitued by either a beta-D-xylopyranose attached by a (1->2) linkage or by a second arabinofuranose attached by a (1->3) linkage. GAX-type polymers are typically located in the non-endospermic tissues of cereal grains such as in wheat, corn, and rice bran 8401598. Its structure is analogous to phosphatidylinositol (PI), but with a glyceryl moiety replacing the inosityl moiety of PI. Within a decade it has been found in higher plants Benson61, Gram-negative bacteria |CITS: [4868364][4295332]| and mammals 5660098. It was later discovered in the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2246|, indicating that it is produced by all three domains of life. The biosynthetic pathway was elucidated in the early 60s 14033231, and a laboratory synthesis was completed a few years later 5916374. The abundance of PG is relatively low compared with phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) in prokaryotes or with either PE or phosphatidylcholine (PC) in eukaryotes |CITS: [18216768][20671299][21172818]|. It is typically more concentrated in plant systems than in animals, forming 1.5-4·5% of the lipid fraction |CITS: [23532185][3592680]| Since its discovery, biochemical research into PG has been dominated by its roles in the surfactant of lung tissue (PG is the second largest lipid constituent of lung surfactant in almost all mammals), chloroplast membranes (PG is the only phospholipid found in chloroplast thylakoids) and in both bacterial and mammalian systems.

It is an abundant anionic lipid in bacteria and in eukaryotes , where it is exclusively present in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Cardiolipin was first isolated from beef heart Pangborn42, hence its name. Many enzymes involved in energy metabolism interact with cardiolipin. |FRAME: EC-7.1.1.9|, also known as Complex IV, requires two associated cardiolipin molecules in order to maintain its full enzymatic function 8389748. |FRAME: EC-7.1.1.8| (cytochrome bc 1 , Complex III) also needs cardiolipin to maintain its quaternary structure and functional role 10413476. |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2| (Complex V) binds four molecules of cardiolipin 2147180.

Compound.name: an adenine-type cytokinin
Comment: Cytokinins are a class of plant hormones that promote cell division, or cytokinesis, in plant roots and shoots. While their main role is to control cell growth and differentiation, they also affect apical dominance, axillary bud growth, and leaf senescence. The cytokinins are structurally diverse, and have been divided into two main types: |FRAME: Adenine-Cytokinins "adenine-type cytokinins"| and |FRAME: Phenylurea-Cytokinins "phenylurea-type cytokinins"|. All the natural cytokinins fall into the first type - phenylurea-type cytokinins are synthetic. The adenine cytokinins are classified further by the configuration of their N6-side chain as isoprenoid or aromatic cytokinins. The most prevalent cytokinins are by far those with an unsaturated isoprenoid side chain, and in particular those with a trans -hydroxylated N6-side chain, such as |FRAME: CPD-4210| and its derivatives. Most of the adenine-type cytokinins are modified by glucosylation of the adenine ring at the 3-, the 7-, or 9-position and conjugation of alanine at the 9-position of zeatin, forming lupinic acid. With the exception of the 3-glucosides, the N -glucosyl and alanyl conjugates generally exhibit no or low activity. The most important modifications are those affecting the N6-side chain, where even small substitutions have pronounced effects on cytokinin activity. The most common modifications of the side chain include reduction (e.g. trans-zeatin to dihydrozeatin), conjugation to O-glycosides (O-glucosides and O-xylosides), and side chain cleavage by cytokinin oxidases 11337393.

In animal tissues heparosan is synthesized attached to cell surface or extracellular matrix proteins, known as "core proteins". Heparosan consists of a repeating disaccharide unit composed of |FRAME: CPD-12521|-(1,4)-|FRAME: CPD-12541|. The disaccharide units are linked by a (1-4) linkage to each other. The polymer chain is attached to the core proteins via a tetrasaccharide linkage region that differs in composition from the rest of the polymer. The heparosan skeleton serves as a starting point in the biosynthesis of several other glycosaminoglycan such as |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate| and |FRAME: HEPARIN|, and bacterial heparosan is sometimes used for the synthesis of non-animal sourced heparin-like products.

Compound.name: a cobamide lower ligand
Comment: |FRAME: Cobamides "A cobamide"| is a corrinoid molecule based on the structure of |FRAME: CPD-20843|, a cobalt-corrinoid hexaamide that is formed from |FRAME: COBINAMIDE| by the attachment of an alpha-D-ribofuranose 3-phosphate residue at the 2 position of the aminopropanol chain. Four of the six coordination sites of the cobalt ion are provided by the corrin ring, while the other two are provided by |FRAME: Cobamide-Upper-Ligands upper| (beta) and |FRAME: Cobamide-Lower-Ligands lower| (alpha) ligands, which are located above and below the ring plane, respectively. The best known cobamide, |FRAME: Cobalamins cobalamin|, contains |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| as the lower ligand and either a methyl group or 5'-deoxyadenosyl group as the upper ligand. At least 16 different cobamides with structural variability in the lower ligand have been described. The 16 bases reported so far are |FRAME: BENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: CPD-18320|, |FRAME: CPD-18321|, |FRAME: CPD-18497|, |FRAME: CPD-18495|, |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: ADENINE|, |FRAME: CPD-18323|, |FRAME: GUANINE|, |FRAME: HYPOXANTHINE|, |FRAME: PHENOL|, |FRAME: CPD-108|, |FRAME: CPD-5723|, |FRAME: CPD-20865|, |FRAME: CPD-20864|, and |FRAME: CPD-20885| 24055007. Compound.name: a [phospholipid] fatty acid containing cis cyclopropane
Comment: Some organisms produce phospholipids in which the fatty acyl chains contain cyclopropane rings. These rings are formed by tenzymes that transfer a methylene moiety from S-adenosylL-methionine to double bonds of unsaturated fatty acyl chains within the lipids. In most organisms the cyclopropane groups are cis -configured and are formed by the action of |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.79|, which acts only on cis double bonds. The |FRAME: MYCOLIC-ACIDS "mycolic acids"| of mycobacteria often contain additional trans -configured cyclopropane groups that are formed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.M101| 16741578. The physiological role of cyclopropane-containing fatty acyl chains (CFA) is to stabilize the membranes by increased ordering of the chains without sacrificing membrane fluidity. This can decrease the proton permeability of phospholipid bilayers, helping the bacteria survive acid shock |CITS: [9310851][18562182][25804677]|. trans -configured CFA in mycolic acids were reported to be correlated with the persistence of the pathogen and to modulate the innate immune response of the host 15710652. The structures shown here depicts a cis -C13:cyclopropane within a phospholipid. This compound was randomly selected to represent a member of this compound class.

Four of the six coordination sites of the cobalt ion are provided by the corrin ring. In many cobinamides a fifth coordination site is provided by |FRAME: Cobamide-Upper-Ligands "an upper ligand"| located above the ring plane. Unlike in |FRAME: Cobamides cobamides|, cobinamides lack |FRAME: Cobamide-Lower-Ligands "a lower ligand"|. Compound.name: a sulfolipid

An abundant class of sulfolipids, found in many photosynthetic organisms, including all photosynthetic plants, algae, cyanobacteria, and purple sulfur and non-sulfur bacteria, is |FRAME: SULFOQUINOVOSYLDIACYLGLYCEROL "sulfoquinovosyl diacylglycerol"| (SQDG), which is composed of a glycoside of |FRAME: CPD-10247| and |FRAME: 1-2-Diglycerides diacylglycerol|. Other important sulfolipids include |FRAME: Cerebroside-3-sulfates sulfatide|, which is abundant in myelin, and |FRAME: Seminolipids seminolipid|, which is the most common glycolipid in mammalian testes.

Compound.name: a cephem
Comment: This compound class stands for |FRAME: Lactams lactams| in which the amide bond is contained within a four-membered ring, which includes the amide nitrogen and the carbonyl carbon. beta-Lactam compounds imitate the naturally occurring |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| substrate for the group of enzymes known as penicillin binding proteins (PBPs), which cross-link the peptidoglycan in bacterial cell wall, and thus act as powerful antibiotics 6109324. Naturally occurring |FRAME: Beta-Lactams "beta-lactam antibiotics"| are classified into several groups according to their chemical structure: In |FRAME: Monolactams monolactams| the beta-lactam ring is not fused to another ring. This class includes compounds such as the |FRAME: Nocardicins nocardicins| 3427723 and the |FRAME: Monobactams monobactams| 3909315. In |FRAME: Penams penams| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a saturated five atom ring (a 4:5 structure). Penams contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring (for example, the |FRAME: PENICILLIN penicillins|) 6335599. Related classes include the |FRAME: Carbapenams carbapenams|, which contain a carbon atom in that position 12890666, and the |FRAME: Clavams oxopenams| (also known as clavams), which contain an oxygen atom at that position (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9261|) 3304182. |FRAME: Penems Penems| are molecues similar to penams in which the five atom ring is unsaturated at positions 2-3. Similarly, penems contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring, while |FRAME: Carbapenems carbapenems| contains a carbon atom in that position 16413506. In |FRAME: Cephams cephams| and |FRAME: Cephems cephems| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a six-atom ring (a 4:6 strcuture) that contains a sulfur atom at position 1. In cephams the ring is saturated, while cephems have an unsaturated bond at positions 3-4 |CITS: [1164170][12722308]|. 1-Oxocephams/1-oxacephems conain an oxygen atom at position 1 |CITS: [11671696][11078187]|.

Compound.name: a furanocoumarin
Comment: The |FRAME: Furanocoumarins furanocoumarins| are one of the main groups of coumarins. Their synthesis starts with the coupling of |FRAME: CPD-4211| to the coumarin |FRAME: CPD-8186|, leading to formation of a skeleton that contains a furan ring fused with coumarin. Furanocoumarins are minor constituents in plants belonging to |FRAME: TAX-4037|, |FRAME: TAX-3803|, |FRAME: TAX-3487|, and |FRAME: TAX-23513| families. They are natural toxins that protect the plants from insects, herbivory, and microbes. Production is triggered by several types of stresses, including fungal infections |CITS: [6682038][8062387]| and stresses such as wounding Zangerl90 or acid fog Dercks90 . Furanocoumarins are also toxic to humans. Direct contact with the sap from some plants containing furanocoumarins (such as |FRAME: TAX-380077|) causes inflammation, burns and irritating sensitivity to sunlight 33174568. Some naturally occurring methoxy derivatives of furanocoumarins have been applied clinically, coupled with exposure to sunlight, to cure dermatological diseases for more than 2000 years. Linear furanocoumarins such as |FRAME: CPD-13042| and |FRAME: 5-METHOXYFURANOCOUMARIN| are used in the clinic in combination with UV radiation to treat several diseases, such as mycosis fungoides, vitiligo and psoriasis. Several clinical trials are ongoing to evaluate furanocoumarins potential to treat additional conditions, such as graft versus host disease, Crohn's disease, and several cancer types 33174568. A well documented toxicity of furanocoumarins is related to their inhibition of cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes 14769198. An example is the interaction of furanocoumarins produced by grapefruit with |FRAME: HS08544-MONOMER| (CYP3A4), an enzyme that is involved in the bioinactivation of about 50% of all drugs currently used, resulting in enhanced systemic drug concentration through impaired drug metabolism, and leading to recommendation to avoid grapefruit while taking drugs 23184849.

Compound.name: a coelenteramide
Comment: |FRAME: OPLOPHORUS-LUCIFERIN Coelenterazine| and its analogues are the luciferase substrate (=luciferin) in the light-emitting process of bioluminescent coelenterates as well as various, distantly related, types of organisms such as squids, shrimps, fishes, and some chaetognaths |CITS: [Shimomura80][Campbell90][20972255]|. It is also found in many nonluminous organisms 9336010. In bioluminescent systems, |FRAME: OPLOPHORUS-LUCIFERIN coelenterazine| is bound by either |FRAME: Coelenterazine-binding-proteins "coelenterazine-binding protein"| or by |FRAME: Aequorins "an aequorin"| protein, depending on the species. In the first system, upon binding of Ca 2+ ions the coelenterazine-binding protein releases coelenterazine, which is then oxidized and decarboxylated by the luciferase enzyme, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-20235|. In the second system, aequorin binds and oxidizes coelenterazine, retainning it in the form of bound |FRAME: CPD-20222|. Upon binding of Ca 2+ ions, the enzyme catalyzes the decarboxylation and formation of |FRAME: CPD-20235|. In vitro the excited coelenteramide relaxes to the ground state by emission of blue light. However, in vivo the excitation energy is transferred to |FRAME: GFP| by Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) |CITS: [4151620][33175]|. Coelenterazine is a derivative of imidazopyrazinone. Its biosynthetic origin is not known. However, it has been shown that the hydromedusa |FRAME: TAX-6100| is not able to synthesize it, and is dependent on a dietary supply of this luciferin for bioluminescence 11572972. The only report of de novo biosynthesis of coelenterazine is from the bioluminescent shrimp |FRAME: TAX-576189| Thomson95.

Comment: |FRAME: Kauralexins Kauralexins| are a class of |FRAME: CPD1F-128|-related diterpenoid defense compounds found in maize. They are produced in response to a variety of biotic threats, including the larvae of the European corn borer |FRAME: TAX-29057| and fungi such as |FRAME: TAX-58291| and TAX-5518. Jasmonic acid and ethylene can also work synergistically to promote kauralexin production.

Compound.name: a jasmonate or derivative
Comment: The |FRAME: Jasmonates jasmonates| are a group of important phytohormones, structurally similar to animal |FRAME: Prostaglandins prostaglandins| and ubiquitous in the plant kingdom. Many forms exist, based on the structure of |FRAME: Jasmonic-Acids "Jasmonate"| (jasmonic acid, JA). The jasmonates act as regulatory molecules in many developmental processes that include fertility, sex determination, root elongation and fruit ripening. They are also potent signals activating plant defences against pathogens, herbivory, wounding and abiotic stress. The jasmonate regulation system includes the COI1 receptor protein and several JAZ ( JA smonate Z IM domain) repressors, which, in the absence of jasmonate, are bound to the MYC2 transcription factors, preventing transcription. In the presence of active jasmonate molecules, COI1 interacts with the JAZ repressors, causing their |FRAME: PWY-7511 ubiquitylation|. The ubiquitylated repressors are targeted for proteasome degradation, releasing the MYC2 transcription factors and activating transcription 19716757. Only two of the four stereoisomers of jasmonate occur naturally: |FRAME: CPD-731| and |FRAME: CPD-734| |CITS: [8074303][19349968]|. These two forms are present in equilibrium within cells and can interconvert spontaneously through epimerization |CITS: [8074303][19349968]|. The exact ratio of these stereoisomers within a cell has not been conclusively determined, and it may vary based on species, cell type, and physiological state. But, in the systems tested so far, |FRAME: CPD-734| is found at higher levels than |FRAME: CPD-731| 19349968. The biological activity of these stereoisomers can be quite different 8074303. In addition, enzymes involved in JA metabolism may have different preferences for the different stereoisomers 17291501. This master class includes a large set of cyclopentanone derivatives of |FRAME: Jasmonic-Acids "jasmonate"|. Confusingly, these compounds are often referred to collectively by the name "jasmonates".

Compound.name: a Lewis epitope
Comment: The Lewis blood group antigens, discovered in 1946, are biosynthetically and structurally related carbohydrate structures used as markers of cell differentiation and embryonic development, based on fucosylation carried by a number of fucosyltransferases. The system is named after Mrs. H. D. G. Lewis, in whose serum the first member of the family was discovered 20995492. However, the presence of the Lewis antigens is not limited to erytrocytes, and they are found in different tissues and organs. One of these fucosyltransferases, encoded by the |FRAME: HS10249| gene, is bifunctional and can fucosylate both the 3 and 4 positions of the penultimate sugar in the precursor disaccharide. The gene, also known as the Lewis gene, has a dominant allele (which was named Le) and a recessive non-functional allele (known as le). The alpha(1,4)-fucosyltransferase activity is only relevant when the substrates are derived from the |FRAME: beta-Gal-13-beta-GlcNac-R "type 1 precursor disaccharide"|, as that position is already occupied in the |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R "type 2 disaccharide"|. The first Lewis antigens to be discovered were the |FRAME: Lewis-a-epitope "Lewis a"| and |FRAME: Antigen-Leb "Lewis b"| antigens, which are produced from |FRAME: beta-Gal-13-beta-GlcNac-R "type 1 precursor disaccharides"| (see |FRAME: PWY-7832|). However, the alpha(1,3) fucosylation of the N -acetylglucosaminyl residue of |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R| leads to formation of several related antigens known as the |FRAME: CPD-8594 "Lewis x epitope"| (also known as SSEA-1, for stage-specific embryonic antigen 1), |FRAME: Antigen-Ley "Lewis y epitope"|, and the |FRAME: sLea-Antigen "sialyl-Lewis x epitope"| (see |FRAME: PWY-7831|).

Compound.name: a sphingoid 1-phosphate

They are characterized by the presence of a hydroxyl group at C1 and C3, and an amine group at C2. The commonly known sphingoids include sphingosine, sphinganine (dihydrosphingosine), and phytosphingosine (4-hydroxysphinganine). Sphingoid bases can be phosphorylated at C1. Phosphorylated shingoids, such as sphingosine 1-phosphate, can be important signalling intermediates.

Many types of such acids exist, including |FRAME: Mycosanoic-Acids "mycosanoic acids"|, |FRAME: Mycolipanoic-Acids "mycolipanoic acids"|, |FRAME: Mycolipanolic-Acids "mycolipanolic acids"|, |FRAME: Mycolipenic-Acids "mycolipenic acids"|, |FRAME: Mycolipodienoic-Acids "mycolipodienoic acids"|, |FRAME: Phthioceranic-Acids "phthioceranic acids"|, and |FRAME: Mycocerosic-Acids "mycocerosic acids"|. Hydroxyphthioceranic acids are hepta and octa-methylated alkanoic very-long chain fatty acids with a hydroxyl group on the carbon next to the last methylated carbon. They are the major acyl group found in |FRAME: CPD-18600|, the major sulfolipid of |FRAME: TAX-1773| Cason64. In heptamethylated hydroxyphthioceranic acids R1=OH, R2,R3 = H. Compound.name: a modified nucleobase

The primary nucleobases are |FRAME: CYTOSINE|, |FRAME: GUANINE|, |FRAME: ADENINE| (found in both DNA and RNA), |FRAME: THYMINE| (found only in DNA) and |FRAME: URACIL| (found only in RNA), abbreviated as C, G, A, T, and U, respectively. There are many additional nucleobases, usually derived from the primary ones. Compound.name: a glucosinolate
Comment: |FRAME: Glucosinolates "Glucosinolates"| are secondary metabolites found in 16 plant families, including agriculturally important crop plants of the |FRAME: TAX-3700| such cabbage, mustard, oilseed rape, and broccoli, as well as the model plant |FRAME: TAX-3702|, and are responsible for the typical sharp taste and odor of these plants. The glucosinolates are substituted beta-thioglucoside N -hydroxysulfates that are formed from any one of eight amino acids, namely, L-ALPHA-ALANINE, |FRAME: VAL|, |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: ILE|, |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: MET|, |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: TRP|. Over 115 naturally occurring glucosinolates have been identified. Much of the diversity amongst glucosinolates arises from the addition of different sized alkyl groups to the side chain of the amino acids, principally valine, phenylalanine and methionine 18458837. They are grouped into aliphatic, aromatic, and indolic types, depending on whether they are derived from methionine, phenylalanine and tyrosine, or tryptophan. Indolylmethyl glucosinolates are found mainly in leaves. For a review, see 12049923. Glucosinolates are stored in the vacuole and come into contact with the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147| (myrosinase) upon breakage of the cell. Myrosinase de-glucosylates the glucosinolates, resulting in formation of nitriles, isothiocyanates and thiocyanates. The precise product that is formed depends on the glucosinolate and whether an epithiospecifier protein is present. The breakdown products give the typical sharp taste and odor to many of the members of brassicaceae that are eaten, such as raddish and mustard. Arabidopsis has been shown to accumulate at least 23 different glucosinolates in both seeds and leaves.

Comment: |FRAME: Heparosan "Heparosan"| (also known as heparan) is a member of the |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycan"| family. It consists of a repeating disaccharide unit composed of |FRAME: CPD-12521|-(1,4)-|FRAME: CPD-12541|. The disaccharide units are linked by a (1-4) linkage to each other. Heparosan is a bacterial glycosaminoglycan produced and found in the capsule of some pathogenic bacteria such as Escherichia coli K5 and Pasteurella multocida. The heparosan skeleton serves as a starting point in the biosynthesis of several other glycosaminoglycan such as |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate| and |FRAME: HEPARIN|, and bacterial heparosan is sometimes used for the synthesis of non-animal sourced heparin-like products.

Mucin-type O -glycosylation, consisting of glycans attached via O-linked |FRAME: CPD-3604|, is one of the most abundant forms of protein glycosylation in animals. Eight core-type structures of mucin-type O -glycans have been proposed, including |FRAME: Core1 "core 1"|, |FRAME: Core2 "core 2"|, |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINYL-13-N-ETCETERA-GALACTOSAMINY "core 3"|, |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINYL-16-ETCETERA-GALACTOSAMINYL- "core 4"|, |FRAME: Core5 "core 5"|, |FRAME: Core6 "core 6"|, |FRAME: Core7 "core 7"| and |FRAME: Core8 "core 8"| 16413314. Many enzymes that act on fatty acids, as well as the corresponding |FRAME: Fatty-Acyl-CoAs "fatty acyl-CoAs"|, |FRAME: Fatty-Alcohols alcohols|, and |FRAME: Fatty-Aldehydes aldehydes|, have evolved to recognize substrates with a limited range of chain lengths. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Short-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Medium-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Long-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "fatty acids that have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: VERY-LONG-CHAIN-FATTY-ACYL-COA "Very-long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Ultra-Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Ultra-long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain"|.

Compound.name: a strigolactone
Comment: Strigolactones are plant hormones that stimulate the branching and growth of symbiotic arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, but inhibit plant shoot branching. They promote the probability of establishment of a symbiotic association between the plant and the fungi. The first strigolactone (|FRAME: CPD-14655|) was described from |FRAME: TAX-3635| (cotton) infected by the root parasitic weeds |FRAME: TAX-4169| (witchweed) (hence the name). It has been shown that the seeds of the parasites germinated only if they were exposed to stimulant molecules present in the root exudate of the host. Although the nature of strigol was not understood at the time, it was observed that it was active at hormonal levels 17780042. Discovery of additional strigolactones from other plants followed, such as |FRAME: CPD-14659| from |FRAME: TAX-4558| Hauck92, |FRAME: CPD-14660| from |FRAME: TAX-3917| Mueler92 and |FRAME: CPD-14657| from |FRAME: TAX-57577| (red clover) Yokota98. The real purpose of strigolactones, which was understood 40 years after the discovery of strigol, is to promote the formation of symbiotic associations known as arbuscular mycorrhiza, which consist of close interaction between the plants roots and |FRAME: TAX-214504| fungi |CITS: [15944706][16574693]|. Arbuscular mycorrhiza, which are found in more than 80% of higher plant species, are one of the most ancient symbioses of land plants. The fungi acquire and deliver nutrients to the plants, which in return provides the fungi with carbohydrates produced by photosynthesis 15944687. The lactones induce extensive hyphal branching in germinating spores of the fungi, which increases the chance of contact with the root and subsequently infecting it. The branching phenomenon has been known for more than 30 years before the identity of the chemical signal that promotes it has been traced to strigolactone Mosse73. Since strigolactones are very labile and active at concentrations as low as picomolar, they are active only in close proximity to potential host roots, ensuring successful interactionbetween the fungi the roots. Study of mutants lacking strigolactones suggest that the hormones are also involved in the regulation of shoot branching, acting as branch-inhibiting hormones |CITS: [15268852][15342640]|.

Compound.name: heparan sulfate
Comment: |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate "Heparan sulfate"| (also known as heparitin sulfate) is a member of the |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycan"| family. It consists of a variably sulfated repeating disaccharide unit composed of a hexuronic acid and a hexosamine. The most common repeating unit, which makes up around 50% of the total disaccharide units in heparan sulfate, is composed of |FRAME: CPD-12521| linked to |FRAME: CPD-12541|. In other units |FRAME: CPD-12521| may be substituted by |FRAME: CPD-12515| or its sulfated form |FRAME: CPD-12518|, and |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| may be sulfated to |FRAME: CPD-12565|, or may be substituted by |FRAME: N-sulfo-D-glucosamine| or |FRAME: CPD-12533|. Heparan sulfate binds to specific proteins such as antithrombin and several growth factors, thereby regulating various biological processes including anticoagulation and angiogenesis 9151776. The unique sulfation pattern of a monosaccharide sequence within HS is believed to be critical for binding to the target protein. The structure of heparan sulfate is very similar to that of |FRAME: HEPARIN|. Heparan sulfate contains lower amounts of sulfate and less iduronic acid than heparin 5484472. In addition, heparan sulfates disaccharide units are organized into distinct sulfated and non-sulfated domains, while heparin disaccharides are sulfated randomly 15047699. |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate "Heparan sulfate"| chains comprise three different types of domains: S-domains that contain contiguous N -sulfated residues, unmodified N -acetyl-rich regions, and mixed transition zones between the S-domains and the unmodified segments. Only the S-domains have binding capacities for growth factors and other proteins 11489926.

Compound.name: λ-carrageenan
Comment: |FRAME: Carrageenans Carrageenans| and |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| are sulfated polysaccharides that are extracted from sea weeds belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-2763| (red algae), mainly from |FRAME: TAX-2769|, and species from the |FRAME: TAX-31444| and |FRAME: TAX-33664| genera. They are laid out in the cell wall at a high density and can constitute up to 50% of the algae dry mass. The basic units of |FRAME: Carrageenans carrageenans| are repeats of alternating alpha-1,3-linked D-galactose and beta-1,4-linked D-galactose units, which are often substituted by sulfate. Carrageenans are classified according to the number and the position of sulfated ester 1367970. In |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| the alpha-1,3-linked galactose units are modified by having a 3,6-anhydro bridge. These bridges, which form a double helix during aggregation, are responsible for the gelation that is typical to these compounds. Despite this distinction, carrageenoses are often referred to as carrageenans. The three most industrially exploited carrageenans, namely, |FRAME: kappa-Carrageenan|, |FRAME: iota-Carrageenan| and |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan|, are distinguished by the presence of one, two or three ester-sulfate groups per repeating disaccharide unit respectively. |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan| is sulfated at position 2 of the beta-1,4 linked D-galactose units and positions 2 and 6 of the alpha-1,3-linked galactose units. Some carrabiose units of the λ-carrageenan from |FRAME: TAX-2765380| are substituted with four sulfate groups (D2S,6S-G2S,4S) 16716278. Since λ-carrageenans do not feature 3,6-anhydro-bridges, they do not make physical gels.

Compound.name: a tricothecene

The trichothecene family has been divided into four groups: Type A, B, C, and D. The most important structural features causing the biological activities of trichothecenes are the 12,13-epoxy ring, the presence of hydroxyl or acetyl groups at appropriate positions on the trichothecene nucleus, and the structure and position of the side-chain. Type D trichothecenes, which have an additional ring between carbon 4 and carbon 15, are thought to be the most toxic 22069741. The toxicity of tricothecenes primarily results from their interaction with ribosomes, acting as protein synthesis inhibitors Kiessling86. Various |FRAME: TAX-5506| species such as |FRAME: TAX-5518|, |FRAME: TAX-5514|, |FRAME: TAX-36050| and |FRAME: TAX-61235| produce tricothecenes on many different grains like wheat, oats or maize. An outbreak in Orenburg, Russia in 1932 affected ~100,000 people, with a mortality rate of 60%. Some producers, such as |FRAME: TAX-74722|, grow in damp indoor environments such as wallpaper, and produce trichothecenes that become airborne and contribute to health problems among occupants |CITS: [11798344][15640178][16269780]|.

Compound.name: a [phospholipid] fatty acid containing cyclopropane
Comment: Some organisms produce phospholipids in which the fatty acyl chains contain cyclopropane rings. These rings are formed by tenzymes that transfer a methylene moiety from S-adenosylL-methionine to double bonds of unsaturated fatty acyl chains within the lipids. In most organisms the cyclopropane groups are cis -configured and are formed by the action of |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.79|, which acts only on cis double bonds. The |FRAME: MYCOLIC-ACIDS "mycolic acids"| of mycobacteria often contain additional trans -configured cyclopropane groups that are formed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.M101| 16741578. The physiological role of cyclopropane-containing fatty acyl chains (CFA) is to stabilize the membranes by increased ordering of the chains without sacrificing membrane fluidity. This can decrease the proton permeability of phospholipid bilayers, helping the bacteria survive acid shock |CITS: [9310851][18562182][25804677]|. trans -configured CFA in mycolic acids were reported to be correlated with the persistence of the pathogen and to modulate the innate immune response of the host 15710652. Comment: Green sulfur bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-191412|) and green flimentous bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-1106|) contain chlorosomes - large organelles that are believed to be the most efficient light-harvesting antennae in nature |CITS: [20130996][Saga10]|. Green sulfur bacteria can grow at light intensities that are too low to support growth of any other phototroph, up to a million times lower light than normal sunlight Overmann92. Chlorosomes contain about 1,500 bacteriochlorophyll molecules per reaction center. They are filled with 10 30 rod-shaped elements which are oriented parallel to the long axis of the chlorosomes and have a diameter of 10 nm. Each rod consists of a tubular bilayer formed by self-organization of the antenna bacteriochlorophyll molecules. Unlike all other known photosynthetic antenna, in which the chlorophyll molecules are bound to proteins, chlorosomes do not contain accessory proteins. The chlorosomal bacteriochlorophyll pigments are able to self-aggregate due to their unique chemical characteristics. The bacteriochlorophylls found in chlorosomes are either |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d "| or |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e "|, depending on the species. In addition, all of these bacteriochlorophylls lack C-13 2 -methylcarboxyl side chains, which are found in all other (bacterio)chlorophylls but would interfere with the ability to form aggregates 16245042. Despite of their names, |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d "| and |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e "| are actually chlorins rather than bacteriochlorins. All three are usually found with an unsaturated farnesyl tail rather than phytyl tails |CITS: [2350541][Borrego99]|, although exceptions have been reported. In chlorosomes of |FRAME: TAX-191412| (but not |FRAME: TAX-1106| |CITS: [Risch79][3442679]|) all three types of bacteriochlorophyll appear in several forms with different degrees of methylation at the C-8 2 and C-12 1 carbons |CITS: [12656478][14610639]|. Comment: Iron-sulfur clusters are cofators of |FRAME: FeS-Proteins "iron-sulfur proteins"| and consist of a cluster of two to four iron atoms linked to sulfides, some of which are cysteine residues of the protein. Several cluster types have been described, including |FRAME: CPD-6|, |FRAME: CPD-23|, |FRAME: 3FE-4S| and |FRAME: CPD-7|. The [3Fe-4S] cluster is relatively rare, and 3Fe/4Fe interconversion may occur with minimal protein reorganization. In another type of Fe-S cluster, known as |FRAME: CPD0-1098|, two of the 4 cysteine residues that are coordinated with the iron atoms in regular |FRAME: CPD-6| are substituted by histidine residues. Although the clusters contain several iron atoms, each one usually transfers only one electron, so, for example, a protein with two [4Fe-4S] clusters will usually transfer two electrons. Small electron transfer proteins that contain only [2Fe-2S] or [4Fe-4S] clusters are called |FRAME: Ferredoxins ferredoxins|. When Fe-S clusters occur in larger (and sometimes membrane-bound) proteins together with other prosthetic groups and/or metal cofactors, the proteins are designated as complex Fe-S proteins. In addition to their roles in electron t ransfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes and the storage of iron and sulfur. They can also act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression 16466637. In some cases iron-sulfur clusters serve as sources of sulfur in enzymatic reactions. In such cases the cluster needs to be reassembled before the enzyme can catalyze the next round 29051382.

Compound.name: compound 0
Comment: |FRAME: Compound-0 "Compound 0"|, |FRAME: Compound-I|, and |FRAME: Compound-II| are the names given to intermediate states of the heme-iron center that is formed at the active sites of cytochrome P-450 enzymes and peroxidases during catalysis. I. Cytochrome P-450 In cytochrome P-450 the proximal coordinatioin position of the heme iron, which is bound to the 4 nitrogen atoms of the tetrapyrrole ring, is tethered to the protein via a cysteine thiolate ligand. At its rest state, the iron is found at a low-spin ferric state (III valency). At this state the iron also binds a water molecule as a sixth ligand at the distal axial coordination position. Binding of a substrate to the low-spin ferric enzyme leads to displacement of the water as the sixth ligand and a high spin shift. The substrate-bound complex has a greater reduction potential and more easily accepts a single electron from the redox partner, which can be either |FRAME: EC-1.6.2.4 "a cytochrome P450 reductase"|, |FRAME: Ferredoxins|, or |FRAME: Cytochromes-b5|). After the first reduction, the heme iron binds oxygen, forming an oxy-heme complex. The oxygen is bound at the distal axial coordination position, from which the water molecule has been displaced. Following the transfer of the second electron from the redox partner and two subsequent protonations, a peroxo adduct is formed, known as |FRAME: Compound-0|. Next, the O-O bond is cleaved heterolytically, releasing a water molecule and leaving behind an oxygen atom with only six valence electrons. This highly active oxene oxygen removes one electron from the iron and one from the porphyrin, oxidizing the iron to the unusual valency of IV (ferryl iron) and generating an additional oxidizing equivalent that is delocalized over the porphyrin and thiolate ligands. This ferryl/porphyrin radical cation complex is known as |FRAME: Compound-I| 21071661. When the substrate nears the active site, |FRAME: Compound-I| abstracts an electron from it, converting the substrate into a radical and becoming a protonated non-radical ferryl compound known as |FRAME: Compound-II|. At this point the substrate radical reacts with the oxygen of |FRAME: Compound-II|, forming a new carbon oxygen bond. The product is released, and the iron returns to a valency of III (compound III) OrtizdeMontellano15. II. preoxidases In peroxidases the proximal coordinatioin position of the heme iron, which is bound to the 4 nitrogen atoms of the tetrapyrrole ring, is tethered to the protein via a histidine residue. |FRAME: Compound-I "Compound I"| is produced when the heme iron is oxidized by |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|. A single one-electron reduction step of |FRAME: Compound-I| from an electron donor substrate yields |FRAME: Compound-II|, followed by a second one-electron transfer that returns the enzyme to the ferric oxidation state, thus completing the catalytic cycle. Each electron transfer event converts a substrate molecule to a radical cation, forming two such radicals during a catalytic cycle. In the presence of high concentrations of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| and the absence of a reducing substrate, |FRAME: Compound-II| can be oxidized to |FRAME: Compound-III|, a catalytically inactive form of the enzyme. |FRAME: Compound-III "Compound III"| is converted back to the resting state by spontaneous autoxidation or by oxidation with two molecules of the substrate radical cation 18581264.

Compound.name: a ganglioside
Comment: |FRAME: Gangliosides "Gangliosides"| are molecules composed of |FRAME: Glycosphingolipids| (|FRAME: Ceramides| and |FRAME: Oligosaccharides|) with one or more sialic acids (usually |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE|) linked to the sugar chain. They are components of the cell plasma membrane that modulates cell signal transduction events, and appear to concentrate in lipid rafts. The name ganglioside is derived from the ganglion cells of the brain, from which the first gangliosides were isolated by the German scientist Ernst Klenk in 1942 Klenk42. Indeed, gangliosides dominate the composition of the glycocalyces of most of the cells of the vertebrate nervous system. Although gangliosides with various glycan structures are found in every vertebrate tissue, they are markedly more abundant in the nervous system, where each cell has on average about 10 million cell surface gangliosides 27261254. Variations in the sialoglycan and lipid components of the gangliosides result in hundreds of distinct ganglioside structures with a variety of functions that ranges from regulating receptor tyrosine kinases to directing cell-cell communication, cell-substrate interaction, adhesion, and protein targeting 17991443. Mammalian brain gangliosides, however, are dominated by only four types of gangliosides - |FRAME: CPD-7188 "ganglioside GM1a|, |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINYL-ETCETERA-GLUCOSYLCERA "ganglioside GD1a"|, |FRAME: Ganglioside-GD1b "ganglioside GD1b"| and |FRAME: Ganglioside-GT1b "ganglioside GT1b"| 22735313. The ceramide lipid components of brain gangliosides are dominated by a single fatty acid (|FRAME: STEARIC_ACID|) attached to one of two sphingoid bases, |FRAME: SPHINGOSINE| and |FRAME: CPD-19684| 21113547. While many non-human mammals synthesize gangliosides that contain two types of sialic acids - |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| and |FRAME: CPD-273|, mammalian brain gangliosides almost exclusively carry the former. Like other glycosphingolipids, gangliosides are biosynthesized stepwise by a series of glycosyltransferases that use nucleotide sugar donors to first glucosylate ceramide and then elongate the saccharide chain .|FRAME: Lactosyl-Ceramides Lactosylceramide|, a product of the second glycosylation step in the biosynthesis of many glycosphingolipids, is an important branching point, being a common precursor for the synthesis of the four major classes of glycosphingolipids: the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|, the |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs "globo series"|, the |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs "lacto series"|, and the |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs "neolacto series"| 10320813. The ceramide lipid of glycosphingolipids is embedded in the outer leaflet of the lipid bilayer of the plasma membrane, with the glycan extending 2-2.5 nm outward, perpendicular to the plane of the lipid bilayer 19056784. What makes gangliosides different from other glycosphingolipids is the incorporation of sialic acids. With a mean Pka value of around 2.6, sialic acids are more acidic than the majority of carboxylic acids and negatively charged at most physiological pH values. About the nomenclature of gangliosides Ganglioside naming is somewhat complex. Two ganglioside nomenclature systems are currently in use. The most commonly used is a short-hand nomenclature suggested by Svennerholm, which was initially based on the migration order of |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio-series"| gangliosides in chromatography 14066623. The more comprehensive system formulated by IUPAC 9826173 is applied much less frequently. A typical ganglioside name using the old system looks like |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"|. The first letter refers to the glycosphingolipid series. For example, the "G" stands for the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|. The next letter describes the number of sialic acid residues: (A = 0, M =1, D = 2, T = 3, Q = 4, P = 5, H = 6, S = 7). The following number describes the number of the non-sialic residues, and is derived in a rather complex manner. It was initially assumed that the number of such residues does not exceed 5. The number in the name was calculated as (5 - the number of uncharged carbohydrates). In addition, several sub-series of gangliosides have been defined based on the number of sialic acids attached to the galactose residue of the lacosylceramide core. If no sialic residues are present at that position, the compounds belong to the |FRAME: 0-Series-Ganglioside "0-series |. Those with one sialic acid at that position are named the |FRAME: A-Series-Gangliosides a-series |, those with two sialic acids belong to the |FRAME: B-Series-Gangliosides b-series |, and so on. |FRAME: C-Series-Gangliosides "C-series"| or higher gangliosides are rare in adult mammals and birds, but are abundant in fish and amphibians. Confusingly, GM1b and GD1c are both 0-series gangliosides, despite having a b and c in their names. So, for example, the |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"| is named as follows: G = belongs to the ganglio series, Q = 4 sialic acids, 1 = 4 non-sialic residues, and b = belongs to the b-series, meaning two of the sialic acids are attached to the inner galactose.
