Compound.name: a type 6 histo-blood group antigen precursor disaccharide
Comment: The histo-blood group antigen precursor disaccharides are found at the terminal end of oligosaccharide chains attached to proteins or sphingolipids, and serve as the actual substrates for various glycosyltransferases that terminate the chain elongation process, forming the ABH or Lewis antigens. Five types of precursor disaccharides are known to carry ABH activity - type 1 through type 4 and type 6. Type 1 precursors are widely expressed on endodermally-derived tissues such as lining epithelia and glandular epithelia. Type 2 precursors are found mainly on ecto- or mesodermally-derived tissues, including erythrocytes Mollicone86. Type 3 and 4 precursors are found on ecto- or endodermally-derived tissues, including the salivary glands and kidneys 2464874. Since ABH antigens are present not only on erythrocytes, but also on various organs such as the salivary glands and kidneys |CITS: [3965299][6172274]|, they are called histo-blood group ABH antigens. Compound.name: a 1,2-beta-D-glucan
Comment: beta-1,2-Glucan is a homopolymer composed of glucose residues connected by beta(1,2) linkages. This type of glucan has been reported from some Gram-negative bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-357|, |FRAME: TAX-379|, |FRAME: TAX-28105|, and |FRAME: TAX-234|, where it exists mainly in cyclic form |CITS: [Hisamatsu82][2117876][8078434][15880113][22583376]|. Cyclic beta-1,2-glucans have been reported to play a role in osmotic regulation |CITS: [3941890][2318812][10779706]|, but were also reported to act as commensal factors in |FRAME: TAX-379| 18052882 and as infectious factors in |FRAME: TAX-235| 11401996. Cyclic beta-1,2-glucans are usually found with a degree of polymerization (DPs) around 20, although a much longer glucan (DPs of around 40) has been reported from |FRAME: TAX-382| Koizumi84. Linear beta-1,2-glucans have been found in |FRAME: TAX-434| and |FRAME: TAX-338| |CITS: [Amemura85][3540204]|, and linear glucans with beta-1,6-glucosyl branches was reported in |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-317| (see |FRAME: CPD-16398|) |CITS: [3941890][7961404][10779706]|.

Compound.name: a medium chain fatty acid
Comment: The term "fatty acid" was originally coined to describe aliphatic monocarboxylic acids derived from or contained in esterified form in an animal or vegetable fat, oil or wax. However, over the years the term has been expanded to refer to additional, shorter monocarboxylic acids with an aliphatic tail such as |FRAME: PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| (but not the shorter |FRAME: FORMATE| and |FRAME: ACET|). The length of a fatty acid is determined by the length of the longest carbon chain, including the carbon of the carboxy group. Common natural fatty acids usually have an even number of carbons in the longest chain and can be either saturated or unsaturated. In many organisms they are often modified by branching, hydroxylation, methylation, epoxidation and other types of modifications. Inside living cells fatty acids are rarely found in free form. They are usually bound to coenzyme A or acyl-carrier proteins, or form part of |FRAME: Triacylglycerides triglycerides|, |FRAME: Phospholipids phospholipids|, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides|, and |FRAME: Cholesterol-esters cholesterol esters|. Many enzymes that act on fatty acids, as well as the corresponding |FRAME: Fatty-Acyl-CoAs "fatty acyl-CoAs"|, alcohols, and aldehydes, have evolved to recognize substrates with a limited range of chain lengths. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "Short-chain fatty acids"| (SCFA) have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "Medium-chain fatty acids"| (MCFA) have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "Long-chain fatty acids"| (LCFA) have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "Very-long-chain fatty acids"| (VLCFA) have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "Ultra-long-chain fatty acids"| (ULCFA) have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain. Most of the natural fatty acids have an even number of carbon atoms, since their biosynthesis involves the addition of two-carbon-atom units. When a fatty acid contains only single bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Saturated-Fatty-Acids|. When it contains one or more double bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Unsaturated-Fatty-Acids|. If it contains a double bond in the trans configuration, it is often referred to as a trans fatty acid. Most fatty acids in the trans configuration are not found in nature and are the result of human processing.

Compound.name: a phthiotriol A
Comment: |FRAME: Phthiotriols Phthiotriols| are intermediates in |FRAME: Phthiocerols phthiocerol| biosynthesis. They contain a hydroxyl group where phthiocerols contain a methoxyl group. Two types of phthiotriol exist. In |FRAME: Phthiotriols-A "phthiotriol A"| the first hydroxyl group and the methyl group are attached at positions 3 and 4, respectively, and the other hydroxyl groups are at positions 9 and 11. In |FRAME: Phthiotriols-B "phthiotriol B"| a methyl group is missing from the beginning of the molecule, and thus the first hydroxyl group and the methyl group are attached at positions 2 and 3, respectively, and the other hydroxyl groups are at positions 8 and 10.

Compound.name: an aminoglycoside
Comment: An aminoglycoside is a molecule composed of a sugar group and an amino group. Several aminoglycoside function as antibiotics that are used to treat certain bacterial infections. Anthracyclines are another group of aminoglycosides, which are used in chemotherapy.

Compound.name: a lactone
Comment: A |FRAME: Lactones "lactone"| is a cyclic ester, the product of condensation of an alcohol group and a carboxylate group within the same molecule. It is characterized by a closed ring consisting of two or more carbon atoms and a single oxygen atom, with a ketone group in one of the carbons adjacent to the ring oxygen. There are several types of lactones - |FRAME: Beta-lactones| contain 3 carbons in the ring, Gamma-lactones contains 4, Delta-lactones contains 5, and Epsilon-lactones contains 6 carbons. The most stable structure for lactones are gamma-lactones and delta-lactones, because of the minimal angle strain in their structure. In fact, gamma-lactones are so stable that, in the presence of dilute acids at room temperature, 4-hydroxy acids esterify and cyclize spontaneously to form lactones. beta-lactones, on the other hand, are not very stable. The name lactone is derived from the lactone of |FRAME: L-LACTATE|, which is called |FRAME: CPD-9549|, although it is really a di-lactone.

Compound.name: a phenolphthiotriol B
Comment: |FRAME: Phenolphthiotriol Phenolphthiotriols| are intermediates in |FRAME: Phenolphthiocerols phenolphthiocerol| biosynthesis. Phenolphthiocerol glycolipids have been found in many Mycobacterium species, including |FRAME: TAX-1769|, |FRAME: TAX-1768|, |FRAME: TAX-1765|, |FRAME: TAX-1781|, and |FRAME: TAX-78331| 3113946. Two types of phenolphthiotriol exist. In |FRAME: Phenolphthiotriol-A "phenolphthiotriol A"| the first hydroxyl and the methyl groups are attached at positions 3 and 4, respectively, and the other hydroxyl groups are at positions 9 and 11. In |FRAME: Phenolphthiotriol-B "phenolphthiotriol B"| a methyl group is missing from the beginning of the molecule, and thus the first hydroxyl and the methyl groups are attached at positions 2 and 3, respectively, and the other hydroxyl groups are at positions 8 and 10.

Compound.name: alpha-carrageenose
Comment: |FRAME: Carrageenans Carrageenans| and |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| are sulfated polysaccharides that are extracted from sea weeds belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-2763| (red algae), mainly from |FRAME: TAX-2769|, and species from the |FRAME: TAX-31444| and |FRAME: TAX-33664| genera. They are laid out in the cell wall at a high density and can constitute up to 50% of the algae dry mass. The basic units of |FRAME: Carrageenans carrageenans| are repeats of alternating alpha-1,3 linked D-galactose and beta-1,4-linked D-galactose units, which are often substituted by sulfate. Carrageenans are classified according to the number and the position of sulfated ester 1367970. In |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| the alpha-1,3-linked galactose units are modified by having a 3,6-anhydro bridge. These bridges, which form a double helix during aggregation, are responsible for the gelation that is typical to these compounds. Despite this distinction, carrageenoses are often referred to as carrageenans. The three most industrially exploited carrageenans, namely, |FRAME: kappa-Carrageenan|, |FRAME: iota-Carrageenan| and |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan|, are distinguished by the presence of one, two or three ester-sulfate groups per repeating disaccharide unit respectively. |FRAME: alpha-Carrageenan| is sulfated only at position 2 of the alpha-1,3-linked 3,6-anhydrogalactose units.

Compound.name: a [glycerolipid]-pinolenate

Compound.name: an N 1 -methyl- N 3 -aminocarboxypropyl-pseudouridine in 18S rRNA

Compound.name: a [glycerolipid]-(8Z,11Z,14Z,17Z)-icosatetraenoate
Comment: |FRAME: CPD-8121 Icosatetraenoate| (also spelled eicosatetraenoate, or ETA) is a polyunsaturated fatty acid that contains four cis double bonds at positions 8, 11, 14 and 17. The last double bond is located at the third carbon from the end of the molecule, making it an ω-3 fatty acid. |FRAME: CPD-8121 Icosatetraenoate| is an intermediate between |FRAME: CPD-12653| and |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE|. It appears to act as as a dual inhibitor of |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| oxygenation by both the cyclooxygenase (COX) and lipoxygenase pathways, and may be responsible for the anti-inflammatory effect of |FRAME: TAX-38949| (green-lipped mussels), in which it is found in high concentrations 12042477. Like other fatty acids, |FRAME: CPD-8121| is rarely found in its free form. It is usually found as either |FRAME: CPD-14394| or |FRAME: CPD-17281 "incorporated into a lipid"|.

Compound.name: a sialyl-Lewis a epitope
Synonyms: an sLe a antigen // alphaNeuNAc-(2->3)-betaGal-(1->3)-[alphaFuc-(1->4]-betaGlcNAc-[protein] // a histo-blood group sialyl Lewis a epitope
Comment: The |FRAME: sLea-Antigen "sialyl-Lewis a epitope"| (SLe a ) was discovered in 1979 with the use of a monoclonal antibody 94699. While the antigen is believed to play an important role during embryogenesis 6381330, in adults only low amounts of the antigen are present on normal epithelial cells |CITS: [6751528][6381289]|. When the selectin family of adhesion molecules was described, it was found that SLe a , along with the |FRAME: sLex-Antigen "sialyl-Lewis x antigen"|, is a ligand for E-selectin. Higher expression of the SLe a antigen in adults is strongly associated with cancer. It was found in high amounts on the surface of human pancreatic, colon and gastric cancer cell lines |CITS: [7142214][6188455]| and in human adenocarcinomas of the colon, stomach, pancreas and gall-bladder |CITS: [94699][6751528][2910493]|. The expression of the antigen has been linked to tumor progression. A gradual increase in SLe a was found in colon and rectum during neoplastic transformation and progression 2863413, and its presence was restricted to tumorigenic and invasive human urothelial cell lines 8900435. The antigen is responsible for adhesion of colon, pancreas, urinary bladder and gastric cancer cells to endothelium via its interaction with selectin E |CITS: [1716885][7687590][7678075][8900435][9578490]|. The expression level of the SLe a antigen is used as a prognostic factor for colorectal carcinoma, and is associated with high incidence of recurrence and the length of survival time |CITS: [8273774][7697593][9303355]|.

Compound.name: a dithiopyrrolone
Comment: Dithiolopyrrolone group antibiotics are characterized by an electronically unique bicyclic structure, which contains a compact disulfide bridge between two ene-thiols. The dithiolopyrrolones exhibit very broad-spectrum antibiotic activity and potent antiangiogenic effects 24835149. The family comprises more than 25 natural variants, isolated from a variety of soil and marine-derived bacteria, including both Gram-positives and Gram-negatives. The earliest dithiopyrrolone to be reported was |FRAME: CPD-17938|, which was isolated from a strain of |FRAME: TAX-37329| (referred to as Actinomyces farcinicus in the original paper) in 1948 Umezawa48.

Compound.name: a rhodoquinol
Comment: Rhodoquinone (RQ) is a modified ubiquinone, where the methoxyl group in position 3 is replaced by an amino group. The compound was originally isolated from TAX-1085 |CITS:[Glover62][14293762] [14285535]|, where is it used for the reduction of fumarate to succinate under anaerobic conditions. Rhodoquinone is not limited to prokaryotes. It was soon discovered that some eukaryotic parasites such as the nematodes |FRAME: TAX-6253| and |FRAME: TAX-6252| |CITS: [5796154][811785]|, as well as parasitic helminths 4795616 also contain rhodoquinone, which is essential for fumarate reduction under anaerobic conditions 2843227. Later it was shown that rhodoquinone is present in all eukaryotes that reduce fumarate during anoxia, including freshwater snails, mussels, lugworms, and oysters 8537365. The reduced form of rhodoquinone is rhodoquinol.

Compound.name: a secoiridoid

Compound.name: an aminated amino group donor
Comment: |FRAME: Amine-Donors "An amino group donor"| is a compound that can donate an amino group to another compound in a reaction catalyzed by enzymes that belong to the |FRAME: EC-2.6.1 transaminase group"| (often called aminotransferases). Prior to donating the amino group the compound is |FRAME: Aminated-Amine-Donors| and after donating it the compound is |FRAME: Deaminated-Amine-Donors|. Since tranmination reactions are reversible, the distinction between an amino group donor and an amino group acceptor is not determined by the actual chemical entity, but by the role it plays in a particular reaction. However, some compounds, such as |FRAME: GLT| and |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, are often used as amino group donors by the aminotransferases in reactions that are physiologically unidirectional. This particular entry is used when the identity of the amino group donor (or acceptor) is not known or cannot be defined.

Compound.name: a heteroarene
Comment: An aromatic compound contains one or more aromatic rings. The pi orbitals of the ring's atoms form a conjugated system and are in resonance, giving increased stability compared to saturated compounds having a similar structure. As a result aromatic rings are very stable and do not break apart easily. Similar structures in which at least one of the ring's carbon atoms is replaced by one of the heteroatoms oxygen, nitrogen, or sulfur, are called heteroarenes.

Compound.name: a glycerolipid

Compound.name: a chaxalactin

The Chaxa Lagoon is a hyper-arid and hypersaline lake and possesses an extremely high content of sodium, sulfate, magnesium, bicarbonate, chlorine, nitrate and arsenic ions. |FRAME: TAX-1437453| produces a variety of specialized metabolites, some of which were shown to possess antibiotic, anti-cancer and anti-inflammatory activities. Among those are two families of polyketide antibiotics, the chaxalactins 21879726 and the ansamycin-like |FRAME: Chaxamycins chaxamycins| 21553813 (see |FRAME: PWY-8036|) 26122045. The chaxalactins belong to the family of 22-membered macrolactone polyketides, which is rather rare in nature (most macrocyclic lactones have a 34-member ring). They were shown to have strong activity against the Gram-positive bacteria |FRAME: TAX-1280| , |FRAME: TAX-1639|, and |FRAME: TAX-1423|, and only weak activity against the Gram-negative bacteria |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-670| 21879726.

Compound.name: an ansamycin
Comment: |FRAME: Ansamycins Ansamycins| are a class of bacterial secondary metabolites that includes several important antibiotics such as the |FRAME: Streptovaricins streptovaricins| and |FRAME: Rifamycins rifamycins|. They are named ansamycins (from the Latin ansa, handle) because of their unique structure, which consists of an aromatic moiety bridged at nonadjacent positions by an aliphatic chain 4148590. The different members of the ansamycin family differ mainly in their aromatic moiety, which can include a naphthalene ring, a naphthoquinone ring, a benzene ring or or a benzoquinone ring.

Compound.name: an XXXG xylogulcan
Comment: |FRAME: Xyloglucan Xyloglucan| is the major hemicellulose in dicotyledon type I cell walls. The cross-linking between xyloglucan chains is a major factor in the stability of the three-dimensional matrix between adjacent cellulose microfibrils Whitney95. Xyloglucan has a backbone of beta-1,4-linked cellotetraose units, which are substituted in C-6 by alpha-D-xylosyl residues at two or three of the first three glucosyl residues, but not in the position closest to the reducing end 8252539. Some of the xylosyl residues are subsequently further substituted by (1,2)-beta-D-galactosyl residues at the second and/or third xylose residue and by (1,2)-alpha-L-fucose at the galactosyl unit of the third xylose residue |CITS:[12837954] [17011813]|. A common terminology uses G for basic non-substituted glucosyl units within a xylosylglycan, X for glucose residues substituted by alpha-D-xylose, L for glucose residues substituted by alpha-D-xylose and beta-D-galactose, and F for glucose residues substituted by alpha-D-xylose, beta-D-galactose and alpha-L-fucose Fry93. Most xylosylglucans consist of repeating heptasaccharide |FRAME: Xyloglucans-Xylose XXXG| units.

Compound.name: NAD(P)H
Comment: |FRAME: NADH-P-OR-NOP| is a class of compounds including the instances |FRAME: NADH| and |FRAME: NADPH|. |FRAME: NAD-P-OR-NOP| is a class of compounds including the instances |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP|. |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP| are dinucleotides containing one |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| base and one |FRAME: ADENINE| base. Each nucleotide is connected to a ribose sugar at position 1, and the two riboses are connected at their 5 position via a diphosphate. The only difference between the two is that in NADP there is an additional phosphate group at the 2' position of the ribose that carries the adenine moiety. These molecules are biological carriers of reductive equivalents (i.e. high potential electrons). They are often referred to as coenzymes, although in most of their reactions they function as cosubstrates rather than true coenzymes. The most common function of |FRAME: NAD| is to accept two electrons and a proton (a hydride ion) from a substrate that is being oxidized. This reduction converts |FRAME: NAD| to |FRAME: NADH|, the reduced form. NADH then diffuses or is transported to a terminal oxidase, where the electrons are passed on, regenerating the oxidized form. |FRAME: NADPH|, on the other hand, is mostly involved in biosynthetic reactions, where it serves as an electron donor. NADPH is formed by reduction of |FRAME: NADP|, which occurs by different mechanisms in different types of organisms. In photosynthetic organisms |FRAME: NADP| is reduced by |FRAME: CPLX-84|. In heterotrophic organisms it is reduced by central metabolism processes such as the pentose phosphate pathway (see |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY|).

Compound.name: Man 6 (GlcNAc) 2 -[protein] (isomer 6A 1,2,3 )

Compound.name: an oxidized flavin

The |FRAME: Oxidized-Flavins "fully oxidized form"| (or quinone form) accepts two electrons and two protons to become the |FRAME: Reduced-Flavins "fully reduced form"| (hydroquinone form). The reduced form can be oxidized to a semireduced form (semiquinone) by donating one electron and one proton. A second oxidation results in restoring the initial quinone form. The conjugated ring system of fully oxidized flavin confers a bright yellow color, and its name is derived from flavus , Latin for yellow. Flavins are synthesized from |FRAME: GTP| in the form of |FRAME: RIBOFLAVIN|, which is later modified into |FRAME: FMN| or |FRAME: FAD|. The plant homeodomain-containing ING2 protein, a candidate tumor suppressor, was shown to act as a nuclear PI5P receptor, a function that regulates its ability to activate p53 12859901. PI5P has also been tied to tumor suppression via its potential regulation of Akt. It was demonstrated that the loss of PI5P, via a conversion to |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA|, resulted in a decrease in Akt activity 12897244. In addition, PI5P was shown to enhance the activity of various myotubularin phosphatases (MTM1, MTMR3, and MTMR6) toward their preferred substrate |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-35-BISPH|, presumably through allosteric regulation 12646134). Chitosan is mostly produced commercially by deacetylation of |FRAME: CHITIN| , which is the structural element in the exoskeleton of crustaceans. The most popular technique for obtaining chitosan is alkaline deacetylation of chitin: this involves boiling chitin in concentrated alkali (50% w/v) for several hours. This process also yields chitosan with a degree of acetylation between 20-30%. However, in such a chitosan, unlike the naturally occurring chitosan, the acetyl groups are uniformly distributed along the polymer chain. Completely de-acetylated forms of chitosan do not exist naturally, but can be synthesized by special chemical treatment.

The first nitrile to be synthesized (in 1782 by Carl Wilhelm Scheele) was that of formate, |FRAME: HCN|, which is an extremely toxic compound (it is an inhibitor of |FRAME: EC-7.1.1.9|). The name nitrile originates from the nitrile of benzoate, |FRAME: CPD-15582|, which was synthesized in 1844 by Hermann Fehling. Nitriles occur naturally in many organisms, and over 120 naturally occurring nitriles have been isolated. It is particularly common in fruit seeds. Compound.name: a pectin
Comment: |FRAME: Pectin "Pectin"| is a structural heteropolysaccharide consisting of a complex set of polysaccharides that is present in most primary cell walls and is particularly abundant in the non-woody parts of terrestrial plants. It is involved in crosslinking cellulose and hemicellulose fibers, which provides rigidity to the cell wall. The characteristic structure of pectin is a linear chain of alpha-(1-4)-linked |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| that forms the pectin-backbone, |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl|. Diferent components of pectin have different substitutions and additions. A common type is |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "rhamnogalacturonan I"| (RG-I), which makes up 20-35% of pectin. In RG-I some of the |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| units in the backbone are replaced by (1-2)-linked |FRAME: L-rhamnose|, to which side chains of various neutral sugars branch off, mostly |FRAME: D-Galactose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| and |FRAME: CPD-25028|. Another common type is |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan II"| (RG-II), which makes up about 10% of pectin. RG-II is based on a backbone of 8-9 galacturonate units, which are decorated by four side chains consisting of 12 different types of sugars in more than 20 different linkages. RG-II usually forms dimeric structures via the formation of crosslinks by a 1:2 borate diol ester between apiosyl residues in one of the side chains. Other types of pectin include chains of |FRAME: Apiogalacturonans apiogalacturonan|, |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl homogalacturonan|, and |FRAME: Xylogalacturonan xylogalacturonan|. There is currently no consensus as to how the pectic polysaccharides are linked to each other, or to other polymers, in the wall. However, it is thought that the different peptides are covalently linked to each other via their backbones, forming a large linear structure with many side branches |CITS: [11423143][12162553][Coenen07]|. In nature, around 80% of the carboxyl groups of the galacturonate units are esterified with |FRAME: METOH|. Some plants, including sugar beet, potatoes and pears, contain pectins with acetylated galacturonate in addition to methyl esters. The salt of partially esterified pectins is called a pectinate, and if the degree of esterification is below 5%, |FRAME: PECTATE|. Pectin is used in the animal feed industry and in the food industry as a gelling agent. Phytopathogenic and saprophytic bacteria and fungi can produce variety of extracellular and intracellular enzymes that degrade pectin and its derivatives. Pectinolytic enzymes such as esterases, hydrolases and lyases, are used in the food, fiber and animal feed industries. There is commercial interest in pectinolytic enzymes to convert the pectin-rich by-products from citrus peel and sugar beet processing to higher value material. In 19618506 18535148 and reviewed in |CITS: [19159926] [REIGNAULT08] [8905080]|. Pectin structure is reviewed in 19616198.

The lipid moiety is mainly two (sometimes one or three) beta-hydroxy fatty acid chains (represented here in part by R1 and R2) linked to each other through an ester bond between the beta-hydroxyl group of the chain distal to the glycosidic bond with the carboxyl group of the chain proximal to the glycosidic bond. The carboxyl group of the distal chain is usually free, but in a few cases it is esterified with a short alkyl group. The fatty acid chains may be saturated, mono-unsaturated, or poly-unsaturated and the chain length may vary from C 8 to C 16 . In rare cases the rhamnose 2-hydroxyl group distal to the glycosidic bond may be acylated with a long chain alkenoate. |CITS: [16160828] [20336292]|. Also see |FRAME: Di-Rhamnolipids| and |FRAME: 3-3-HAAs|.

Compound.name: a dapdiamide
Comment: This family of antibiotics, discovered in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-549|, consists of fumaramoyl and epoxysuccinamoyl dipeptides. It is named for the presence of |FRAME: 23-Diaminopropanoate| (DAP) and two amide linkages in the antibiotic scaffold 20041689. The compounds are similar in structure to synthetic |FRAME: CPD0-1236| dipeptides, which show broad spectrum activity by targeting bacterial and fungal |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.16|, the enzyme that catalyzes the rate-limiting step in the formation of the essential cell-wall building block |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| |CITS: [2111163][1901701]|. These compounds are likely cleaved intracellularly to generate acyl-DAP warheads that interact with the enzyme. The fumaramoyl-DAP warheads which would be derived from |FRAME: CPD-18311|, |FRAME: CPD-17539|, |FRAME: CPD-17540|, |FRAME: CPD-17541| and |FRAME: CPD-17542| provide a conjugated eneamide system that is likely attacked by the thiolate side chain of the active site Cys in the glutaminase domain of the enzyme, leading to alkylation of that residue, preventing the formation of ammonium essential of enzyme activity 2111163. The epoxysuccinamoyl moiety in |FRAME: CPD-18309|, |FRAME: CPD-18310|, and |FRAME: CPD-17543| could function as a similar inactivating electrophile for the catalytic Cys residue 19807062.

This type of ceramide is common in animals, and is produced by desaturation of a sphinganine base within a ceramide (known as |FRAME: CPD3DJ-82|) by |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.17|. Ceramides are found in high concentrations within the cell membrane and are one of the component lipids that make up |FRAME: Sphingomyelins sphingomyelin|, one of the major lipids in the lipid bilayer.

The precursor |FRAME: CPD-195| molecule is first attached to a specific |FRAME: LYS| residue within the lipoyl domain (producing |FRAME: Octanoylated-domains|), and is then converted to lipoate by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.8|, resulting in |FRAME: Lipoyl-Protein-N6-lipoyllysine|. |FRAME: CPLX0-782 "Lipoate synthase"| not only catalyzes the reaction, but is also the source of the two sulfur atoms (see several pathway variants under |FRAME: Lipoate-Biosynthesis|).

Compound.name: a (1->4)-beta-D-xylan
Comment: |FRAME: 1-4-beta-Xylan " (1->4)-beta-D-xylan"| is a polymer of |FRAME: BETA-D-XYLOSE| residues connected by (1->4) links. It is found in the cell walls of plants and some green and red algae, and is the major constituent of |FRAME: Hemicelluloses|. Pure xylan, consisting of only xylopyranosyl residues, is rare. Most forms of |FRAME: 1-4-beta-Xylan| are decorated with other types of sugar.

Compound.name: a GXGG xylogulcan
Comment: |FRAME: Xyloglucan Xyloglucan| is the major hemicellulose in dicotyledon type I cell walls. The cross-linking between xyloglucan chains is a major factor in the stability of the three-dimensional matrix between adjacent cellulose microfibrils Whitney95. Xyloglucan has a backbone of beta-1,4-linked cellotetraose units, which are substituted in C-6 by alpha-D-xylosyl residues at two or three of the first three glucosyl residues, but not in the position closest to the reducing end 8252539. Some of the xylosyl residues are subsequently further substituted by (1,2)-beta-D-galactosyl residues at the second and/or third xylose residue and by (1,2)-alpha-L-fucose at the galactosyl unit of the third xylose residue |CITS:[12837954] [17011813]|. A common terminology uses G for basic non-substituted glucosyl units within a xylosylglycan, X for glucose residues substituted by alpha-D-xylose, L for glucose residues substituted by alpha-D-xylose and beta-D-galactose, and F for glucose residues substituted by alpha-D-xylose, beta-D-galactose and alpha-L-fucose Fry93. Most xylosylglucans consist of repeating heptasaccharide |FRAME: Xyloglucans-Xylose XXXG| units.

Compound.name: compound III
Comment: |FRAME: Compound-0 "Compound 0"|, |FRAME: Compound-I|, and |FRAME: Compound-II| are the names given to intermediate states of the heme-iron center that is formed at the active sites of cytochrome P-450 enzymes and peroxidases during catalysis. I. Cytochrome P-450 In cytochrome P-450 the proximal coordinatioin position of the heme iron, which is bound to the 4 nitrogen atoms of the tetrapyrrole ring, is tethered to the protein via a cysteine thiolate ligand. At its rest state, the iron is found at a low-spin ferric state (III valency). At this state the iron also binds a water molecule as a sixth ligand at the distal axial coordination position. Binding of a substrate to the low-spin ferric enzyme leads to displacement of the water as the sixth ligand and a high spin shift. The substrate-bound complex has a greater reduction potential and more easily accepts a single electron from the redox partner, which can be either |FRAME: EC-1.6.2.4 "a cytochrome P450 reductase"|, |FRAME: Ferredoxins|, or |FRAME: Cytochromes-b5|). After the first reduction, the heme iron binds oxygen, forming an oxy-heme complex. The oxygen is bound at the distal axial coordination position, from which the water molecule has been displaced. Following the transfer of the second electron from the redox partner and two subsequent protonations, a peroxo adduct is formed, known as |FRAME: Compound-0|. Next, the O-O bond is cleaved heterolytically, releasing a water molecule and leaving behind an oxygen atom with only six valence electrons. This highly active oxene oxygen removes one electron from the iron and one from the porphyrin, oxidizing the iron to the unusual valency of IV (ferryl iron) and generating an additional oxidizing equivalent that is delocalized over the porphyrin and thiolate ligands. This ferryl/porphyrin radical cation complex is known as |FRAME: Compound-I| 21071661. When the substrate nears the active site, |FRAME: Compound-I| abstracts an electron from it, converting the substrate into a radical and becoming a protonated non-radical ferryl compound known as |FRAME: Compound-II|. At this point the substrate radical reacts with the oxygen of |FRAME: Compound-II|, forming a new carbon oxygen bond. The product is released, and the iron returns to a valency of III (compound III) OrtizdeMontellano15. II. preoxidases In peroxidases the proximal coordinatioin position of the heme iron, which is bound to the 4 nitrogen atoms of the tetrapyrrole ring, is tethered to the protein via a histidine residue. |FRAME: Compound-I "Compound I"| is produced when the heme iron is oxidized by |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|. A single one-electron reduction step of |FRAME: Compound-I| from an electron donor substrate yields |FRAME: Compound-II|, followed by a second one-electron transfer that returns the enzyme to the ferric oxidation state, thus completing the catalytic cycle. Each electron transfer event converts a substrate molecule to a radical cation, forming two such radicals during a catalytic cycle. In the presence of high concentrations of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| and the absence of a reducing substrate, |FRAME: Compound-II| can be oxidized to |FRAME: Compound-III|, a catalytically inactive form of the enzyme. |FRAME: Compound-III "Compound III"| is converted back to the resting state by spontaneous autoxidation or by oxidation with two molecules of the substrate radical cation 18581264.

Compound.name: a pyrone
Comment: Pyrones (also called pyranones) are a class of heterocyclic chemical compounds. They contain a six-membered heterocyclic, non-aromatic ring consisting of five carbon atoms and one oxygen atom and containing two double bonds and a ketone functional group. Most pyones belong to either of two isomers based on the |FRAME: CPD-11706| (2-pyrone) or |FRAME: CPD-26550| (4-pyrone) structure. The 2-pyrone structure common in nature as part of the |FRAME: Coumarins "coumarin"| ring system, while the 4-pyrone structure is found in some natural chemical compounds such as |FRAME: CPD-26551|, |FRAME: CPD-15508| and |FRAME: KOJIC-ACID|. 3-Pyrone structures exist, but are far less common.

Compound.name: cyanophycin
Comment: |FRAME: Cyanophycin Cyanophycin| is an amino acid polymer that is found in most cyanobacteria. It is a high-molecular weight copolymer, composed of an |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| backbone and |FRAME: ARG| side groups, with typical size of 25-100 kDa. The arginine moieties are linked to the beta-carboxyl group of each aspartate by their alpha-amino group. Cyanophycin is largely insoluble under physiological conditions and is accumulated in the form of granules in the cytoplasm during phosphate or sulfur starvation, generally in the early and mid-stationary phase 16591901. The polymer serves as a temporary nitrogen reserve, which accumulates during the transition from the exponential- to the stationary-growth phase and disappears when balanced growth resumes. |FRAME: ARG| contains 4 nitrogen atoms per molecule, the highest N:C ratio of any amino acid. Even though cyanophycin is considered largely exclusive for cyanobacteria, it is also found in a few heterotrophic bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-62977| |CITS: [11976746][15289556]|.

Compound.name: a bile acid
Comment: Bile (or gall) is a dark green to yellowish brown fluid, produced by the liver of most vertebrates, that aids the digestion of lipids in the small intestine 14097367. In humans bile is produced continuously by the liver and stored and concentrated in the gall bladder. After eating, the bile is discharged into the the first section of the small intestine (the duodenum). The main active ingredient (about 0.7%) of the bile is bile acids. Bile acids are classified into primary and secondary. The primary bile acids are produced in the liver from |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL|, while the secondary bile acids are produced by gut bacteria that modify the primary acids. About half of the cholesterol produced in the body is used for bile acid synthesis. The primary bile acids are conjugated in the liver with |FRAME: GLY| or |FRAME: TAURINE| before secretion into the bile. The structures and proportions of the different bile acids vary among different species 19638645. Bile acids also act as steroid hormones through their interaction with receptors encoded by the NR1H4 and GPBAR1 genes |CITS: [10334992][10360171][19758712][31984784]|.

Compound.name: a [glycerolipid]-stearate
Comment: Stearate is a saturated fatty acid that occurs in many animal and vegetable fats and oils. It is a large constituent in milk fats, lard, and cocoa and shea butters. The name comes from Greek for "hard fat", reflecting the fact that stearate forms a waxy solid 16477801. Stearate was first described by Michel Eugene Chevreul in 1823. In cells |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| is usually found in the form of |FRAME: Stearoyl-ACPs stearoyl-[acp]|, |FRAME: STEAROYL-COA| or |FRAME: Stearoyl-lipid "incorporated into lipids"|.

Compound.name: a cyanohydrin
Comment: A cyanohydrin is an alpha-hydroxynitrile in which the alpha carbon is further substituted.

Compound.name: a ganglioside GP1c
Comment: The gangliosides |FRAME: Ganglioside-GT3 GT3|, |FRAME: Ganglioside-GT2 GT2|, |FRAME: Ganglioside-GT1c GT1c|, |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b GQ1b|, and |FRAME: Ganglioside-GP1c GP1c| belong to the c-series. The majority of gangliosides of normal mammals and birds belong to the a- and b-series (containing one and two molecules of sialic acids attached to the inner galactose, respectively), whereas gangliosides in lower vertebrates and amphibia are almost exclusively from the c-series (containing three sialic acid residues attached to the inner galactose) |CITS: [500707][7361620][7150621][6697683]|. However, the c-series gangliosides also occur in the serum of patients with neuroblastoma and type I diabetes mellitus |CITS: [3300782][2654294]| and have been found in small amounts in human brain 1879553.

Compound.name: a pyrimidine ribonucleoside 5'-triphosphate
Comment: Pyrimidines are heterocyclic aromatic compounds similar to benzene, containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3 of the ring. Three of the nucleosides found in nucleic acids, cytosine, thymine, and uracil, are pyrimidine derivatives.

Compound.name: an H type 1 histo-blood group antigen
Comment: The |FRAME: H-antigen "H antigens"| are fucosylated oligosaccharides that decorate proteins on the surface of red blood cells in people with O blood type. In people with A or B blood types an additional monosaccharide is attached to one of the beta-D-galactosyl residues of the H antigen (|FRAME: CPD-12557| in |FRAME: A-antigen "A antigens"| and |FRAME: GALACTOSE| in |FRAME: B-antigen "B antigens"|). These fucosylated structures are found not only on blood cells but also on many other cell types (mainly epithehal), and it has been suggested that they should be called histo-blood group antigens. The majority of the A, B and H antigens are linked to the ends of long polylactosamine chains attached mainly to band 3 protein (encoded by SLC4A1), the anion exchange protein of the red blood cells. A minor fraction of the antigens is attached to a ceramide moiety, forming neutral glycosphingolipids. Several H antigens exist, differing in their core disaccharide 2093726. The different types are: |FRAME: Type-1-H-Antigen "Type 1"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->3)-betaGlcNac-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-2-H-Antigen "Type 2"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->4)-betaGlcNac-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-3-H-Antigen "Type 3"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->3)-alphaGalNac-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-4-H-Antigen "Type 4"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->3)-betaGalNac-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-5-H-Antigen "Type 5"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->3)-betaGal-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-6-H-Antigen "Type 6"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->4)-betaGlc-(1->R) Most of the H antigens found in the cell are either type 1 or type 2, followed by type 3 and 4. Type 1 is found in secretions and in the serum, while type 2 is found exclusively on the surface of red blood cells. Type 6 molecules have been described in exocrine secretions. It is not clear if type 5 H antigens exist, although the type 5 precursor has been characterized 2093726.

Compound.name: a purine nucleoside
Comment: Nucleosides are glycosylamines consisting of |FRAME: Bases| bound to a |FRAME: CPD0-1110 ribose| or |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE| sugar via a beta-glycosidic linkage. The nucleosides are called |FRAME: Ribonucleosides ribonucleosides| when the sugar is |FRAME: CPD0-1110 ribose|, and |FRAME: Deoxy-Ribonucleosides deoxyribonucleosides| when it is |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE|. Common |FRAME: Ribonucleosides ribonucleosides| include |FRAME: CYTIDINE|, |FRAME: URIDINE|, |FRAME: ADENOSINE|, |FRAME: GUANOSINE| and |FRAME: INOSINE|. Examples of |FRAME: Deoxy-Ribonucleosides deoxyribonucleosides| include |FRAME: THYMIDINE| and |FRAME: DEOXYADENOSINE|. When nucleosides are phosphorylated on the sugar's primary alcohol group, the resulting phosphonucleosides are called |FRAME: Nucleotides nucleotides|. Purines are heterocyclic aromatic compounds that contain a |FRAME: PYRIMIDINE-RING| ring fused to an |FRAME: IMIDAZOLE-RING| ring. Two of the ribonucleosides in nucleic acids, |FRAME: ADENOSINE| and |FRAME: GUANOSINE|, are purines.

Compound.name: a polyprenol

Compound.name: an epsilon-lactone
Comment: A |FRAME: Lactones "lactone"| is a cyclic ester, the product of condensation of an alcohol group and a carboxylate group within the same molecule. It is characterized by a closed ring consisting of two or more carbon atoms and a single oxygen atom, with a ketone group in one of the carbons adjacent to the ring oxygen. There are several types of lactones - |FRAME: Beta-lactones| contain 3 carbons in the ring, Gamma-lactones contains 4, Delta-lactones contains 5, and Epsilon-lactones contains 6 carbons.

Compound.name: a chondroitin sulfate
Comment: |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates "Chondroitin sulfate"| is a sulfated |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycan"| composed of alternating units of |FRAME: CPD-12557|(beta1,3)|FRAME: CPD-12521| linked to each other by a beta(1,4) linkage. It is usually found attached to proteins as part of a proteoglycan. Chondroitin sulfate is a major component of connective tissue matrix (such as skin and cartilage), but is also found on cell surface and basement membranes and in intracellular granules of certain cells. Functions in matrix locations are mainly structural, while functions in membranes are mainly as receptors. The saccharide units can be sulfated in variable positions and quantities - |FRAME: CPD-12557| can be sulfated at positions 4 and 6 to yield |FRAME: CPD-12516|, |FRAME: CPD-12565| or |FRAME: CPD-12526|, while |FRAME: CPD-12521| can be sulfated at position 2 to form |FRAME: CPD-12527| (the sulfate group is indicated as R3 in the diagram below). The following names have been used to define different sulfation states: |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-A "Chondroitin sulfate A"| contains |FRAME: CPD-12521| and |FRAME: CPD-12516| |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-C "Chondroitin sulfate C"| contains |FRAME: CPD-12521| and |FRAME: CPD-12565| |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-D "Chondroitin sulfate D"| contains |FRAME: CPD-12527| and |FRAME: CPD-12565| |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-E "Chondroitin sulfate E"| contains |FRAME: CPD-12521| and |FRAME: CPD-12526| The term "chondroitin sulfate B" has been used in the past to refer to |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate|, but is not used any more.

Compound.name: a ceramide NdS
Comment: The human skin outermost layer (the stratum corneum) contains 12 main types of free ceramides. Two nomenclature systems have been used for the description of these ceramides. The older numbering system is based on the chromatographic migration (ceramide 1 to ceramide 8) and chronological arrangement of their publication (from ceramide 9 and on). A newer system is based on the molecular structure |CITS: [8357845][7868984]|. In this system each ceramide type is named by two or three letters, where the front letter(s) designate the acyl chain: N (non-hydroxy fatty acid), A (alpha-hydroxy fatty acid), O (ω--hydroxy fatty acid, or EO (an ω-hydroxy fatty acid esterified to linoleic acid), and the last letter designates the sphingoid base: S (|FRAME: SPHINGOSINE|), dS (|FRAME: CPD-13612 sphinganine|), P (|FRAME: PHYTOSPINGOSINE|), or H (|FRAME: CPD-22027|). The 12 types of free stratum corneum ceramides are |FRAME: Ceramide-EOS| (ceramide 1), |FRAME: Ceramide-NS| (ceramide 2), |FRAME: Ceramide-NP| (ceramide 3), |FRAME: Ceramide-EOH| (ceramide 4), |FRAME: Ceramide-AS| (ceramide 5), |FRAME: Ceramide-AP| (ceramide 6), |FRAME: Ceramide-AH| (ceramide 7), |FRAME: Ceramide-NH| (ceramide 8), |FRAME: Ceramide-EOP| (ceramide 9), ,|FRAME: Ceramide-NdS| (ceramide 10), |FRAME: Ceramide-AdS| (ceramide 11), and |FRAME: Ceramide-EOdS| (ceramide 12) |CITS: [7868984][18329855][23954553]|. The four EO types, |FRAME: Ceramide-EOS|, |FRAME: Ceramide-EOH|, |FRAME: Ceramide-EOP|, and |FRAME: Ceramide-EOdS|, are also known as |FRAME: Linoleate-Acylceramides acylceramides|. The four O-type ceramides of the stratum corneum are not found among the free ceramides, as they form an ester-linkage via their ω-hydroxyl group to to glutamate residues of proteins in the cornified envelope 27432202.

Compound.name: a VB type gamma-butyrolactone
Comment: The Gram-positive, soil-inhabiting, filamentous bacteria of the genus |FRAME: TAX-1883| use a number of chemical compounds including |FRAME: Gamma-Butyrolactones "gamma-butyrolactones"|, |FRAME: MMFs "methylenomycin furans"|, |FRAME: CPD-19905|, and |FRAME: Butenolides "gamma-butenolides"|, as chemical signalling molecules or microbial hormones, which, together with their specific receptors, regulate morphological and/or physiological differentiation 2268871. At least 60% of Streptomyces species appear to produce gamma-butyrolactones, although (as of 2011), only a small number of which have been identified 21090718. Based on their structures, these gamma-butyrolactones have been classified into three types: the |FRAME: A-factor-type-lactones "A-factor type"|, |FRAME: Virginiae-butanolides "virginiae butanolide (VB) type"|, and |FRAME: IM-2-type-lactones "IM-2 type"|, all of which share the cyclic butanolide skeleton |CITS: [14523609][19778723]|. The VB-type compounds were originally isolated from |FRAME: TAX-1961|, where they control |FRAME: CPD-19910 virginiamycin| production. They contain a 6-alpha-hydroxy group |CITS: [3108224][3145258][2621168]|.

Compound.name: a hydroxamate siderophore
Comment: Siderophores are small, high-affinity iron chelating compounds usually produced and secreted by microorganisms. Once outside the cell, siderophores bind |FRAME: FE+3| with high affinity, and the iron-siderophore complexes are imported back into the cell by active-transport mechanisms. Siderophores are very common in pathogenic bacteria, since iron in the host organism is usually tightly bound to proteins, resulting in an extremely low concentration of free iron in the blood. Most siderophores belong to one of three major groups: the |FRAME: Catecholate-siderophores "catechols"|, |FRAME: Hydroxamate-siderophores "hydroxamates"| and |FRAME: Thiazoline-siderophores "thiazolines"|. Some grasses are known to make siderophores as well. These |FRAME: Phytosiderophores "phytosiderophores"| are also known as mugineic acids. Hydroxamate siderophores are named based on the presence of a |FRAME: Hydroxamates hydroxamate| element in their structures.

Compound.name: isolichenan
Comment: |FRAME: Isolichenin Isolichenin| is a complex glucan characterized from from Iceland Moss (|FRAME: TAX-78064|). It consists solely of D-glucose residues united by alpha(1-3)- and beta(1-4)-glucosidic linkages which are present in the relative proportion of 3:2. The molecule appears to be linear, with an average chain length of 42-44 glucose residues Chanda57.

Compound.name: a pteroate
Comment: Pteroate is the name given of a specific compund (|FRAME: PTEROATE|), but also serves as the name of a class of compounds that are based on the |FRAME: PTEROATE| skeleton. When conjugated to a |FRAME: GLT| molecule,pteroates form |FRAME: All-Folates folates|.

Compound.name: rubber
Comment: Natural rubber is an important raw material in an enormous number of products. The backbone of natural rubber comprises a ( cis )-1,4-polyisoprene with two or three trans -isoprene units at the ω-terminus, formed by the sequential condensation of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (IPP) units in cis configuration onto a short all-trans prenyl diphosphate. It is very similar in structure to |FRAME: DOLICHOL dolichols|, but the chain length is much longer (C>1500). Natural rubber is produced from latex - a material that makes up the cytoplasmic content of the latecifers or latex vessels of |FRAME: TAX-3981| (the Brazilian rubber tree) 17545224. Although over 2000 plant species capable of producing rubber have been identified, only a few synthesize the high molecular weight rubber that is required for the production of high quality rubber products, and natural rubber is currently produced commercially only from |FRAME: TAX-3981|. A potential alternative source is the Russian rubber-producing dandelion (|FRAME: TAX-333970|), which was cultivated in the former Soviet Union during World War II to satisfy the demand for natural rubber 22504822. Rubber biosynthesis is carried out by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.20|. The enzyme is localized at the surface of cytosolic vesicles known as rubber particles, and biosynthesis is initiated through the binding of an allylic pyrophosphate primer, such as |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| |CITS: [Tanaka01][14622254][18799172]|. The R in the structure stands for an unspecified number of ( cis )-connected isoprene units.

Compound.name: an O -linked glycoprotein
Comment: O -Linked glycans are polysaccharide or oligosaccharide that are linked to a protein via the oxygen atom in the side chain of a |FRAME: SER| or |FRAME: THR| residue. Most commonly O-glycosylation begins with the attachment of |FRAME: CPD-3604| to the free hydroxyl group of the amino acid, although O-linkages to fucose, glucose, mannose, xylose and other sugars are known. Mucin-type O-glycosylation, consisting of glycans attached via O-linked |FRAME: CPD-3604|, is one of the most abundant forms of protein glycosylation in animals. Eight core-type structures of mucin-type O -glycans have been proposed. In eukaryotes, O -linked glycans are assembled in the Golgi apparatus one sugar at a time, while attached to the core protein. Examples for O -linked glycoproteins include glycophorin, |FRAME: Mucin mucin|, notch, thrombospondin, |FRAME: Factor-VII "factor VII"| and |FRAME: Factor-IX "factor IX"|.

Compound.name: a 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA
Comment: ACYL-COA are oxoacids that have been activated by |FRAME: CO-A|. They are often classified by the length of their acyl moiety. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Medium-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from fatty acids with aliphatic tails of 6-12 carbons. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Long-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from fatty acids with aliphatic tails of 13-21 carbons. |FRAME: VERY-LONG-CHAIN-FATTY-ACYL-COA "Very long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from fatty acids with aliphatic tails of 22 carbons or longer.

Compound.name: a 2'-deoxyribonucleotide
Comment: A nucleotide is composed of |FRAME: Bases| (nitrogenous base), a five-carbon sugar (either |FRAME: CPD0-1110 ribose| or |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE|), and one to three phosphate groups. When joined together, nucleotides make up the structural units of RNA and DNA. The nucleotides are called |FRAME: Ribonucleotides| when the sugar is |FRAME: CPD0-1110 ribose|, and |FRAME: Deoxynucleotides| when it is |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE|.

Compound.name: cellulose
Comment: Cellulose is the most common organic compound on Earth. It is a polysaccharide consisting of a linear chain of several hundred to over ten thousand beta(1->4) linked D-glucose units, and is the structural component of the primary cell wall of green plants, many forms of algae and the oomycetes. Cellulose is a straight chain polymer. Unlike |FRAME: Starch starch| or |FRAME: Glycogens glycogen|, there is no coiling or branching, and the molecule adopts an extended and stiff rod-like conformation. The multiple hydroxyl groups on the glucose moieties from one chain form hydrogen bonds with oxygen atoms on neighbor chains, holding the chains firmly together side-by-side and forming microfibrils with high tensile strength. Several different crystalline structures of cellulose are known, corresponding to the location of hydrogen bonds between and within strands. Known crystalline forms are named cellulose I, cellulose II, cellulose III and cellulose IV. Cellulose I is further divided into Ialpha and Ibeta, with the former formed by bacteria and algae and the latter by higher plants. Crystalline cellulose is not soluble. It is converted to a soluble, amorphus structure only at a temperature of 320 °C. Molecules with very small chain length, known as |FRAME: Cellodextrins cellodextrins|, are typically soluble in water and organic solvents.

Compound.name: an aralkylamine
Comment: This compound class collects various arylalkylamines.

Compound.name: beta-D-glucosyluronate-[heparan sulfate]
Comment: This compounds describes an |FRAME: CPD-12521| residue located at the non-reducing end of |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate|.

Compound.name: monogalactosyldiacylglycerol-34:3
Comment: In this group of monogalactosyldiacylglycerols, the length of the two acyl chains, and the location and number of the double bonds varies. For each of the group members, the total number of carbon atoms in the two acyl chains adds up to 34, and the total number of double bonds in the two acyl groups adds up to 3.

Compound.name: a high-mannose N -linked glycoprotein
Comment: High-mannose glycans typically contain between five and nine mannose residues attached to a chitobiose (GlcNAc 2 ) core, which links the glycan to an |FRAME: ASN| residue of a protein.

Compound.name: acetylxylan
Comment: |FRAME: 1-4-beta-Xylan (1->4)-beta-D-xylan| is present in some trees and other plants in a partially acetylated form. Angiosperm (hardwood) xylans (e.g. from beechwood) have a high rate of substitution (70-80%) by acetyl groups at position 2 and/or 3 of the beta-D-xylopyranosyl residues, conferring on the xylan its partial solubility in water 8338637.

Compound.name: an oxacycle
Comment: An oxacycle is an organic heterocyclic compound containing at least one ring oxygen atom.

Compound.name: a glyco-amino acid
Comment: The glycation reaction, also known as the Maillard reaction, as first identified by the French chemist L. Maillard, is ubiquitous in nature. The reaction involves the formation of Schiff's bases between reducing sugars (such as glucose) and biological amines such as an amino acid, which then rearrange to form stable ketoamine products, or amadori compounds.

Compound.name: a lipoxin
Comment: Lipoxins belong to the icosanoid family. They are generated from |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| during inflammation and have a distinct structure containing 4 conjugated double bonds. Lipoxins consist of two distinct isomers, as exemplified by |FRAME: CPD66-51| (LXA4) and |FRAME: CPD66-56| (LXB4). These lipid-derived mediators play an important role in modulating the inflammatory response. |FRAME: CPD66-51 "Lipoxin A4"| (LXA4) dampens the immune response by inhibiting leukocyte chemotaxis, transmigration and adhesion 83260192548801. It also promotes the resolution phase of inflammation by enhancing phagocytosis of apoptotic leukocytes by macrophages 10657608. These activities are brought about through the G protein-coupled receptor ALX 16968948. See |FRAME: PWY66-392|.

Compound.name: a triterpenoid
Comment: |FRAME: Terpenoids Terpenoids| make up a very large family of natural products containing more than 50,000 structurally diverse compounds. They are categorized by the number of C5 isoprene units as follows: |FRAME: Hemiterpenes Hemiterpenoids| (one C5 unit), |FRAME: Monoterpenes monoterpenoids| (C10; two C5 units), |FRAME: Sesquiterpenes sesquiterpenoids| (C15; three C5 units), |FRAME: Diterpenes diterpenoids| (C20; four C5 units), |FRAME: Sesterterpenes sesterterpenoids| (C25; five C5 units), |FRAME: Triterpenes triterpenoids| (C30; six C5 units), |FRAME: C35-Terpenes "sesquarterpenoids"| (C35; seven C5 units), and |FRAME: Tetraterpenes tetraterpenoids| (C40; eight C5 units).

Compound.name: an HOTrE
Comment: HOTrE is an acronym for HydroxyOctadecaTriEnoate. It describes a family of monohydroxylated fatty acids containing three double bonds that originate from |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| or |FRAME: CPD-8117|. HOTrEs are usually derived from the respective hydoperoxylated compounds.

Compound.name: a poly[( R )-3-hydroxyalkanoate]
Synonyms: a polyhydroxyalkanoate // PHA // a polyhydroxyalkanoic acid
Comment: Polyhydroxyalkanoates or PHAs are linear polyesters produced in nature by bacteria as a means of carbon and energy storage. The building blocks for PHA are coenzyme A - thioesters of ( R )-hydroxy fatty acids. Two classes of PHA synthases exist, and differ in their specificity towards short- or medium-chain substrates. Depending on the enzyme, the resulting PHAs are divided into two main categories: Poly (HA SCL) are formed from hydroxy fatty acids with short chain lengths of three to five carbon atoms. Poly (HA MCL) are formed from hydroxy fatty acids with medium chain lengths of six to 14 carbon atoms. A few bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-644| and |FRAME: TAX-1057|, can synthesize PHAs that contain both short- and medium-chain hydroxy fatty acids.

Compound.name: a phthiodiolone B
Comment: |FRAME: Phthiodiolones Phthiodiolones| are intermediates in |FRAME: Phthiocerols phthiocerol| biosynthesis. They contain an oxo group where phthiocerols contain a methoxyl group. Two types of phthiodiolone exist. In |FRAME: Phthiodiolone-A "phthiodiolone A"| the oxo and the methyl groups are attached at positions 3 and 4, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 9 and 11. In |FRAME: Phthiodiolone-B "phthiodiolone B"| a methyl group is missing from the beginning of the molecule, and thus the oxo and methyl groups are attached at positions 2 and 3, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 8 and 10.

Compound.name: an aliphatic diamine
Comment: This compound class collects various aliphatic diamines.

Compound.name: an IM-2 type gamma-butyrolactone
Comment: The Gram-positive, soil-inhabiting, filamentous bacteria of the genus |FRAME: TAX-1883| use a number of chemical compounds including |FRAME: Gamma-Butyrolactones "gamma-butyrolactones"|, |FRAME: MMFs "methylenomycin furans"|, |FRAME: CPD-19905|, and |FRAME: Butenolides "gamma-butenolides"|, as chemical signalling molecules or microbial hormones, which, together with their specific receptors, regulate morphological and/or physiological differentiation 2268871. At least 60% of Streptomyces species appear to produce gamma-butyrolactones, although (as of 2011), only a small number of which have been identified 21090718. Based on their structures, these gamma-butyrolactones have been classified into three types: the |FRAME: A-factor-type-lactones "A-factor type"|, |FRAME: Virginiae-butanolides "virginiae butanolide (VB) type"|, and |FRAME: IM-2-type-lactones "IM-2 type"|, all of which share the cyclic butanolide skeleton |CITS: [14523609][19778723]|. The original |FRAME: CPD-19915| compound was isolated from |FRAME: TAX-74574|, where it controls the production of the nucleoside antibiotics |FRAME: CPD-19916| and |FRAME: CPD-19917| Hashimoto92.

Compound.name: elemental selenium
Comment: Selenium is an essential trace element that is crucial for the normal development of bacteria and animals. High concentrations of selenium are however toxic, largely because transporters and enzymes involved in sulfur and sulfo-compound metabolism can often erroneously substitute |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| for sulfur and can misincorporate seleno-amino acids into proteins 21913064. In humans the safety threshold between acute selenium poisoning (>400 mug/day) and selenium deficiency (<40 mug/day) is very narrow. The natural forms of selenium include |FRAME: SELENATE| [Se(VI)], |FRAME: SELENITE| [Se(IV)], |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| [Se(0)], and |FRAME: SE-2| [Se(-II)]. Selenite is the most toxic, while elemental selenium is insoluble and is generally considered to be non-toxic 25631289. However, selenium rarely occurs in its elemental state in nature. Elemental selenium can be formed by certain organisms, usually by reduction of the oxidized forms |FRAME: SELENATE| and |FRAME: SELENITE|. Some bacterial species are known to form selenium nanoparticles that consist of elemental selenium coated by a mixture of proteins, lipids, and carbohydrates |CITS: [26801915][32854560][35398797]|. Elemental selenium occurs in nature in two main allotropic forms. The most stable allotrope is a polymeric form that appears as a dense purplish-gray solid. It forms polyselenides in the presence of strong reducing agents. The second major allotrope is red selenium which, similar to |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|, forms individual molecules of eight-membered rings (although rings composed of more or less than 8 selenium atoms have been reported). Red selenium converts to the gray polymeric allotrope upon heating.

Compound.name: a monoterpenoid indole alkaloid
Comment: Monoterpenoid indole alkaloids (MIAs) are a very large class of terpenoid indole alkaloids synthesized by the Apocynaceae, Loganiaceae, and Rubiaceae plant families. Almost all of the 2000 known members are derived from |FRAME: STRICTOSIDINE|, which is biosynthesized from |FRAME: TRP| and |FRAME: SECOLOGANIN-CPD|. Though more than 42 skeletons have been described, they can be classified according to their carbon skeleton and biogenetic branch points into five major subgroups - the Aspidosperma, Ajmalan, Corynanthe, Iboga, and Quinoline alkaloids. Some of the MIAs exhibit a broad range of biological activities including anticancer, antimalarial, and antiarrhythmic properties.

Compound.name: a holothin
Comment: Dithiolopyrrolone group antibiotics are characterized by an electronically unique bicyclic structure, which contains a compact disulfide bridge between two ene-thiols. The dithiolopyrrolones exhibit very broad-spectrum antibiotic activity and potent antiangiogenic effects 24835149. The family comprises more than 25 natural variants, isolated from a variety of soil and marine-derived bacteria, including both Gram-positives and Gram-negatives. The earliest dithiopyrrolone to be reported was |FRAME: CPD-17938|, which was isolated from a strain of |FRAME: TAX-37329| (referred to as Actinomyces farcinicus in the original paper) in 1948 Umezawa48. The holothins are |FRAME: Dithiopyrrolones dithiopyrrolones| based on the core structure of |FRAME: CPD-17948|.

Compound.name: a sialyl-Lewis x epitope
Synonyms: an sLe x antigen // alphaNeuNAc-(2->3)-betaGal-(1->4)-[alphaFuc-(1->3]-betaGlcNAc-[protein] // a sialyl Lewis x antigen // a histo-blood group sialyl Lewis x antigen
Comment: The sialyl Lewis-X (SLeX) antigen is expressed on glycolipids and glycoproteins on the cell surfaces. In adults, SLeX antigen is expressed principally on the surfaces of granulocytic cells. It plays an important role during early steps of inflammatory response as a ligand of the three known selectins - E-selectin (also known as endothelial leucocyte adhesion molecules, ELAM-1), P-Selectin, and L-selectin, resulting in the capture of leucocytes from the plasma and their attachment to blood endothelial cells |CITS: [2210723][7591266]|. In the case of L-selectin, the antigen needs to be sulfated first, forming |FRAME: 6-Sulfo-sLex-Antigen| 9556613. The antigen is expressed in high frequency in tumor tissue where it plays a role in adhesion between tumor cells and blood endothelial cells during tumor metastases |CITS: [6386148][12029441][1699667][1701275]|. The SLeX antigen is synthesized from |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R| by the action of two enzymes, |FRAME: EC-2.4.3.6| and |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.152| |CITS: [1339443][25498912]|.

Compound.name: a guaiacol
Synonyms: an O -methoxyphenol // a catechol monomethyl ether
Comment: This class includes any phenol carrying an additional methoxy substituent at the ortho-position.

Compound.name: a bacterial endotoxin
Comment: This compound class stands for generic and unspecified bacterial endotoxins. These are components from the outer membrane and cell wall of bacteria, which are toxic to humans and can cause sepsis. The Gram negative bacteria produce lipopolysaccharides, whereas the Gram positive bacteria produce the less active lipoteichoic acids and muramyl peptides.

Compound.name: a [glycerolipid]-vaccenate
Comment: |FRAME: CPD-9247 " cis -Vaccenate"| is produced from |FRAME: CPD-9245| by bacteria and plants. It is one of only two unsaturated fatty acids in |FRAME: TAX-562| 6988423 (see |FRAME: PWY-5973|). Some plant species such as |FRAME: TAX-48545| and |FRAME: TAX-73871| ( Doxantha unguis-cati L.) produce relatively high levels of |FRAME: CPD-9245| and |FRAME: CPD-9247| in their seed oils |CITS: [CHISHOLMMJ60][CHISHOLMMJ65]|. The plant pathway is likely identical to the bacterial one (in 20943853). Like other fatty acids, |FRAME: CPD-9247| is rarely found in its free form. It is usually found as either |FRAME: Cis-vaccenoyl-ACPs " cis -vaccenoyl-[acp]"| or |FRAME: Vaccenoyl-Lipid "incorporated into a lipid"|.

Compound.name: a di-rhamnolipid
Comment: This class contains glycosides composed of a di-rhamnose moiety joined in an O -glycosidic linkage to a lipid moiety. The rhamnose moieties are linked to each other through an alpha-1,2-glycosidic linkage. The lipid moiety is mainly two (sometimes one or three) beta-hydroxy fatty acid chains (represented here in part by R1 and R2) linked to each other through an ester bond between the beta-hydroxyl group of the chain distal to the glycosidic bond with the carboxyl group of the chain proximal to the glycosidic bond. The carboxyl group of the distal chain is usually free, but in a few cases it is esterified with a short alkyl group. The fatty acid chains may be saturated, mono-unsaturated, or poly-unsaturated and the chain length may vary from C 8 to C 16 . In rare cases the rhamnose 2-hydroxyl group distal to the glycosidic bond may be acylated with a long chain alkenoate. |CITS: [16160828] [20336292]|. Also see |FRAME: Mono-Rhamnolipids| and |FRAME: 3-3-HAAs|.

Compound.name: a saturated fatty acid
Comment: |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "A fatty acid"| is a carboxylic acid with a long unbranched aliphatic tail. Even though fatty acids derived from natural fats and oils, such as CPD-195, are usually at least 8 carbon atoms long, carboxylic acids as short as BUTYRIC_ACID (4 carbon atoms) are considered to be fatty acids. When a fatty acid contains only single bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Saturated-Fatty-Acids|. When it contains one or more double bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Unsaturated-Fatty-Acids|. If it contains a double bond in the trans configuration, it is often referred to as a trans fatty acid. Most fatty acids in the trans configuration are not found in nature and are the result of human processing.

Compound.name: a carbapenem
Comment: This compound class stands for |FRAME: Lactams lactams| in which the amide bond is contained within a four-membered ring, which includes the amide nitrogen and the carbonyl carbon. beta-Lactam compounds imitate the naturally occurring |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| substrate for the group of enzymes known as penicillin binding proteins (PBPs), which cross-link the peptidoglycan in bacterial cell wall, and thus act as powerful antibiotics 6109324. Naturally occurring |FRAME: Beta-Lactams "beta-lactam antibiotics"| are classified into several groups according to their chemical structure: In |FRAME: Monolactams monolactams| the beta-lactam ring is not fused to another ring. This class includes compounds such as the |FRAME: Nocardicins nocardicins| 3427723 and the |FRAME: Monobactams monobactams| 3909315. In |FRAME: Penams penams| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a saturated five atom ring (a 4:5 structure). Penams contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring (for example, the |FRAME: PENICILLIN penicillins|) 6335599. Related classes include the |FRAME: Carbapenams carbapenams|, which contain a carbon atom in that position 12890666, and the |FRAME: Clavams oxopenams| (also known as clavams), which contain an oxygen atom at that position (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9261|) 3304182. |FRAME: Penems Penems| are molecues similar to penams in which the five atom ring is unsaturated at positions 2-3. Similarly, penems contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring, while |FRAME: Carbapenems carbapenems| contains a carbon atom in that position 16413506. In |FRAME: Cephams cephams| and |FRAME: Cephems cephems| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a six-atom ring (a 4:6 strcuture) that contains a sulfur atom at position 1. In cephams the ring is saturated, while cephems have an unsaturated bond at positions 3-4 |CITS: [1164170][12722308]|. 1-Oxocephams/1-oxacephems conain an oxygen atom at position 1 |CITS: [11671696][11078187]|.

Compound.name: a 1,2-diacyl-3-O-[beta-D-galactosyl-(1->6)-beta-D-galactosyl]- sn -glycerol
Synonyms: a (beta-D-galactosyl-(1->6)-beta-D-galactosyl)-1,2-diacyl- sn -glycerol // an beta-D-galactosyl-beta-D-galactosyldiacylglycerol // DGDG // a beta,beta digalactosyldiacylglycerol
Comment: Note, this is different from the most commonly found DGDG, the alpha-D-galactosyl-(1->6)-beta-D-galactosyl)-1,2-diacyl- sn -glycerol (|FRAME: Galactosyl-galactosyl-diacyl-glycerols|).

Compound.name: fucose
Comment: Fucose is a hexose deoxy sugar. It received its name from the brown algae genus |FRAME: TAX-3011|, from which it was first decribed. The alga was named because of its dark redish color, as one of the meanings of the Latin word fucus is "red paint". Algae of the |FRAME: TAX-3009| order produce fucose-rich polysaccahrides known as |FRAME: Fucoidans fucoidans|. However, fucose is a common sugar, found in N -linked glycans on the mammalian, insect and plant cell surface, in many bacterial glycans, and in other biomolecules. Most of the fucose found in biology is in the |FRAME: L-fucoses "L conformation"|, and the use of |FRAME: D-Fucoses| is rather rare (for example in some |FRAME: Cardenolide-Glycosides "cardenolide glycosides"|).

Compound.name: a flavanone glycoside
Comment: A member of the class of flavanones having one or more glycosyl residues attached at unspecified positions.

Compound.name: a phthiodiolone
Comment: |FRAME: Phthiodiolones Phthiodiolones| are intermediates in |FRAME: Phthiocerols phthiocerol| biosynthesis. They contain an oxo group where phthiocerols contain a methoxyl group. Two types of phthiodiolone exist. In |FRAME: Phthiodiolone-A "phthiodiolone A"| the oxo and the methyl groups are attached at positions 3 and 4, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 9 and 11. In |FRAME: Phthiodiolone-B "phthiodiolone B"| a methyl group is missing from the beginning of the molecule, and thus the oxo and methyl groups are attached at positions 2 and 3, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 8 and 10.

Compound.name: a medium-chain 3-hydroxy fatty acyl-CoA
Comment: Fatty acyl-CoAs are |FRAME: ACYL-COA "acyl-CoAs"| derived from |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "fatty acids"|. Many enzymes that act on fatty acids, as well as the corresponding |FRAME: Fatty-Acyl-CoAs "fatty acyl-CoAs"|, |FRAME: Fatty-Alcohols alcohols|, and |FRAME: Fatty-Aldehydes aldehydes|, have evolved to recognize substrates with a limited range of chain lengths. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Short-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Medium-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Long-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "fatty acids that have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: VERY-LONG-CHAIN-FATTY-ACYL-COA "Very-long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Ultra-Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Ultra-long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain"|.

Compound.name: a uronate
Comment: Uronic acids are carbohydrate acids formally derived by oxidation of the terminal hydroxyl group of any |FRAME: Aldoses aldose| or |FRAME: Ketoses ketose| to a carboxy group.

Compound.name: a 1-lysophosphatidylcholine
Synonyms: a 2-acylglycero-3-phosphocholine // a L-1-lysolecithin // a 1-lyso-2-acyl- sn -glycero-3-phosphocholine // a 1-lysolecithin // a beta-lysophosphatidylcholine // a 2-acylglycerophosphocholine // a 2-acyl 1-lyso- sn -glycero-3-phosphatidylcholine // a 2-acyl- sn -glycero-3-phosphocholine

Compound.name: a chrysogenamide
Comment: |FRAME: CPD-25433 "Chrysogenamide A"| was isolated from the fungus |FRAME: TAX-5076|, an endophytic fungus associated with |FRAME: TAX-161395|, a parasitic plant commonly known as desert-broomrape. The compound exhibited a neurocyte protection effect against oxidative stress-induced cell death in SH-SY5Y cells 18408327. The chrysogenamides belong to a diverse family of biologically active prenylated indole alkaloids isolated mainly from various |FRAME: TAX-5073| and |FRAME: TAX-5052| species of fungi that contains a unique bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane core ring system, and are derived from |FRAME: TRP|, a cyclic amino acid (|FRAME: PRO|, |FRAME: L-PIPECOLATE| or a derivative of one of those compounds), and one or two isoprene units. In addition to their structural diversity, members of this family have been attributed a variety of bioactivities, including (but not limited to) insecticidal, cytotoxic, anthelmintic, and antibacterial properties. The bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane-containing compounds can be divided into two sub-categories: the diketopiperazines (DKPs) and the monoketopiperazines (MKPs). DKPs include the |FRAME: Stephacidins stephacidins|, |FRAME: Brevianamides brevianamides|, and |FRAME: Notoamides notoamides|, while MKPs include the |FRAME: Paraherquamides paraherquamides|, |FRAME: Asperparalines asperparalines|, |FRAME: Marcfortines marcfortines|, |FRAME: Chrysogenamides chrysogenamides|,and |FRAME: Malbrancheamides malbrancheamides|. Two distinct stereochemical configurations have been noted with respect to the relative configuration of the bridging amide of the bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane core. Most compounds have a syn -configuration (in which the the C-19 position (brevianamide numbering) and the bridging amide point at the same direction), but a few (such as |FRAME: CPD-25433| and |FRAME: CPD-25434|) have an anti configuration. |FRAME: CPD-25433 "Chrysogenamide A"| is closely related to the marcfortines in that it contains not only a bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane ring system but also a spiro-oxindole moiety and a pipecolate unit with C-17 methylation. It also displays the rare anti configuration and an isoprene unit at the C-7 indole position 22502590.

Compound.name: a very long-chain alkane
Comment: Alkanes are saturated acyclic hydrocarbons. They consist only of hydrogen and saturated carbon atoms and are bonded exclusively by single bonds. They could be either branched or unbranched. Linear alkanes are often classified by the length of their acyl moiety. |FRAME: Short-Chain-Alkanes "Short-chain alkanes"| contain less than 6- carbons. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Alkanes "Medium-chain alkanes"| contain 6-12 carbons. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Alkanes "Long-chain alkanes"| contain 13-22 carbons. |FRAME: Very-Long-Chain-Alkanes "Very-long-chain alkanes"| contain 23 carbons or longer.

Compound.name: a ganglioside LM1
Synonyms: a alphaNeuAc-(2->3)-betaGal-(1->4)-betaGlucNAc-(1->3)-betaGal-(1->4)-betaGlc-ceramide // a alpha- N -acetylneuraminyl-(2->3)-beta-D-galactosyl-(1->4)- N -acetyl-beta-D-glucosaminyl-(1->3)-beta-D-galactosyl-(1->4)-beta-D-glucosyl-(1HARR:1)-ceramide // a sialosylparagloboside (ambiguous) // IV 3 Neu5Ac-nLc4Cer // a sialosylneolactotetraosylceramide
Comment: |FRAME: ACETYLNEURAMINYL-23-BETA-D-GALACTOSYL-ET "Ganglioside LM1"| is the predominant ganglioside (61%) of the peripheral nerve myelin |CITS: [3989569][1402926][10526188]|.

Compound.name: a diol
Comment: Diols are compound that contain two hydroxy groups. Aliphatic diols in which the two hydroxyls reside on different carbons are also called |FRAME: glycols glycols|.

Compound.name: a sesterterpenoid
Comment: |FRAME: Terpenoids Terpenoids| make up a very large family of natural products containing more than 50,000 structurally diverse compounds. They are categorized by the number of C5 isoprene units as follows: |FRAME: Hemiterpenes Hemiterpenoids| (one C5 unit), |FRAME: Monoterpenes monoterpenoids| (C10; two C5 units), |FRAME: Sesquiterpenes sesquiterpenoids| (C15; three C5 units), |FRAME: Diterpenes diterpenoids| (C20; four C5 units), |FRAME: Sesterterpenes sesterterpenoids| (C25; five C5 units), |FRAME: Triterpenes triterpenoids| (C30; six C5 units), |FRAME: C35-Terpenes "sesquarterpenoids"| (C35; seven C5 units), and |FRAME: Tetraterpenes tetraterpenoids| (C40; eight C5 units).

Compound.name: an oleanonic-acid-type saponin ginsenoside
Comment: |FRAME: Ginsenosides Ginsenosides| or panaxosides are a class of steroid glycosides and triterpene saponins found exclusively in the plant genus |FRAME: TAX-4053| (ginseng). They are the principal components responsible for the pharmaceutical activities of ginseng. Ginsenosides are composed of an aglycone and sugar moieties. Based on the structure of their aglycones, ginsenosides have been categorized into three broad types; |FRAME: Protopanaxadiol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxadiol-type ginsenosides"| (PPD), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3 and 20, |FRAME: Protopanaxatriol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxatriol-type ginsenosides"| (PPT), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3, 6 and 20, and |FRAME: Oleanonic-acid-type-ginsenosides "oleanonic-acid-type saponins"|. Although ginsenosides only have three kinds of aglycones, more than 60 kinds of ginsenosides have been identified by now due to the variability in the type of sugar moieties, their number, and the carbon positions they link to. The biological activity of ginsenoside increases with the decrease of the number of the sugar moieties. All of the ginsenosides found in large quantities in wild ginseng (known as major ginsenosides) are heavily glycosylated, while the more active less-glycosylated ginsenosides are found in much smalller quantities (and are commonly referred to as the minor ginsenosides). Following oral intake of ginseng, the large low-solubility and poor-permeability major ginsenosides cannot be absorbed by the human body directly Su06, and are deglycosylated into smaller forms in the gastrointestinal tract by intestinal bacteria and/or digestive enzymes 8923812. Glycosidase enzymes that can convert the major ginsenosides to minor ginsenosides are not common and are of commercial interest.
