Comment: Arabinogalactans (AGs) are widely spread throughout the plant kingdom. Many edible and inedible plants are rich sources of these polysaccharides. AGs are associated with the pectin cell-wall component by physical bonds, and some of them are covalently linked to the complex pectin molecule as neutral side chains Ebringerova05. AGs have been classified into two general forms, named |FRAME: Plant-Arabinogalactans-I "type I"| and |FRAME: Plant-Arabinogalactans-II "type II"|. AGs of type I have a linear beta-(1->4)-D-Gal p backbone, while those of type II have a beta-(1->3)-D-Gal p backbone. In type II AGs, known also as arabino-3,6-galactan, the (beta-1->3)-D-Gal p backbone is heavily substituted at position 6 by mono- and oligosaccharide side chains composed of arabinosyl and galactosyl units. It is more widespread than the AG type I and occurs in cell walls of dicots and cereals often linked to proteins (known as arabinogalactan proteins). AG type II, along with galactomannans and cellulose, comprises the predominating polysaccharides of green arabica coffee beans 11217967. In some case type II AG contains a small amount of beta-glucuronate. There are many variations of AG type II produced by different plants. Two forms that have been studied thoroughly are |FRAME: Gum-Arabic "gum arabic AG"|, which is produced by acacia trees, and |FRAME: Larch-AG "larch AG|, produced by larch trees (members of the genus |FRAME: TAX-3325|). AG is very abundant in the wood of larch trees - certain parts of the western larch (|FRAME: TAX-3327|) contain up to 35% AG Whistler93. Larch AG type II is located in the lumen of the tracheids and ray cells, and is thus not a cell-wall component and by definition, not part of the |FRAME: Hemicelluloses| of these trees. Carrageenans are classified according to the number and the position of sulfated ester 1367970. In |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| the alpha-1,3-linked galactose units are modified by having a 3,6-anhydro bridge. These bridges, which form a double helix during aggregation, are responsible for the gelation that is typical to these compounds. Despite this distinction, carrageenoses are often referred to as carrageenans. The three most industrially exploited carrageenans, namely, |FRAME: kappa-Carrageenan|, |FRAME: iota-Carrageenan| and |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan|, are distinguished by the presence of one, two or three ester-sulfate groups per repeating disaccharide unit respectively. |FRAME: kappa-Carrageenan| is sulfated only at position 4 of the beta-1,4 linked D-galactose units.

The names are often followed by the number of the prenoid units in the side chain (e.g. Q-8), or the number of carbons in the chain. For example, the name Q-8 may be substituted with ubiiquinone(40). The first clue to mycofactocin's identity came in 2011 when bioinformatic analysis demonstrated the co-occurrence of the genes mftABCDEF in over 600 bacterial species, including pathogens such as |FRAME: TAX-1773|, |FRAME: TAX-1764|, and |FRAME: TAX-1809|, with genes encoding the dehydrogenases of the above mentioned families 21223593. Further studies have shown that mycofactocins originate from a ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptide (MftA). The C terminus of the peptide, consisting of |FRAME: VAL|-|FRAME: TYR|, is oxidatively decarboxylated and cyclized by a radical SAM enzyme and cleaved, followed by oxidative deamination to generate the |FRAME: CPD-22872| aglycone, which contains the redox center of MFT. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-Chain-Aldehydes "Short-chain fatty aldehydes"| are derived from |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Aldehydes "Medium-chain fatty aldehydes"| are derived from |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Aldehydes "Long-chain fatty aldehydes"| are derived from |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "fatty acids that have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Very-Long-Chain-Aldehydes "Very-long-chain fatty aldehydes"| are derived from |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Ultra-Long-Chain-Aldehydes "Ultra-long-chain fatty aldehydes"| are derived from |FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain"|.

Compound.name: a colanic acid
Comment: |FRAME: CPD0-1099 "Colanic acid"| is an exopolysaccharide secreted by |FRAME: TAX-562| and a number of other |FRAME: TAX-543| that encapsulates the organism, resulting in a mucoid appearance 13963285. Colanic acid is thought to promote biofilm formation and to protect the organism when exposed to harsh environments such as acidic conditions |CITS: [11371548][16706906]|. Even though it wasn't identified as such, colanic acid was first described in 1927 by Dorothea Smith, who isolated a polysaccharide from a mucoid strain of |FRAME: TAX-562| 19869322. Fourteen years later, in a study on the antigens of the Enterobacteriaceae , it was noticed that one antigen was common to several mucoid strains of |FRAME: TAX-57045| Kauffmann41. It was soon reported that the same antigen, which was named "M" antigen, is produced by mucoid Escherichia coli strains 15406247. In 1954 Kauffmann reported that the antigen was common to all mucoid Salmonella species Kauffmann54. Similar exopolysaccharides were reported from a number of mucoid strains and species |CITS: [13475241][13641209][13963285][14073028][5324934]|. In the early 60s it was reported that a large number of Salmonella and Escherichia strains that are not normally mucoid can be induced to form slime exopolysaccharides when grown at 15 to 20°C in high phosphate concentration |CITS: [Anderson61][Anderson63]|, and the exopolysaccharide was named "colanic acid" after |FRAME: TAX-562| from which it was isolated 13963285. In a paper describing the discovery of the same polysaccharide in |FRAME: TAX-83333| it was suggested that colanic acid and the "M antigen" reported in the earlier studies are identical 14206589. A confirmation was obtained in 1969 when it was shown that colanic acid of identical composition is produced by strains from the genera Salmonella , Escherichia , and Aerobacter . At that time the exact structure was not known, though it was known that the polysaccharide contains glucose, galactose, fucose, and glucuronate, as well as some O -acetyl groups 4902806. Additional structural studies have shown that colanic acid from different organisms is very similar, with the polysaccharide composed of a hexasaccharide repeating unit consisting of glucose, two fucoses, two galactoses, and glucuronate. In addition, one fucose and one galactose may be acetylated to varying degrees, and the terminal galactose residue is modified. The repeat units are connected by a linkage between the first and third residues, with the remaining three residues forming a side chain |CITS: [4311825][4902692]|. Differences are found in the modifications of the terminal galactose residue, which was found to contain a 4,6-pyruvoyl group, a 3,4-pyruvoyl group, a 3,4-ethylidene group, or a 4,6-methylene group in different strains 4941627. The structure shown here was published in 2007, correcting several errors in earlier reports 17227761. While colanic acid was considered exclusively an exopolysaccharide that is only loosely associated with the cell surface, the 2007 study also found that colanic acid can be attached to the lipid A core of lipopolysaccharide instead of the O antigen, forming a novel type of lipopolysaccharide which was named |FRAME: CPD0-1101 M LPS | 17227761.

Compound.name: a (6 S )-5-formyltetrahydrofolate
Synonyms: a folinic acid // an (6 S )- N 5 -formyltetrahydrofolate
Comment: |FRAME: THF-GLU-N Tetrahydrofolate| (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are required in a variety of reactions in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, where they act as carriers of one-carbon units in various oxidation states. These one-carbon units are utilized in the biosynthesis of several cellular components, including glycine, methionine, formylmethionine, thymidylate, pantothenate and purine nucleotides. During folate biosynthesis (as described in FOLSYN-PWY) the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.12|, adds a glutamate residue to |FRAME: 7-8-DIHYDROPTEROATE|, resulting in |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE|, also known as H 2 PteGlu 1 . This molecule in turn is reduced by EC-1.5.1.3 (FolA) to |FRAME: THF| (H 4 PteGlu 1 , or tetrahydrofolate), which can be converted to several other folate molecules 11501996. Most folate molecules are modified in cells by successive additions of glutamate residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-gamma-glutamates). The glutamate residues are added by an amide linkage to the gamma-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are not the normal amide bonds they are not hydrolyzed by peptidases or proteases, which are specific for alpha-carboxyl-linked peptide bonds. The addition of glutamyl residues probably occurs after the reduction of newly synthesized dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and its conversion to other tetrahydrofolate derivatives. The glutamylation of folate residues serves several goals: it prevents the efflux of folates out of the cell, it increases the binding of folate cofactors to the enzymes of folate interconversion and biosynthesis, and in mammals, it allows the accumulation of folates in the mitochondria, which is required for glycine synthesis 10598551. Among the many folates 5-FORMYL-THF is the most enigmatic compound involved in the folate biosynthesis. 5-FORMYL-THF is the only folate derivative that does not serve as a cofactor in C1-metabolism, but it is the most frequent and stable form of folates found in plants 8480361. Moreover, 5-FORMYL-THF is known to inhibit most of the folate dependent enzymes at physiological concentrations. The biological role of this compound is still poorly understood but it has been discussed as factor involved in the regulation of essential biosynthetic steps such as the formation of serine during photorespiration |CITS: [15888445][12207015]|. This class stands for (6 S )-5-formyltetrahydrofolates with an unspecified number of glutamate residues.

Comment: |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13| is a vitamin B12-dependent zinc metalloenzyme that catalyzes the transfer of a methyl group from |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N| to homocysteine. Methionine synthase is one of two eukaryotic enzymes that require a cobalamin prosthetic group for activity. Unlike the other enzyme (|FRAME: EC-5.4.99.2|), which requires adenosylcobalamin, the cobalamin cofactor of methionine synthase needs to be methylated. Upon the initial transfer of a cob(II)alamin cofactor from a |FRAME: CPD-20918|, it is methylated to the active methylcob(III)alamin form by |FRAME: EC-1.16.1.8|, which uses |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| as the methyl donor. The methyl group is subsequently transferred to homocysteine to form methionine, leaving the cofactor briefly in a cob(I)alamin form, which is regenerated to the active methylcob(III)alamin form by a transfer of a methyl group from |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N "5-methyltetrahydrofolate"| 2407589. The enzyme becomes inactivated occasionally during its cycle by oxidation of Co(I) to Co(II). Reactivation by reductive methylation is catalysed by the enzyme itself, with S-adenosyl-L-methionine as the methyl donor and a reducing system. For the mammalian enzyme, the reducing system involves NADPH and |FRAME: EC-1.16.1.8|. In bacteria, the reducing agent is flavodoxin, and no further catalyst is needed (the flavodoxin is kept in the reduced state by NADPH and |FRAME: EC-1.18.1.2|). A histidine residue embedded in the canonical B 12 -binding DxHxxG motif in methionine synthase serves as the lower axial ligand to the cobalt, which is bound in the "base-off/His-on" state 7992050.

Compound.name: heparin
Comment: |FRAME: HEPARIN "Heparin"| is a glycosaminoglycan polymer with a molecular weight ranging from 3 to 30 kDa. It is composed of a variable sulfated repeating disaccharide units composed of hexuronic (either iduronic or glucuronic) acid and glucosamine residues, in which the 2 position of the hexuronic acid and the 2, 3, or 6 positions of glucosamine may be sulfated. The two residues within a disaccharide are linked by a (1->4) bond, as are the disaccharides to each other. The main disaccharide unit consists of |FRAME: CPD-12518| and |FRAME: CPD-12533| [it is often referred to as IdoA(2S)-(1->4)-GlcNS(6S)]. However, |FRAME: CPD-12518| can be substituted by |FRAME: CPD-12521|, and |FRAME: CPD-12533| can be replaced by |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, |FRAME: N-sulfo-D-glucosamine|, |FRAME: CPD-12545| or |FRAME: CPD-12565|. The basic IdoA(2S)-(1->4)-GlcNS(6S) disaccharide accounts for at least 85% of heparin isolated from beef lung and about 75% of heparin from porcine intestinal mucosa |CITS: [Casu89][Gatti79]|. Variations in the extent and location of sulfation, as well as the conformation of the alternating hexuronic acid residues, lead to a high degree of heterogeneity. By convention, heparin refers to molecules which possess a high sulfate content and large amounts of iduronic acid. The structure of |FRAME: HEPARIN| is very similar to that of |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate| (also known as heparitin sulfate). Heparan sulfate contains lower amounts of sulfate and less iduronic acid than heparin 5484472. In addition, heparan sulfates disaccharide units are organized into distinct sulfated and non-sulfated domains, while heparin disaccharides are sulfated more uniformly 15047699.

Comment: |FRAME: Xyloglucan Xyloglucan| is the major component of the |FRAME: Hemicelluloses| in cell walls of dicotyledon type I and non-graminaceous monocotyledon plants. It also exists in some seeds of trees growing in the tropical zone. Xyloglucan interacts with cellulose microfibrils via hydrogen bonds to form a structural network that is assumed to play a key role in cell wall integrity. Cross-linking between the xyloglucan chains is a major factor in the stability of the resulting three-dimensional matrix Whitney95. Xyloglucan has a backbone of beta-1,4-linked glucose residues, most of which are substituted in C-6 by alpha-D-xylosyl residues 8252539. In most plants some of the xylosyl residues are further substituted by (1,2)-beta-D-galactosyl residues, and some of the galactosyl residues are capped by (1,2)-alpha-L-fucose |CITS:[12837954] [17011813]|. Other types of xyloglucans, for example those found in the Poaeceae and Solanaceae, feature xylose units that bear alpha-L-arabinosyl instead of beta-D-galactosyl residues. A common terminology uses G for basic non-substituted glucosyl units within a xylosylglycan, X for glucose residues substituted by alpha-D-xylose, L for glucose residues substituted by alpha-D-xylose and beta-D-galactose, and F for glucose residues substituted by alpha-D-xylose, beta-D-galactose and alpha-L-fucose Fry93. Fucosyl residues are typically absent from seed xyloglucans but present on the xyloglucans in the vegatative portions of the same plant Mishra09. Most xylosylglucans consist of repeating heptasaccharide |FRAME: Xyloglucans-Xylose XXXG| units. The average molecular weight of xyloglucan is more than 50,000 Mishra09. Compound.name: a lankacidin-group antibiotic
Comment: The |FRAME: Lankacidins "lankacidins"| are a class of unique 17-membered carbocyclic polyketide natural products isolated from Streptomyces spp. that show promising antimicrobial activity. |FRAME: CPD-27267 "Lankacidin C"| was originally isolated in 1960 from |FRAME: TAX-68280| under the name lankacidin Gaumann60. It was subsequently isolated from multiple other species such as |FRAME: TAX-146922| Sakamoto62 and Streptomyces sp. 6642-GC 5796585, sometimes under the name bundlin A. In 1971 a group of related antibiotics, which included lankacidin C, was isolated from |FRAME: TAX-885435| (previously named strain T-2636). These compounds, which were referred to as "T-2636 antibiotics", have been studied extensively. The antibiotics were found to be active against a number of organisms, particularly Gram-positive bacteria, including many strains that are resistant to macrolide antibiotics |CITS: [5541329][5541328][5541330][4833376][1212749][4792112][4792113][1126865][240790]|. X-ray crystallographic analysis revealed that lankacidin C and |FRAME: CPD-27278| (a 14-membered macrolide antibiotic also produced by |FRAME: TAX-885435|) inhibit peptide formation synergistically by binding to neighboring sites in the large bacterial ribosomal subunit |CITS: [20080686][21282615]|. In addition, the lankacidins were shown to have considerable antitumor activity against certain cell line models |CITS: [4801122][1148][27718573]|. |FRAME: CPD-27267 "Lankacidin C"| is currently used in veterinary medicine. In 1994 it was found that the genes encoding the biosynthesis of the lankacidin-group antibiotics reside on the linear plasmid pSLA2-L 7844039. Sequencing of the region suggested that lankacidin biosynthesis is mediated by one PKS/NRPS hybrid (LkcA) and three PKSs (LkcC, LkcF, and LkcG) 10767533. A starter glycine molecule is extended by eight malonyl-[acp] molecules. The methyl groups at C-2, C-4, C-10, and C-16 are added by C-methylation from |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| Uramoto78. The formation of the delta-lactone ring is catalyzed by the thioesterase domain of LkcG. Once removed from the PKS machinary, the molecule is cyclyzed by an |FRAME: MONOMER-124699 "amine oxidase"| (LkcE) |CITS: [15734652][18057700][21953738]|.

Comment: |FRAME: Ginsenosides Ginsenosides| or panaxosides are a class of steroid glycosides and triterpene saponins found exclusively in the plant genus |FRAME: TAX-4053| (ginseng). They are the principal components responsible for the pharmaceutical activities of ginseng. Ginsenosides are composed of an aglycone and sugar moieties. Based on the structure of their aglycones, ginsenosides have been categorized into three broad types; |FRAME: Protopanaxadiol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxadiol-type ginsenosides"| (PPD), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3 and 20, |FRAME: Protopanaxatriol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxatriol-type ginsenosides"| (PPT), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3, 6 and 20, and |FRAME: Oleanonic-acid-type-ginsenosides "oleanonic-acid-type saponins"|. Although ginsenosides only have three kinds of aglycones, more than 60 kinds of ginsenosides have been identified by now due to the variability in the type of sugar moieties, their number, and the carbon positions they link to. The biological activity of ginsenoside increases with the decrease of the number of the sugar moieties. All of the ginsenosides found in large quantities in wild ginseng (known as major ginsenosides) are heavily glycosylated, while the more active less-glycosylated ginsenosides are found in much smalller quantities (and are commonly referred to as the minor ginsenosides). Following oral intake of ginseng, the large low-solubility and poor-permeability major ginsenosides cannot be absorbed by the human body directly Su06, and are deglycosylated into smaller forms in the gastrointestinal tract by intestinal bacteria and/or digestive enzymes 8923812. Glycosidase enzymes that can convert the major ginsenosides to minor ginsenosides are not common and are of commercial interest.

Compound.name: a polyketide quinone
Comment: |FRAME: Polyketide-quinones "Polyketide quinones"| are used by some organisms as a functional alternative to |FRAME: Menaquinones menaquinone| under specific conditions such as low oxygen environments or sporulation. Though the existence of polyketide quinones was known since 2008 18364359, their role was not understood at the time. A new understanding of polyketide quinones was achieved in 2015, when it was reported that these molecules can serve as alternate mobile electron carriers in the respiratory electron transport chain during respiration in oxygen-deficient niches. The authors, who studied the enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-1772|, found that the enzymes are specifically expressed in biofilms and other oxygen-deficient niches. They also reported that the system is conserved in all mycobacteria as well as in several other Actinobacterial and a few Proteobacterial species 26585386. A study of the freshwater bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1573406| has shown that the organism switches from using menaquinone to using polyketide quinone during its development cycle. The gene cluster was significantly upregulated during the dormant sporulation stage, while the menaquinone biosynthetic genes were downregulated during this period. A metabolite extract from the spores showed 10 times more polyketide quinone molecules than menaquinones 36507669.

Compound.name: a methanofuran
Comment: Methanofurans are a group of related carbon-carrier cofactors involved in the first step of the methanogenic reduction of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| (see |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|). Methanofurans react with |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| to form the carbamate N -carboxymethanofuran, which is reduced to |FRAME: Formyl-methanofurans| by |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.12|. In addition, the cofactor also participates at a later stage of all methanogenesis pathways. These pathways converge at the compound Me-CoM, which is then disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|; the latter process involves methanofuran (see |FRAME: PWY-5209|). Methanofuran is also used by methylotrophic bacteria as a coenzyme to oxidize formaldehyde to formate |CITS: [9651254][11532013]|. Methanofurans are the only cofactors known to contain a furan moiety, although furans have been identified in polyketides and fatty acid derived natural products, and are often formed during the heating or oxidation of carbohydrates 12013276. The chemical structure of methanofuran varies among different methanogens. At this time (2014) five variants have been characterized: |FRAME: CPD-17181| (from |FRAME: TAX-145262|) 1517208, CPD-7628 (from |FRAME: TAX-2208|) 2883935, CPD-7629 (from |FRAME: TAX-2173|) 3170480, |FRAME: methanofuran-d| (from |FRAME: TAX-2190|) 24977328 and |FRAME: CPD-17182| (from |FRAME: TAX-39152|, |FRAME: TAX-2187| and |FRAME: TAX-155863|) 25203397. All methanofurans contain the basic core structure of 4-[ N -gamma-L-glutamyl-gamma-L-glutamyl)- p -(beta-aminoethyl)phenoxymethyl]-2-(aminomethyl)furan, but with different attached side chains.

Compound.name: starch
Comment: Starch is a glucose-based polysaccharide produced by plants, green algae, and cyanobacteria. Starch combines two polymeric carbohydrates (polysaccharides) called |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses "alpha-amylose"| and |FRAME: CPD-7043|. |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses "alpha-Amylose"| contains up to several thousand alpha-glucosyl units linked almost exclusively in linear alpha(1->4) linkages, with very few branches of alpha(1->6) linkages. In |FRAME: CPD-7043|, on the other hand, branching is common, and occurs approximately every 24-30 glucose monomer units. Amylopectin is one of (if not the) largest biological polymer known and contains from 10 5 –10 6 glucose residues 9730163. Unlike |FRAME: Glycogens glycogen| molecules, which is limited to ~55,000 glucose units, the starch branched structure leads to clusters of chains that allow for indefinite growth of the polysaccharide. |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses "alpha-Amylose"| accounts for 30% of starch, while |FRAME: CPD-7043| accounts for the other 70%. The dense packing of branches at the root of the clusters generates tightly packed glucan chains that are close enough to align and form parallel double helical structures. The helices within a single cluster and neighbouring clusters align and form sections of crystalline structures separated by sections of amorphous material (containing the branches) thereby generating the semi-crystalline nature of amylopectin and of the ensuing starch granule. The crystallized chains become insoluble and typically collapse into a macrogranular solid that is osmotically inert 9730163. The enzymes of starch synthesis and mobilization are unable to interact directly with the solid structure, with the exception of |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.242 "granule-bound starch synthase"| 14502990. The solid semi-crystalline starch and hydrosoluble |FRAME: Glycogens glycogen| define two distinct physical states of the same type of storage polysaccharide. Glycogen is by far the most widespread form of storage, as it is found in Archaea, Bacteria, and Eukaryotes. The appearance of semi-crystalline storage polysaccharides appears linked to the requirement of unicellular diazotrophic cyanobacteria to fuel nitrogenase and protect it from oxygen through respiration of large amounts of stored carbon 21220783.

Compound.name: a quinone
Comment: Quinones are organic compounds derived from aromatic compounds, with two carbonyl groups incorporated into the ring structure with rearrangement of the double bonds where necessary. Quinones are conjugated but not aromatic. A classic example of a quinone is |FRAME: P-BENZOQUINONE|. Quinones are commonly named with a prefix that indicates the parent aromatic hydrocarbon (for example, "benzo-" for benzene, "naphtho-" for naphthalene, and "anthra-" for anthracene) with a "-quinone" suffix. Several types of quinones serve as electron acceptors in electron transport chains. Those quinones are usually prenylated with a lipid-soluble isoprenyl tail that anchors them in the membrane lipid bilayer. Quinones can carry two electrons, and when fully reduced they are referred to as |FRAME: Reduced-Quinones quinols|. The addition of a single H atom to a quinone results in formation of a free radical called |FRAME: Semiquinones|. Many quinone derivatives often have other biological activities, such as |FRAME: CPD-11501 "vitamin K"|.

Compound.name: a rhamnogalacturonan type II
Comment: Rhamnogalacturonan type II (RG-II) is a relatively small polysaccharide that makes up about 10% of |FRAME: Pectin pectin|. Despite its small size, it, is the most structurally complex pectin component. Its alpha-1,4-linked D-galacturonate backbone is decorated with four side branches (named A D) consisting of 12 different types of sugars in over 20 different linkages 18486536. Some of the sugars are quite rare, including |FRAME: CPD-13046|, |FRAME: CPD-20946| (3-C-carboxy-5-deoxy-L-xylose), and |FRAME: CPD-20949| (Dha). RG-II exists in the primary wall as a dimer that is cross linked by a 1:2 borate-diol diester 12226238. The borate diester cross link is formed between the apiosyl residue in side chain A of each monomer subunit |CITS: [8798473][10224062]|. Despite this complexity the structure of RG-II is largely conserved across plant species. It has been reported that the structure is virtually the same in members of the Brassicacea, Cucurbitaceae, Leguminoseae, Apiaceae, Liliaceae, Araceae, Amaryllidaceae, Gramineae, and more families 12765781. However, later work reported some variation in the side chains and methylation status within and across different plant speces 23802881. Please note that the structure shown here is not entirely accurate, due to the inability of software to depict unusual monosaccharides. |FRAME: CPD-13046|, |FRAME: CPD-20946| and |FRAME: CPD-20949| are depicted as generic pentose, hexuronate, and heptose, respectively.

Compound.name: a Lewis y epitope
Synonyms: a histo-blood group Le y antigen // AH6 antigen
Comment: The Lewis y epitope (Le y ) is a difucosylated oligosaccharide derived from |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R "type 2 precursor disaccharides"| carried by glycoconjugates on the cell surface. Le y is expressed predominately during embryogenesis, and expression on adult tissue is restricted to granulocytes and epithelial surfaces 11037972, where it acts as a ligand for lectin-like proteins |CITS: [18711002][22101897]|. However, Le y is overexpressed in the majority of carcinomas, including breast, ovary, pancreas, prostate, colon, and non-small cell lung cancers, and has been correlated to the pathological staging and prognosis |CITS: [2537068][7714977][8621218][9824007][21512109]|. In these cases, Le y occurs either at the plasma membrane as a glycolipid or linked to surface receptors |CITS: [2436750][14871842]|. Le y was shown to play an important role in promoting cell proliferation, tumorigenecity and adhesion |CITS: [21152298][18205178]|, and several clinical trials were conducted using Le y monoclonal antibodies for targeted immunotherapy of tumors |CITS: [1327079][8577771][8640770][10829049][10861456][16963623][17545534][17909358][19825951][26026738]|. The human pathogenic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-210| is known to express the Le y antigen in its lipopolysaccharide, mimicking human cell surface glycoconjugates |CITS: [8890213][10096092][11237846][11741906]|.

Compound.name: a steroid
Comment: Steroids are compounds possessing the skeleton of cyclopenta[ a ]phenanthrene or a skeleton derived therefrom by one or more bond scissions or ring expansions or contractions. Methyl groups are normally present at C-10 and C-13. An alkyl side chain may also be present at C-17. Steroids are abundant in the environment. Large amounts of steroids and their derivatives are synthesized by eukaryotes, and these molecules play very important and diverse roles and include hormones, detergents that facilitate the absorption of lipids by the intestine, and membrane constituents. Some of them, |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| and related compounds, are ubiquitous as membrane constituent of eukaryotes (for instance, up to 10% of the dry mass of yeast is |FRAME: ERGOSTEROL|) and as the precursors of all steroid hormones, vitamin D, and the bile acids. Interestingly, with exception of methane-oxidizing bacteria that contain relatively large amounts of sterols, sterols are absent from most prokaryotes. However, many bacterial membranes contain |FRAME: Hopanoids hopanoids|, which are similar pentacyclic sterol-like molecules 18039763.

Compound.name: a menaquinone
Comment: Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are isoprenoid quinones of the naphthalene series, and are constituents of bacterial plasma membranes, where they play important roles in electron transfer and oxidative phosphorylation. Menaquinones are the most widespread respiratory quinones in biological systems Fujimoto12. Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are named MK- n or DMK- n , respectively, where the n refers to the number of prenyl units present in the side chain. The most common length of the side chain in bacteria is 8, although minor amounts of MK-1 through MK-14 have been found 7022156. Many bacteria and archaea have |FRAME: Dihydromenaquinones "dehydrogenated menaquinones"|, which are named MK- n (H 2 ). The degree and location of dehydrogenation depends on the species. Some organisms have menaquinones with modifications of the head group, for example |FRAME: TAX-2302| possess both |FRAME: CPD-15875 thermoplasmaquinones| (TPQ), which contains an extra methyl group, and |FRAME: CPD-15876 methionaquinones| (MTK), which contains a methylthio group 11157962. Menaquinones are also known as vitamin K 2 . Vitamin K is a name given to a group of derivatives of 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone that are required by mammals for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins, mostly involved in blood coagulation. These compounds, while essential for mammals, are not synthesized by them, and are thus considered vitamins. The natural forms of the vitamin are vitamin K 1 (|FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE|) and vitamin K 2 (|FRAME: Menaquinones "menaquinone"|). Since menaquinones produced by different organisms have different tail lengths there are many variations of vitamin K 2 , usually specified based on the number of carbons in their tails, such as in Vitamin K 2 (45). The reduced form of menaquinone is called |FRAME: Menaquinols|.

However, the term is now used in a much wider sense and includes |FRAME: Monosaccharides monosaccharides|, |FRAME: Disaccharides disaccharides|, |FRAME: Oligosaccharides oligosaccharides| and |FRAME: Polysaccharides polysaccharides| as well as substances derived from monosaccharides by reduction of the carbonyl group (|FRAME: Sugar-alcohols alditols|), by oxidation of one or more terminal groups to |FRAME: Carboxylates "carboxylic acids"|, or by replacement of one or more hydroxy group(s) by a hydrogen atom, an amino group, a sulfhydryl group or similar heteroatomic groups. It also includes oligo- and polysaccharides consisting of such modified monosaccharides, as well as derivatives of these compounds. An exception is |FRAME: Cyclitols cyclitols|, which are generally not regarded as carbohydrates.

Most compounds have a syn -configuration (in which the the C-19 position (brevianamide numbering) and the bridging amide point at the same direction), but a few (such as |FRAME: CPD-25433| and |FRAME: CPD-25434|) have an anti configuration.

For a complete list of aerobic bacteria that contain bacteriochlorophyll, see 12483616. Much of the knowledge about bacteriochlorophyll biosynthesis comes from the organisms |FRAME: TAX-1061| and |FRAME: TAX-1063|, which produce mainly CPD-9067, the most common form of the bacteriochlorophylls. |FRAME: Bacteriochlorophyll-a "Bacteriochlorophyll a "| is the most common type of bacteriochlorophyll, and is found in light-harvesting antenna systems and reaction center complexes of most anoxygenic photosynthetic bacteria, except for some purple bacteria that produce giving CPD-9091 and heliobacteria that produce CPD-9095. Different forms of bacteriochloropyll a have been reported. The green sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1097| synthesizes two types - one with an esterified |FRAME: PHYTOL| side chain (|FRAME: CPD-9067|) and one with a |FRAME: CPD-18893| side chain (|FRAME: CPD-18892|). Comment: The brevianamides are a class of indole alkaloids originally isolated from |FRAME: TAX-5074|. They are derived from |FRAME: PRO|, |FRAME: TRP|, and one or two isoprene units |CITS: [5419195][4751807][1186436][16345847]|. The two main producers of |FRAME: CPD-15274| are |FRAME: TAX-5074| and |FRAME: TAX-60134|. The brevianamides belong to a diverse family of biologically active prenylated indole alkaloids isolated mainly from various |FRAME: TAX-5073| and |FRAME: TAX-5052| species of fungi that contains a unique bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane core ring system, and are derived from |FRAME: TRP|, a cyclic amino acid (|FRAME: PRO|, |FRAME: L-PIPECOLATE| or a derivative of one of those compounds), and one or two isoprene units. In addition to their structural diversity, members of this family have been attributed a variety of bioactivities, including (but not limited to) insecticidal, cytotoxic, anthelmintic, and antibacterial properties. The bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane-containing compounds can be divided into two sub-categories: the diketopiperazines (DKPs) and the monoketopiperazines (MKPs). DKPs include the |FRAME: Stephacidins stephacidins|, |FRAME: Brevianamides brevianamides|, and |FRAME: Notoamides notoamides|, while MKPs include the |FRAME: Paraherquamides paraherquamides|, |FRAME: Asperparalines asperparalines|, |FRAME: Marcfortines marcfortines|, |FRAME: Chrysogenamides chrysogenamides|,and |FRAME: Malbrancheamides malbrancheamides|. Two distinct stereochemical configurations have been noted with respect to the relative configuration of the bridging amide of the bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane core. Most compounds have a syn -configuration (in which the the C-19 position (brevianamide numbering) and the bridging amide point at the same direction), but a few (such as |FRAME: CPD-25433| and |FRAME: CPD-25434|) have an anti configuration. The brevianamides display the anti configuration, as well as a spiro-indoxyl moiety and an unsubstituted indole ring 22502590. |FRAME: CPD-15274 "Brevianamide A"| possesses antifeedant and insecticidal effects Paterson87. |FRAME: CPD-15265 "Brevianamide F"| (cyclo-L-Trp-L-Pro) serves as the precursor for several secondary metabolites that lack the bridging bicycle, such as the |FRAME: CPD-15266 fumitremorgins| and spirotryprostatins in |FRAME: TAX-746128| 18763205.

Compound.name: chitosan
Comment: |FRAME: Chitosan Chitosan| is a linear polysaccharide composed of randomly distributed beta-(1-4)-linked D-glucosamine and N-acetyl-D-glucosamine units. Chitosan is found in the cell walls of some phytopathogenic fungi. The natural occuring chitosan has a degree of acetylation between 20-30%, with the acetyl residues grouped into clusters. Chitosan is mostly produced commercially by deacetylation of |FRAME: CHITIN| , which is the structural element in the exoskeleton of crustaceans. The most popular technique for obtaining chitosan is alkaline deacetylation of chitin: this involves boiling chitin in concentrated alkali (50% w/v) for several hours. This process also yields chitosan with a degree of acetylation between 20-30%. However, in such a chitosan, unlike the naturally occurring chitosan, the acetyl groups are uniformly distributed along the polymer chain. Completely de-acetylated forms of chitosan do not exist naturally, but can be synthesized by special chemical treatment.

Compound.name: a monounsaturated fatty acid

Even though fatty acids derived from natural fats and oils, such as CPD-195, are usually at least 8 carbon atoms long, carboxylic acids as short as BUTYRIC_ACID (4 carbon atoms) are considered to be fatty acids. When a fatty acid contains only single bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Saturated-Fatty-Acids|. When it contains one or more double bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Unsaturated-Fatty-Acids|. If it contains a double bond in the trans configuration, it is often referred to as a trans fatty acid. Most fatty acids in the trans configuration are not found in nature and are the result of human processing. About nomenclature : Several nomenclatures are used for unsaturated fatty acids, and are not complementary. Systematic names (or IUPAC names) begin counting the carbon atoms from the carboxylic acid end, and the double bonds are labelled with cis / trans or E/Z notation, e.g. 8 E ,10 E ,12 Z -octadecatrienoate. However, unsaturated fatty acids are often described using the omega nomenclature, which begins counting the carbon atoms from the terminal methyl carbon (designated as n or ω). In addition, unsaturated fatty acids are often referred to by trivial names, or by the "lipid number" as in 18:3, where 18 is the number of carbons, and 3 is the number of double bonds. This notation is ambiguous, as it does not specify the location of the double bonds.

Compound.name: a lipopolysaccharide
Comment: This compound class stands for generic and unspecified lipopolysaccharides. The structure shown here is intended to provide a general overview and does not describe a lipopolysaccharide from a specific species. Lipopolysaccharides (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of almost all Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. Lipopolysaccharides that comprise all three regions are called |FRAME: Smooth-Form-LPS "smooth (S)-form LPS"|, while LPS lacking the O -antigen are named |FRAME: LOS "rough (R)-form LPS"| or lipooligosaccharide (LOS). Lipid A, which is common to most Gram negative bacteria, is the most toxic part. The core polysaccharide is genus specific, and contains unusual 7-carbon and 8-carbon sugars, and the O -antigen's side chains are variable in structure and toxicity. The O -antigen usually consists of about 20-40 repeated subunits.

This conjugation results in very active antibiotics: mupirocin is an effective protein synthesis inhibitor, while holomythin inhibits transcription.

Comment: The dissimilatory sulfite reductase, DsrAB, is an essential enzyme in prokaryotic sulfur-based energy metabolism. In sulfur reducers it catalyzes the reduction of sulfite to sulfide, while in sulfur oxidizers it catalyzes the opposite reaction Schedel79. This reaction involves the small protein DsrC, which is present in all organisms that contain DsrAB, including sulfate/sulfite reducing organisms, sulfur-oxidizing bacteria, and organosulfonate reducers. DsrC contains two redox-active conserved cysteines in a flexible C-terminal arm. A crystal structure of |FRAME: TAX-881| DsrAB in complex with DsrC has shown that the C-terminal arm of DsrC projects inside DsrAB in a way that brings its last Cys (CysA) right next to the active site. In the sulfur-oxidizing bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1049| DsrC is the final sulfur-accepting protein, receiving the sulfur from the sulfur-carrier protein |FRAME: DsrE-Protein DsrE| and forming |FRAME: DsrC-persulfides "a perthiol on CysA"|. This perthiol is oxidized to form a trisulfide bridge with CysB. This trisulfide bridge then serves as a direct substrate for |FRAME: CPLX-7133| (DsrAB), which catalyzes an oxidation reaction. The oxidized middle sulfur is released in the form of sulfite, leaving DsrC with two reduced cysteine residues |CITS: [18656485][20952577]|. In sulfite reducers DsrAB catalyzes the opposite reaction, adding the sulfur atom of sulfite to DsrC and forming the trisulfide bridge with the two cysteine residues. This third sulfur atom is then released in the form of hydrogen sulfide in a reaction catalyzed by DsrK, restoring DsrC to its reduced form 26680199. Compound.name: a neomycin
Comment: Neomycins are a family of broad-spectrum highly toxic antibiotics produced by |FRAME: TAX-1906|. They were discovered in 1949 by Waksman and Lechevalier (Waksman later received the 1951 Nobel Prize in Physiology and medicine) 17782716. Neomycin usually exists as a complex composed of two stereoisomers, |FRAME: CPD-14142| and |FRAME: CPD-14141|, which are the two active components. A third component, |FRAME: CPD-14137 "neomycin A"|, which is a degradation product, is present in small quantities. Neomycin was originally used as a treatment for tuberculosis, but serious side effects soon became apparent, including ototoxicity 8170691, which sometimes developed to complete loss of hearing, and nephrotoxicity. Thus systemic use of neomycin is limited, and the most common mode of use is via topical application 6224608.

Compound.name: an estrogen
Comment: Estrogens are hormones that stimulate or control the development and maintenance of female sex characteristics in mammals by binding to estrogen receptors. They are important in both the menstrual and the estrous reproductive cycles. Estrogens are synthesized in all vertebrates as well as some insects, suggesting that estrogenic sex hormones have an ancient evolutionary history. The estrogens that occur naturally in the body are steroids, however other types of molecules acquired in the diet are known to bind to the estrogen receptors and are thus also considered estrogens. They include molecules produced by plants (phytoestrogens), molecules produced by fungi (mycoestrogens), and synthetic compounds (xenoestrogens). The main steroidal |FRAME: Estrogens estrogens| in humans are |FRAME: ESTRONE|, |FRAME: CPD-352| and |FRAME: ESTRIOL|, which differ in the number of hydroxyl groups (one for |FRAME: ESTRONE|, two for |FRAME: CPD-352| and three for |FRAME: ESTRIOL|). |FRAME: CPD-352| is about 10 times as potent as |FRAME: ESTRONE| and about 80 times as potent as |FRAME: ESTRIOL| in its estrogenic effect. |FRAME: CPD-352| is the predominant estrogen in non-pregenant women during their reproductive years in terms of serum levels. |FRAME: ESTRONE Estrone| is the predominant circulating estrogen in women during menopause and |FRAME: ESTRIOL| is the predominant circulating estrogen during pregnancy.

Compound.name: a lignin
Comment: |FRAME: Lignins Lignin| is a complex phenolic biopolymer and an integral part of the secondary cell walls of plants and some algae. It is one of the most abundant organic polymers on Earth, exceeded only by |FRAME: CELLULOSE|, and constitutes from a quarter to a third of the dry mass of wood. During the formation of the secondary cell wall, lignin fills the spaces in the cell wall between the |FRAME: CELLULOSE|, |FRAME: Hemicelluloses|, and |FRAME: Pectin pectin| components, driving out water and strengthening the wall. Lignin is heterogeneous, and lacks a defined primary structure. The illustration below is meant to provide a general concept rather than describe an exact structure. The main basic monomers (known as monolignols) are the phenylpropanoids |FRAME: COUMARYL-ALCOHOL|, |FRAME: CONIFERYL-ALCOHOL|, and |FRAME: SINAPYL-ALCOHOL| (see |FRAME: PWY-361|). The composition and relative abundance of the lignols differ among different organisms. The monolignols are glycosylated for the purpose of transport to the lignification zone, but the glucose moiety is removed prior to polymerization (see |FRAME: PWY-83|). The biosynthesis of lignin is not well understood. It consists of radical-radical coupling, and is catalyzed by oxidative enzymes (peroxidases and/or laccases). Lignin is covalently linked to the hemicellulose fibers, and thus crosslinks different components of the cell wall, conferring mechanical strength. Lignin can be degraded by certain fungi and bacteria that produce the enzymes |FRAME: MANGANESE-PEROXIDASE-RXN "manganese peroxidase"|, |FRAME: RXN-17136 "lignin peroxidase"| and |FRAME: CELLOBIOSE-DEHYDROGENASE-ACCEPTOR-RXN "cellobiose dehydrogenase"|.

Compound.name: laminaran
Comment: Laminaran (also known as laminarin) is a storage glucan produced by brown algae. It is a highly water soluble, branched polysaccharide based on a linear beta-(1->3)-linked glucose-based chain with an average degree of polymerization (DP) of 20-30 glucose units and beta-(1->6)-linked side chains consisting of one or more glucose residues. The ratio of beta(1->3) to beta(1->6) linkages is 3:1. Measurements conducted in 2019 along transects in the Arctic, Atlantic, and Pacific oceans revealed a median concentration of 26 +/- 17% laminarin within the particulate organic carbon pool 32170018.

Compound.name: a wax ester
Comment: Natural waxes are biosynthesized by many plants and animals and are typically esters of fatty acids and long chain alcohols. The composition depends not only on species, but also on geographic location of the organism. Common animal wax esters include |FRAME: CPD-7776|, a major component of beeswax; |FRAME: CPD-14317|, which occurs in the head oil of the sperm whale, and lanolin, obtained from wool. It is estimated that there may be between 8,000 and 20,000 different types of lanolin esters, resulting from combinations between 200 different lanolin acids and 100 different lanolin alcohols that have so far been identified. Plants also produce many types of waxes, often as a way to control evaporation and hydration (see |FRAME: PWY-282|).

Fatty acids are often classified into four groups by their lengths: |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "Short-chain fatty acids"| (SCFA) are fatty acids with aliphatic chains of fewer than six carbons. |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "Medium-chain fatty acids"| (MCFA) are fatty acids with aliphatic chain of 6-12 carbons. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "Long-chain fatty acids"| (LCFA) are fatty acids with aliphatic chains of 13-22 carbons. |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "Very-long-chain fatty acids"| (VLCFA) are fatty acids with aliphatic chains of 23 carbons or longer.

Compound.name: a galactomannan
Comment: Mannans are polymers composed of beta(1->4)-linked |FRAME: MANNOSE| residues. Pure mannans are rarely found, and most contain alpha(1,6)-linked galactopyranosyl side chains. The extent of galactosylation varies greatly, and the mannose : galactose ratio is one of the main characteristics of the polymer as it determines their physicochemical properties, such as solubility in water, density, and the viscosity of the solution Ebringerova05. On one hand, slightly galactosylated linear mannans (about 4% galactose), have been isolated from the seed endosperm of vegetable ivory nut (|FRAME: TAX-115507|) and date (|FRAME: TAX-42345|). They are water-insoluble, resemble cellulose in conformation of the individual molecular chains, and occur in cellulose microfibrils of the plant tissues Reid95. On the other hand, heavily galactosylated polymers (up to 96%) are abundant in the cell walls of storage tissues (endosperm, cotyledons, perisperm) of many seeds. Those from the endosperm of some leguminous seeds, such as guar (|FRAME: TAX-3832|), locust bean or carob (|FRAME: TAX-20340|), and tara gum (|FRAME: TAX-191904|), are widely used commercially Reid95. Another important feature is the distribution of the galactopyranose residues along the mannan backbone, which affects the molecular interactions of the chains among themselves (self-association) and with other polysaccharides (cooperative associations) in solution Ebringerova05.

Compound.name: a plant arabinogalactan
Comment: Arabinogalactans are biopolymers consisting of arabinose and galactose residues. Two main classes of arabinogalactans are found in nature: |FRAME: Plant-Arabinogalactans "plant arabinogalactan"| and |FRAME: Mycobacterial-Arabinogalactans "microbial arabinogalactan"|. |FRAME: Plant-Arabinogalactans "Plant arabinogalactans"| (AGs) are widely spread throughout the plant kingdom. Many edible and inedible plants are rich sources of these polysaccharides. AGs are associated with the pectin cell-wall component by physical bonds, and some of them are covalently linked to the complex pectin molecule as neutral side chains Ebringerova05. AGs occur in two structurally different forms described as |FRAME: Plant-Arabinogalactans-I "type I"| and |FRAME: Plant-Arabinogalactans-II "type II"|. AG of type I has a linear (1->4)-beta-D-Galp backbone, bearing 20-40% of alpha-L-Araf residues (1->5)-linked in short chains, in general at position 3. It is commonly found in pectins from citrus, apple and potato. Type I AG has been isolated from the skin of Opuntia ficus indica pear fruits 15063212. AG of type II, known as arabino-3,6-galactan, has a (1->3)-beta-D-Galp backbone heavily substituted at position 6 by mono- and oligosaccharide side chains composed of arabinosyl and galactosyl units. It is more widespread than the AG type I and occurs in cell walls of dicots and cereals often linked to proteins (known as arabinogalactan proteins). AG type II, along with galactomannans and cellulose, comprises the predominating polysaccharides of green arabica coffee beans11217967. In some case type II AGt contains a small amount of beta-glucuronate. AG type II occurs as minor, water-soluble components in softwoods. It is very abundant in the wood of larch trees (members of the genus |FRAME: TAX-3325|) - certain parts of the western larch (|FRAME: TAX-3327|) contain up to 35% AG Whistler93. However, larch AG type II is located in the lumen of the tracheids and ray cells, and is thus not a cell-wall component and by definition, not part of the |FRAME: Hemicelluloses| of these trees.

Unlike lipopolysaccharides, which are attached to a lipid anchor, EPS refers to extracellular polysaccharides with slight or no cell association.

Compound.name: a pyrimidine base
Comment: Nucleobases are the parts of nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) that are involved in pairing of the two strands. The primary nucleobases are |FRAME: CYTOSINE|, |FRAME: GUANINE|, |FRAME: ADENINE| (found in both DNA and RNA), |FRAME: THYMINE| (found only in DNA) and |FRAME: URACIL| (found only in RNA), abbreviated as C, G, A, T, and U, respectively. There are many additional nucleobases, usually derived from the primary ones. Based on their structure, nucleobases are divided into |FRAME: Purines purines| and |FRAME: Pyrimidine-Bases pyrimidines|. |FRAME: PYRIMIDINE-RING Pyrimidine| is a heterocyclic aromatic compound similar to benzene, containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3 of the ring. The name pyrimidines is also used for compounds derived from the basic pyrimidine compound, including three of the bases found in nucleic acids, namely |FRAME: CYTOSINE|, THYMINE, and |FRAME: URACIL|.

Compound.name: compound I
Comment: |FRAME: Compound-0 "Compound 0"|, |FRAME: Compound-I|, and |FRAME: Compound-II| are the names given to intermediate states of the heme-iron center that is formed at the active sites of cytochrome P-450 enzymes and peroxidases during catalysis. I. Cytochrome P-450 In |FRAME: Cytochrome-P450 "cytochrome P-450"| the proximal coordinatioin position of the heme iron, which is bound to the 4 nitrogen atoms of the tetrapyrrole ring, is tethered to the protein via a cysteine thiolate ligand. At its rest state, the iron is found at a low-spin ferric state (III valency). At this state the iron also binds a water molecule as a sixth ligand at the distal axial coordination position. Binding of a substrate to the low-spin ferric enzyme leads to displacement of the water as the sixth ligand and a high spin shift. The substrate-bound complex has a greater reduction potential and more easily accepts a single electron from the redox partner, which can be either |FRAME: EC-1.6.2.4 "a cytochrome P450 reductase"|, |FRAME: Ferredoxins|, or |FRAME: Cytochromes-b5|). After the first reduction, the heme iron binds oxygen, forming an oxy-heme complex. The oxygen is bound at the distal axial coordination position, from which the water molecule has been displaced. Following the transfer of the second electron from the redox partner and two subsequent protonations, a peroxo adduct is formed, known as |FRAME: Compound-0|. Next, the O-O bond is cleaved heterolytically, releasing a water molecule and leaving behind an oxygen atom with only six valence electrons. This highly active oxene oxygen removes one electron from the iron and one from the porphyrin, oxidizing the iron to the unusual valency of IV (ferryl iron) and generating an additional oxidizing equivalent that is delocalized over the porphyrin and thiolate ligands. This ferryl/porphyrin radical cation complex is known as |FRAME: Compound-I| 21071661. When the substrate nears the active site, |FRAME: Compound-I| abstracts an electron from it, converting the substrate into a radical and becoming a protonated non-radical ferryl compound known as |FRAME: Compound-II|. At this point the substrate radical reacts with the oxygen of |FRAME: Compound-II|, forming a new carbon oxygen bond. The product is released, and the iron returns to a valency of III (compound III) OrtizdeMontellano15. II. preoxidases In peroxidases the proximal coordinatioin position of the heme iron, which is bound to the 4 nitrogen atoms of the tetrapyrrole ring, is tethered to the protein via a histidine residue. |FRAME: Compound-I "Compound I"| is produced when the heme iron is oxidized by |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|. A single one-electron reduction step of |FRAME: Compound-I| from an electron donor substrate yields |FRAME: Compound-II|, followed by a second one-electron transfer that returns the enzyme to the ferric oxidation state, thus completing the catalytic cycle. Each electron transfer event converts a substrate molecule to a radical cation, forming two such radicals during a catalytic cycle. In the presence of high concentrations of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| and the absence of a reducing substrate, |FRAME: Compound-II| can be oxidized to |FRAME: Compound-III|, a catalytically inactive form of the enzyme. |FRAME: Compound-III "Compound III"| is converted back to the resting state by spontaneous autoxidation or by oxidation with two molecules of the substrate radical cation 18581264.

The hydroxy group is often glucosylated, as in |FRAME: Alpha-Glycosylated-Hydroxymethyl-DNAs "alpha-glucosyl-hydroxymethylcytosine"|, |FRAME: Beta-Glycosylated-Hydroxymethylated-DNAs "beta-glucosyl-hydroxymethylcytosine"| and |FRAME: Gluc-Glycosyl-Hydroxymethylcytosine-DNAs "beta-glucosyl-(1->4)-beta-glucosyl-hydroxymethylcytosine"|, so that T4 DNA is typically covered with sugar chains.

Compound.name: a dolichol
Comment: |FRAME: DOLICHOL "Dolichol"| is the name given to a family of long-chain polyprenols that contain a varying number of cis -linked isoprene units, terminating with three isoprene units, two of which are trans -linked. The first (alpha) unit in dolichols is always saturated 11442630. Additional modifications are found. For example, dolichols from certain halobacteria contain an additional saturation in the terminal (omega) isoprene unit |CITS: [9363431][21091511]|. The length of dolichol molecules varies within a range in a species, and the range varies among species (reviewed in 9878760). In mammals dolichols are usually within the range of 80 to 105 carbons. Archaea prefer dolichols of 55-60 carbons. The main function of dolichols is to act as a membrane anchor for the formation of oligosaccharides, which are then transferred to certain asparagine residues within proteins through a modification process known as |FRAME: MANNOSYL-CHITO-DOLICHOL-BIOSYNTHESIS "N-glycosylation"|. In eukaryotes dolichol is also involved in the transfer of some of the monosaccharides to the forming oligosaccharide. Dolichols are the major lipid component (14% by mass) of human substantia nigra |FRAME: CPD-12419| 15686500.

Compound.name: a nucleotide

When joined together, nucleotides make up the structural units of RNA and DNA. The nucleotides are called |FRAME: Ribonucleotides| when the sugar is |FRAME: CPD0-1110 ribose|, and |FRAME: Deoxynucleotides| when it is |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE|. In the absence of phosphate, the combination of |FRAME: Bases| (nitrogenous base) and a five-carbon sugar is called |FRAME: Nucleosides|.

Compound.name: a coelenterazine
Comment: |FRAME: OPLOPHORUS-LUCIFERIN Coelenterazine| and its analogues are the luciferase substrate (=luciferin) in the light-emitting process of bioluminescent coelenterates as well as various, distantly related, types of organisms such as squids, shrimps, fishes, and some chaetognaths |CITS: [Shimomura80][Campbell90][20972255]|. It is also found in many nonluminous organisms 9336010. In bioluminescent systems, |FRAME: OPLOPHORUS-LUCIFERIN coelenterazine| is bound by either |FRAME: Coelenterazine-binding-proteins "coelenterazine-binding protein"| or by |FRAME: Aequorins "an aequorin"| protein, depending on the species. In the first system, upon binding of Ca 2+ ions the coelenterazine-binding protein releases coelenterazine, which is then oxidized and decarboxylated by the luciferase enzyme, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-20235|. In the second system, aequorin binds and oxidizes coelenterazine, retainning it in the form of bound |FRAME: CPD-20222|. Upon binding of Ca 2+ ions, the enzyme catalyzes the decarboxylation and formation of |FRAME: CPD-20235|. In vitro the excited coelenteramide relaxes to the ground state by emission of blue light. However, in vivo the excitation energy is transferred to |FRAME: GFP| by Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) |CITS: [4151620][33175]|. Coelenterazine is a derivative of imidazopyrazinone. Its biosynthetic origin is not known. However, it has been shown that the hydromedusa |FRAME: TAX-6100| is not able to synthesize it, and is dependent on a dietary supply of this luciferin for bioluminescence 11572972. The only report of de novo biosynthesis of coelenterazine is from the bioluminescent shrimp |FRAME: TAX-576189| Thomson95.

Compound.name: a menaquinol
Comment: Menaquinols are the reduced form of |FRAME: Menaquinones "menaquinones"|. Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are isoprenoid quinones of the naphthalene series, and are constituents of bacterial plasma membranes, where they play important roles in electron transfer and oxidative phosphorylation. Menaquinones are the most widespread respiratory quinones in biological systems Fujimoto12. Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are named MK- n or DMK- n , respectively, where the n refers to the number of prenyl units present in the side chain. The most common length of the side chain in bacteria is 8, although minor amounts of MK-1 through MK-14 have been found 7022156. Many bacteria and archaea have |FRAME: Dihydromenaquinones "dehydrogenated menaquinones"|, which are named MK- n (H 2 ). The degree and location of dehydrogenation depends on the species. Some organisms have menaquinones with modifications of the head group, for example |FRAME: TAX-2302| possess both |FRAME: CPD-15875 thermoplasmaquinones| (TPQ), which contains an extra methyl group, and |FRAME: CPD-15876 methionaquinones| (MTK), which contains a methylthio group 11157962. Menaquinones are also known as vitamin K 2 . Vitamin K is a name given to a group of derivatives of 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone that are required by mammals for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins, mostly involved in blood coagulation. These compounds, while essential for mammals, are not synthesized by them, and are thus considered vitamins. The natural forms of the vitamin are vitamin K 1 (|FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE|) and vitamin K 2 (|FRAME: Menaquinones "menaquinone"|). Since menaquinones produced by different organisms have different tail lengths there are many variations of vitamin K 2 , usually specified based on the number of carbons in their tails, such as in Vitamin K 2 (45).

Synonyms: a beta-D-galactosyl-1,3-beta- N -acetyl-D-galactosaminyl-( N -acetylneuraminyl)-D-galactosyl-D-glucosyl- N -acylsphingosine // alpha-N-acetylneuraminosyl-(2->3)-[beta-D-galactosyl-(1->3)-N-acetyl-beta-D-galactosaminyl-(1->4)]-beta-D-galactosyl-(1->4)-beta-D-glucosyl-ceramide // alpha-N-acetylneuraminosyl-(2->3)-[beta-D-galactosyl-(1->3)-N-acetyl-beta-D-galactosaminyl-(1->4)]-beta-D-galactosyl-(1->4)-beta-D-glucosyl-R // a ganglioside GM1 // I 3 Neu5AcGg 4 Cer // Galbeta(1,3)GalNAcbeta(1,4)[Neu5Acalpha(2,3)]Galbeta(1,4)Glcbeta1Cer
Comment: A ganglioside is a molecule composed of |FRAME: Glycosphingolipids| (|FRAME: Ceramides| and |FRAME: Oligosaccharides|) with one or more sialic acids (e.g. |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE|) linked on the sugar chain. Ganglioside are components of the cell plasma membrane that modulates cell signal transduction events, and appear to concentrate in lipid rafts. The name ganglioside is derived from ganglion cells of the brain, from which the first gangliosides were isolated by the German scientist Ernst Klenk in 1942. More than 60 gangliosides are known, which differ from each other mainly in the position and number of |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| residues. The same four structures- |FRAME: CPD-7188 "ganglioside GM1|, |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINYL-ETCETERA-GLUCOSYLCERA "ganglioside GD1a"|, |FRAME: Ganglioside-GD1b "ganglioside GD1b"| and |FRAME: Ganglioside-GT1b "ganglioside GT1b"|, comprise the great majority of gangliosides in mammalian brains 22735313. |FRAME: CPD-7188 "Ganglioside GM1"| (also known as ganglioside GM1a) is one of major gangliosides in vertebrate brain, and shows specific binding with cholera toxin B subunit, resulting in important biological events such as cAMP response 1058471. GM1 is also involved in the receptor functions for peptide hormones such as follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone 185697.

Compound.name: a cepham
Comment: This compound class stands for |FRAME: Lactams lactams| in which the amide bond is contained within a four-membered ring, which includes the amide nitrogen and the carbonyl carbon. beta-Lactam compounds imitate the naturally occurring |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| substrate for the group of enzymes known as penicillin binding proteins (PBPs), which cross-link the peptidoglycan in bacterial cell wall, and thus act as powerful antibiotics 6109324. Naturally occurring |FRAME: Beta-Lactams "beta-lactam antibiotics"| are classified into several groups according to their chemical structure: In |FRAME: Monolactams monolactams| the beta-lactam ring is not fused to another ring. This class includes compounds such as the |FRAME: Nocardicins nocardicins| 3427723 and the |FRAME: Monobactams monobactams| 3909315. In |FRAME: Penams penams| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a saturated five atom ring (a 4:5 structure). Penams contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring (for example, the |FRAME: PENICILLIN penicillins|) 6335599. Related classes include the |FRAME: Carbapenams carbapenams|, which contain a carbon atom in that position 12890666, and the |FRAME: Clavams oxopenams| (also known as clavams), which contain an oxygen atom at that position (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9261|) 3304182. |FRAME: Penems Penems| are molecues similar to penams in which the five atom ring is unsaturated at positions 2-3. Similarly, penems contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring, while |FRAME: Carbapenems carbapenems| contains a carbon atom in that position 16413506. In |FRAME: Cephams cephams| and |FRAME: Cephems cephems| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a six-atom ring (a 4:6 strcuture) that contains a sulfur atom at position 1. In cephams the ring is saturated, while cephems have an unsaturated bond at positions 3-4 |CITS: [1164170][12722308]|. 1-Oxocephams/1-oxacephems conain an oxygen atom at position 1 |CITS: [11671696][11078187]|.

Compound.name: a mannosylerythritol lipid
Comment: |FRAME: CPD-25639 "Mannosylerythritol lipids"| (MELs) are amphiphilic glycolipids that display high surface activity and act as biodetergents (biosurfactants). The compounds are produced by yeast strains that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-5269| and |FRAME: TAX-63261| genera. They show excellent surface-active properties and versatile biochemical actions. The compounds were first described in 1956 from an |FRAME: TAX-5269| species 13276861. However, the most common MEL producing species are members of the |FRAME: TAX-63261| genus, such as |FRAME: TAX-84753|, |FRAME: TAX-84754|, |FRAME: TAX-84752|, and |FRAME: TAX-203536| 25723622. The lipids are acylated at positions O-2' and O-3' by a range of fatty acyl residues. In |FRAME: TAX-5270| the fatty acid at O-2' ranges from C2 to C6, while that at O-3' ranges from C12 to C16. In addition, MELs differ in their acetylation status. Four general types are produced differing in the acetylation of positions O-4' and O-6'. Mel-D has no acetylation, MEL-B is acetylated only at the O-6' position, MEL-C is acetylated only at the O-4' position, and MEL-A is acetylated at both positions |CITS: [Kitamoto90a][Kitamoto90][10570818][17898510]|. The biological function of MELs is still unknown, but they are of growing biotechnological interest as a sustainable alternative for chemical surfactants |CITS: [18585066][22901730]|.

Compound.name: a c-series ganglioside
Comment: c-Series gangliosides are formed during mammalian brain development where they are thought to be involved in growth, differentiation, and migration of neuronal cells. They are abundant in fish brain, and in adult rats; they occur in liver, kidney, and pancreas 10699494 and in tumors such as glioma. About the nomenclature of gangliosides Ganglioside naming is somewhat complex. Two ganglioside nomenclature systems are currently in use. The most commonly used is a short-hand nomenclature suggested by Svennerholm, which was initially based on the migration order of |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio-series"| gangliosides in chromatography 14066623. The more comprehensive system formulated by IUPAC 9826173 is applied much less frequently. A typical ganglioside name using the old system looks like |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"|. The first letter refers to the glycosphingolipid series. For example, the "G" stands for the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|. The next letter describes the number of sialic acid residues: (A = 0, M =1, D = 2, T = 3, Q = 4, P = 5, H = 6, S = 7). The following number describes the number of the non-sialic residues, and is derived in a rather complex manner. It was initially assumed that the number of such residues does not exceed 5. The number in the name was calculated as (5 - the number of uncharged carbohydrates). In addition, several sub-series of gangliosides have been defined based on the number of sialic acids attached to the galactose residue of the lacosylceramide core. If no sialic residues are present at that position, the compounds belong to the |FRAME: 0-Series-Ganglioside "0-series |. Those with one sialic acid at that position are named the |FRAME: A-Series-Gangliosides a-series |, those with two sialic acids belong to the |FRAME: B-Series-Gangliosides b-series |, and so on. |FRAME: C-Series-Gangliosides "C-series"| or higher gangliosides are rare in adult mammals and birds, but are abundant in fish and amphibians. Confusingly, GM1b and GD1c are both 0-series gangliosides, despite having a b and c in their names. So, for example, the |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"| is named as follows: G = belongs to the ganglio series, Q = 4 sialic acids, 1 = 4 non-sialic residues, and b = belongs to the b-series, meaning two of the sialic acids are attached to the inner galactose.

Compound.name: a gaburedin
Comment: The |FRAME: Gaburedins gaburedins| are a family of gamma-aminobutanoate (GABA)-derived ureas whose biosynthesis is encoded by a silent gene cluster in the |FRAME: TAX-54571| genome. The cluster, which consists of the three genes |FRAME: G-124751|, |FRAME: G-124752|, and gbnC , is located adjacent to a putative regulatory system homologous to the the mmfR - mmfLHP - mmyR cluster of |FRAME: TAX-100226|. The products of the mmfLHP genes are the |FRAME: MMFs "methylenomycin furans"|, which act as inducers of |FRAME: CPD-27200 methylenomycin| production in |FRAME: TAX-100226|, while MmfR and MmyR are ArpA-like transcriptional repressors, which repress |FRAME: CPD-27200 methylenomycin| production 18988741. Based on the sequence homology, it was hypothesized that the gbnABC genes encode a natural product(s), whose production is controlled by a regulatory system encoded by the mmfR - mmfLHP - mmyR genes homologs. The gbn cluster contains highly conserved DNA sequence, which were predicted to be binding motifs for the transcriptional repressor GbnR, the mmyR homolog. To test this hypothesis, the gbnR gene was knocked out. Indeed, the mutant produced six new metabolites, the products of the gbnABC genes, which were named gaburedin A-F. The compounds structures were shown to be gamma-aminobutanoate (GABA)-derived ureas, containing an amino acid linked by a ureido bridge Sidda14.

Comment: Xylan is a general name given for polysaccharides composed of xylose residues. It is the principal type of |FRAME: Hemicelluloses| in plant biomass representing the second most abundant polysaccharide in the biosphere after |FRAME: CELLULOSE| 20113432. The most common form of xylan is |FRAME: 1-4-beta-Xylan "(1->4)-beta-D-xylan"|, which is found in the cell walls of plants and some algae. Pure |FRAME: 1-4-beta-Xylan "(1->4)-beta-D-xylan"| is uncommon. In most cases it is acetylated and/or decorated with additional sugars, in the form of |FRAME: Arabinoxylan arabinoxylan|, |FRAME: Glucuronoxylans glucuronoxylan|, |FRAME: Glucuronoarabinoxylans glucuronoarabinoxylan| or |FRAME: Arabinoglucuronoxylans arabinoglucuronoxylan|. The secondary hydroxyl groups on xylose carbons 2 and 3 can be substituted by a number of residues, the type and degree of substitution depending on xylan's botanical source. Arabinose and glucuronic acid are linked to the backbone by glycosidic bonds. Other substituents form ester bonds: acetate groups are bound directly to the backbone, while cinnamoyl (feruloyl and coumaroyl) residues are linked to the side chain arabinoses JOSELEAU. Due to its heterogeneous structure, the biodegradation of xylan requires the concerted action of a complex set of enzymes 17008082. These enzymes are mainly extracellular and are secreted by numerous fungi and bacteria BIELY. The endoxylanases and beta xylosidases hydrolyze the main chain; the former generating short chain oligosaccharides and the latter acting on these products to liberate xylose. The side chains are hydrolyzed by glycanases, alpha-glucuronidases, acetyl xylan esterases and feruloyl esterases 11729262. |FRAME: 13-BETA-D-XYLANS "(1->3)-beta-D-xylan"| is found only in cell walls of some red and green algae.

Compound.name: a 5-methyltetrahydrofolate
Comment: |FRAME: THF-GLU-N Tetrahydrofolate| (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are required in a variety of reactions in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, where they act as carriers of one-carbon units in various oxidation states. These one-carbon units are utilized in the biosynthesis of several cellular components, including glycine, methionine, formylmethionine, thymidylate, pantothenate and purine nucleotides. During folate biosynthesis (as described in FOLSYN-PWY) the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.12|, adds a glutamate residue to |FRAME: 7-8-DIHYDROPTEROATE|, resulting in |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE|, also known as H 2 PteGlu 1 . This molecule in turn is reduced by EC-1.5.1.3 (FolA) to |FRAME: THF| (H 4 PteGlu 1 , or tetrahydrofolate), which can be converted to several other folate molecules 11501996. Most folate molecules are modified in cells by successive additions of glutamate residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-gamma-glutamates). The glutamate residues are added by an amide linkage to the gamma-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are not the normal amide bonds they are not hydrolyzed by peptidases or proteases, which are specific for alpha-carboxyl-linked peptide bonds. The addition of glutamyl residues probably occurs after the reduction of newly synthesized dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and its conversion to other tetrahydrofolate derivatives. The glutamylation of folate residues serves several goals: it prevents the efflux of folates out of the cell, it increases the binding of folate cofactors to the enzymes of folate interconversion and biosynthesis, and in mammals, it allows the accumulation of folates in the mitochondria, which is required for glycine synthesis 10598551. This class stands for 5-methyltetrahydrofolates with an unspecified number of glutamate residues.

Comment: About the nomenclature of gangliosides Ganglioside naming is somewhat complex. Two ganglioside nomenclature systems are currently in use. The most commonly used is a short-hand nomenclature suggested by Svennerholm, which was initially based on the migration order of |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio-series"| gangliosides in chromatography 14066623. The more comprehensive system formulated by IUPAC 9826173 is applied much less frequently. A typical ganglioside name using the old system looks like |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"|. The first letter refers to the glycosphingolipid series. For example, the "G" stands for the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|. The next letter describes the number of sialic acid residues: (A = 0, M =1, D = 2, T = 3, Q = 4, P = 5, H = 6, S = 7). The following number describes the number of the non-sialic residues, and is derived in a rather complex manner. It was initially assumed that the number of such residues does not exceed 5. The number in the name was calculated as (5 - the number of uncharged carbohydrates). In addition, several sub-series of gangliosides have been defined based on the number of sialic acids attached to the galactose residue of the lacosylceramide core. If no sialic residues are present at that position, the compounds belong to the |FRAME: 0-Series-Ganglioside "0-series |. Those with one sialic acid at that position are named the |FRAME: A-Series-Gangliosides a-series |, those with two sialic acids belong to the |FRAME: B-Series-Gangliosides b-series |, and so on. |FRAME: C-Series-Gangliosides "C-series"| or higher gangliosides are rare in adult mammals and birds, but are abundant in fish and amphibians. Confusingly, GM1b and GD1c are both 0-series gangliosides, despite having a b and c in their names. So, for example, the |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"| is named as follows: G = belongs to the ganglio series, Q = 4 sialic acids, 1 = 4 non-sialic residues, and b = belongs to the b-series, meaning two of the sialic acids are attached to the inner galactose.

Unlike many other aldoses, which are more abundant in nature as the "D"-form, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| is far more common in nature than |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|. Free |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| rarely exists in the nature (though it has been found in the core of coniferous trees Pingman57). However, it is widely distributed as a component of complex nonstarch polysaccharides in plant cell walls, including many plants common in the human diet such as maize, wheat, rye, rice, sugar beets, and plant gums, and in bacterial polysaccharides. L-arabinose has many biomedical and health effects, especially intestinal sucrase inhibition effect 8931641. In recent years it has been used as a low-caloric sweetener, with approximately 50% of the sweetness of sucrose Hu18.

Compound.name: an alpha-limit dextrin
Synonyms: a glycogen phosphorylase-limit dextrin // a glycogen phosphorylase-limited dextrin

These enzymes shorten the chains, but are not able to hydrolyze the alpha-1,6 bonds at branch points. Since the branching residues block the enzymes from getting close, the enzymes leave a tail of 4 alpha-1,4-linked residues next to the branch points.

Compound.name: a gamma-lactone
Comment: A |FRAME: Lactones "lactone"| is a cyclic ester, the product of condensation of an alcohol group and a carboxylate group within the same molecule. It is characterized by a closed ring consisting of two or more carbon atoms and a single oxygen atom, with a ketone group in one of the carbons adjacent to the ring oxygen. There are several types of lactones - |FRAME: Beta-lactones| contain 3 carbons in the ring, Gamma-lactones contains 4, Delta-lactones contains 5, and Epsilon-lactones contains 6 carbons.
